concepts: Position vector of the intersection of two lines in a regular hexagon
questions.question: Let $OABCDE$ be a regular hexagon, $O$ is the origin and the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ respectively. The position vector of the point of intersection of $OB$ and $AC$ is:
questions.key_idea: In a regular hexagon the long diagonal $OC$ is parallel to $AB$ and twice its length, so $\overrightarrow{OC}=2(\vec b-\vec a)$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\vec b-\vec a$.
In a regular hexagon the length of $OC$ is double the length of a side and $OC\parallel AB$.
Hence $\overrightarrow{OC}=2(\vec b-\vec a)$.
Line $OB$: $\vec r=\lambda\vec b$.
Line $AC$: $\vec r=\vec a+\mu(\overrightarrow{OC}-\vec a)=\vec a+\mu(2\vec b-2\vec a-\vec a)$.
At the common point $P$, equate the coefficients of the independent vectors $\vec a,\vec b$: $\lambda=2\mu$ and $1-3\mu=0$.
So $\mu=\frac13$ and $\lambda=\frac23$.
Therefore $\vec r=\frac23\vec b$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Since $OC\parallel AB$ and $OC=2AB$, triangles $POC$ and $PBA$ are similar with ratio $2:1$.
solution: Let $P=OB\cap AC$. The vertical angles at $P$ are equal and $OC\parallel BA$ gives equal alternate angles.
So $\triangle POC\sim\triangle PBA$ and $\frac{PO}{PB}=\frac{OC}{BA}=2$.
Thus $P$ divides $OB$ internally in the ratio $2:1$, i.e. $OP=\frac23\,OB$.
Hence the position vector of $P$ is $\frac23\vec b$.

useful_results: In a regular hexagon $OABCDE$: the long diagonal $OC\parallel AB$ and $OC=2AB$ (also $AD\parallel BC$, $BE\parallel CD$ with the same factor 2).
Two lines cut by a pair of parallel lines meet at a point that divides them in the ratio of the parallel segments: here $OP:PB=OC:AB=2:1$.
To intersect two lines $\vec r=\lambda\vec p$ and $\vec r=\vec a+\mu\vec d$, express everything in two independent vectors and equate coefficients.

concepts: Vector product and vector area of a square and equilateral triangles
questions.question: The figure shows a square. On each side of the square an outward equilateral triangle is constructed. The vectors $\vec a_1,\vec a_2,\vec a_3,\vec a_4,\vec a_5,\vec a_6,\vec a_7,\vec a_8,\vec p$ and $\vec q$ are as shown in the figure. If $\vec a_2\times\vec a_1+\vec a_4\times\vec a_3+\vec a_6\times\vec a_5+\vec a_8\times\vec a_7=\lambda\,\vec p\times\vec q$, then $\lambda$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Each cross product $\vec a_{i+1}\times\vec a_i$ is the same vector $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}l^2\hat n$, while $\vec p\times\vec q=l^2\hat n$.
solution: Let the side of the square be $l$ and let $\hat n$ be the unit vector perpendicular to the plane (towards the reader).
Two sides of an equilateral triangle make $60^\circ$, so $|\vec a_{i+1}\times\vec a_i|=l\cdot l\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}l^2$.
In the figure each of the four pairs is taken in the same (anticlockwise) sense, so $\vec a_{i+1}\times\vec a_i=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}l^2\hat n$ for all four pairs.
$\vec p\times\vec q=l^2\hat n$ ($\vec p$ and $\vec q$ are adjacent sides of the square).
The left side of the equation is $4\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}l^2\hat n=2\sqrt3\,l^2\hat n$.
So $2\sqrt3\,l^2\hat n=\lambda\,l^2\hat n$, giving $\lambda=2\sqrt3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put numbers on the figure: take $l=1$, $\vec p=\hat i$, $\vec q=\hat j$ and write the sides of the left triangle in components.
solution: Take the square $[0,1]\times[0,1]$ with $\vec p=\hat i$, $\vec q=\hat j$; the left apex is $\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)$.
Then $\vec a_1=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)$ (apex to top-left corner) and $\vec a_2=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},-\frac12\right)$ (apex to bottom-left corner).
$\vec a_2\times\vec a_1=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac12-\left(-\frac12\right)\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ along $\hat k$.
A rotation by $90^\circ$ about the centre of the square maps this triangle to the next one and keeps the cross product unchanged, so all four terms equal $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\hat k$.
Sum $=2\sqrt3\,\hat k$ and $\vec p\times\vec q=\hat k$, so $\lambda=2\sqrt3$.

useful_results: $|\vec u\times\vec v|$ is twice the area of the triangle on $\vec u,\vec v$; for an equilateral triangle of side $s$ it equals $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}s^2$.
For vectors in one plane, every cross product is a multiple of the same unit normal $\hat n$, so compare coefficients of $\hat n$ (signs follow the sense of rotation).
Symmetry: a rotation of the whole configuration about the normal does not change $\vec u\times\vec v$.

concepts: Solving a vector equation using dot product
questions.question: Four vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ and $\vec x$ satisfy the relation $(\vec a\cdot\vec x)\vec b=\vec c+\vec x$ where $\vec b\cdot\vec a\neq1$. The value of $\vec x$ in terms of $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is equal to:
options: $\frac{(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b-1)}{(\vec a\cdot\vec b-1)}$
$\frac{2(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b+\vec c}{\vec a\cdot\vec b-1}$
$\frac{2(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec c+\vec c}{\vec a\cdot\vec b-1}$
questions.key_idea: Take the dot product of the relation with $\vec a$ to find the scalar $\vec a\cdot\vec x$, then substitute back.
solution: Given $(\vec a\cdot\vec x)\vec b=\vec c+\vec x$ ......(1).
Dot (1) with $\vec a$: $(\vec a\cdot\vec x)(\vec b\cdot\vec a)=(\vec c\cdot\vec a)+(\vec a\cdot\vec x)$.
$\Rightarrow(\vec a\cdot\vec x)(\vec b\cdot\vec a-1)=\vec c\cdot\vec a$.
$\Rightarrow\vec a\cdot\vec x=\frac{\vec c\cdot\vec a}{\vec b\cdot\vec a-1}$ ......(2).
Put (2) in (1): $\left(\frac{\vec c\cdot\vec a}{\vec b\cdot\vec a-1}\right)\vec b=\vec c+\vec x$.
$\Rightarrow\vec x=\left(\frac{\vec c\cdot\vec a}{\vec b\cdot\vec a-1}\right)\vec b-\vec c$.
$=\frac{(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-\vec c(\vec a\cdot\vec b-1)}{\vec a\cdot\vec b-1}$, which is option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the options on two simple choices of vectors; the wrong options fail at once.
solution: Take $\vec a=\hat i$, $\vec b=2\hat i$ (so $\vec a\cdot\vec b-1=1$) and $\vec c=\hat i$. Then $x_1\cdot2\hat i=\hat i+\vec x$ forces $\vec x=\hat i$ ($x_1=1$).
Options (A), (B) both give $\hat i$, but (C) gives $5\hat i$ and (D) gives $3\hat i$, so (C), (D) are out.
Now take $\vec c=\hat j$ with the same $\vec a,\vec b$: $2x_1\hat i=\hat j+\vec x$ gives $x_1=0$ and $\vec x=-\hat j$.
Option (B) gives $+\hat j$ (wrong sign) while option (A) gives $\frac{0\cdot\vec b-\hat j(1)}{1}=-\hat j$.
Only (A) survives both tests.

useful_results: For equations of the form $(\vec a\cdot\vec x)\vec b=\vec c+\vec x$, dot with $\vec a$ first to turn the vector unknown into the scalar $\vec a\cdot\vec x$.
General solution of $\vec x=k\vec u+\vec v$ with $k=\vec a\cdot\vec x$: put $\vec x$ back into the definition of $k$ and solve the linear equation for $k$.
Two well-chosen numerical examples (one aligned, one perpendicular component) eliminate wrong vector formulas quickly in an MCQ.

concepts: Magnitude of a sum of vector products of unit vectors
Direction cosines of a line
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are three unit vectors and $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are the angles between the vectors $\vec a;\vec b$ ; $\vec b;\vec c$ ; $\vec c;\vec a$ respectively and also $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are the angles which the unit vector $l\hat i+m\hat j+n\hat k$ makes with the positive $x$-axis, $y$-axis and $z$-axis respectively, then the value of $|\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a|$ equals:
questions.key_idea: The three angles are also direction angles, so $\cos\alpha=l,\cos\beta=m,\cos\gamma=n$ with $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$; square the magnitude and use $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=\vec a\cdot\vec b\,\vec b\cdot\vec c-\vec a\cdot\vec c$.
solution: Since $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are direction angles of a unit vector, $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$, and $(l+m+n)^2=1+2(lm+mn+nl)$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec b=\cos\alpha=l$, $\ \vec b\cdot\vec c=\cos\beta=m$, $\ \vec c\cdot\vec a=\cos\gamma=n$.

$|\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a|^2=|\vec a\times\vec b|^2+|\vec b\times\vec c|^2+|\vec c\times\vec a|^2+2(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)+2(\vec b\times\vec c)\cdot(\vec c\times\vec a)+2(\vec c\times\vec a)\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)$.

Using $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\gamma$ and its cyclic forms: $=\sin^2\alpha+\sin^2\beta+\sin^2\gamma+2[\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\beta\cos\gamma+\cos\gamma\cos\alpha-\cos\alpha-\cos\beta-\cos\gamma]$.
$=2+2(lm+mn+nl)-2(l+m+n)$ using $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$ (the PDF prints $2-2(lm+mn+nl)-\ldots$, a sign slip).
$=(1-\sum l)^2$, so the required magnitude is $\left|\sum l-1\right|$.
questions.correction_note: PDF line '= 2 - 2(lm+mn+nl) - 2(l+m+n)' has a sign error: 3-(l^2+m^2+n^2)+2(lm+mn+nl)-2(l+m+n) equals 2 + 2(lm+mn+nl) - 2(l+m+n). The following lines of the PDF (1+(l+m+n)^2-2(l+m+n)=(1-sum l)^2) are correct, so the answer (A) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=(\vec a-\vec c)\times(\vec b-\vec c)$, i.e. twice the vector area of the triangle with vertices at the tips of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$.
solution: Expand $(\vec a-\vec c)\times(\vec b-\vec c)=\vec a\times\vec b-\vec a\times\vec c-\vec c\times\vec b+\vec c\times\vec c=\vec a\times\vec b+\vec c\times\vec a+\vec b\times\vec c$.
So the required modulus is $2\times$ area of the triangle whose vertices are the tips of the three unit vectors.
With $\vec a\cdot\vec b=l,\ \vec b\cdot\vec c=m,\ \vec c\cdot\vec a=n$: $|\vec a-\vec c|^2=2-2n$, $|\vec b-\vec c|^2=2-2m$ and $(\vec a-\vec c)\cdot(\vec b-\vec c)=1+l-m-n$.
Lagrange's identity: $|\vec u\times\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2-(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2=(2-2n)(2-2m)-(1+l-m-n)^2$.
Expanding and using $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$, this equals $2+2(lm+mn+nl)-2(l+m+n)$.
Since $2(lm+mn+nl)=(l+m+n)^2-1$, it becomes $(l+m+n)^2-2(l+m+n)+1=\left(\sum l-1\right)^2$.
Hence $|\ldots|=\left|\sum l-1\right|$.

useful_results: $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=(\vec a-\vec c)\times(\vec b-\vec c)$: twice the vector area of the triangle on the tips of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$; it is zero iff the three tips are collinear.
$(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(\vec c\times\vec d)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)(\vec b\cdot\vec d)-(\vec a\cdot\vec d)(\vec b\cdot\vec c)$ (Lagrange's identity).
The direction angles of a line satisfy $\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma=1$; here this is the hidden condition that makes the answer collapse to one expression.
Quick check by special case: $l=1,m=n=0$ (i.e. $\vec a=\vec b\perp\vec c$) gives modulus $0=|1-1|$, which eliminates options (B), (C), (D).

concepts: Common chord of two circles that bisects the circumference of one
Intersection (coplanarity) of two lines in 3D
questions.question: If the circle $x^2+y^2+4x+22y+c=0$ bisects the circumference of the circle $x^2+y^2-2x+8y-d=0$. If the lines $\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y-3}{1}=\frac{4-z}{\lambda}$ and $\frac{x-1}{\lambda}=\frac{y-4}{2}=\frac{z-\alpha}{1}$ intersect, then the value of $\alpha\lambda$ is (where $\alpha$ is equal to $\frac{c+d}{10}$):
questions.key_idea: The common chord is a diameter of the second circle, so it passes through its centre; then intersecting lines are coplanar: $(\vec P_2-\vec P_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)=0$.
solution: The first circle bisects the circumference of the second, so their common chord is a diameter of the second circle and passes through its centre $(1,-4)$.
Common chord $S_1-S_2=0$: $6x+14y+c+d=0$.
Passing through $(1,-4)$: $6-56+c+d=0\Rightarrow c+d=50$.
Hence $\alpha=\frac{c+d}{10}=5$ (the PDF writes this value as '$\lambda=5$', a slip of notation).
The lines pass through $P_1(2,3,4)$ with direction $(1,1,-\lambda)$ and $P_2(1,4,5)$ with direction $(\lambda,2,1)$.
They intersect, so $(\vec P_2-\vec P_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)=0$, i.e. $\left|\begin{matrix}1&-1&-1\\1&1&-\lambda\\\lambda&2&1\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
$(1+2\lambda)+(1+\lambda^2)-(2-\lambda)=0\Rightarrow\lambda^2+3\lambda=0\Rightarrow\lambda=0$ or $-3$.
So $\alpha\lambda=0$ or $-15$. Only $0$ is among the options, so the answer is (D).
questions.correction_note: PDF used the symbol lambda for alpha (writes 'lambda=(c+d)/10, lambda=5') and wrote 'l=0,-3'. Corrected to alpha=5 and lambda in {0,-3}; the second root gives alpha*lambda=-15 which is not an option, so (D) 0 still stands.

alternate_solutions.idea: Intersection means a common point: solve the two parametric lines directly for the parameters instead of a determinant.
solution: Line 1: $(2+s,\,3+s,\,4-\lambda s)$. Line 2: $(1+\lambda t,\,4+2t,\,5+t)$ (using $\alpha=5$).
Equate coordinates: $2+s=1+\lambda t$ ......(i); $3+s=4+2t$ ......(ii); $4-\lambda s=5+t$ ......(iii).
From (ii): $s=1+2t$. Put in (i): $3+2t=1+\lambda t\Rightarrow t(\lambda-2)=2$ ($\lambda\neq2$, otherwise (i) is impossible).
Put $s=1+2t$ in (iii): $4-\lambda-2\lambda t=5+t\Rightarrow t(1+2\lambda)=-(1+\lambda)$.
Eliminate $t=\frac{2}{\lambda-2}$: $2(1+2\lambda)=-(1+\lambda)(\lambda-2)=-\lambda^2+\lambda+2$.
$\lambda^2+3\lambda=0\Rightarrow\lambda=0$ or $-3$, the same as the determinant condition; $\alpha\lambda=0$ (or $-15$), so (D).

useful_results: Two lines $\vec r=\vec p_1+s\vec d_1$, $\vec r=\vec p_2+t\vec d_2$ intersect iff $(\vec p_2-\vec p_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)=0$ AND $\vec d_1\nparallel\vec d_2$.
A circle $S_1$ bisects the circumference of $S_2$ iff the common chord $S_1-S_2=0$ passes through the centre of $S_2$.
Read the symbols carefully: an unknown can appear in both a circle part and a line part of a mixed question; keep each letter's meaning fixed.

concepts: Scalar and vector products with given projections
questions.question: If $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ are non-zero, non-collinear vectors such that $|\vec a|=2$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b=1$ and the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$. If $\vec r$ is any vector such that $\vec r\cdot\vec a=2$, $\vec r\cdot\vec b=8$, $(\vec r+2\vec a-10\vec b)\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=4\sqrt3$ and $\vec r+2\vec a-10\vec b=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)$ then $\lambda$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Dot $\vec r+2\vec a-10\vec b=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)$ with $\vec a\times\vec b$ to get $\lambda|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=4\sqrt3$; find $|\vec b|$ from $\vec a\cdot\vec b=1$.
solution: Dot $\vec r+2\vec a-10\vec b=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)$ with $\vec a\times\vec b$: $\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=4\sqrt3$.
From $\vec a\cdot\vec b=ab\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=1$ with $a=2$: $2b\cdot\frac12=1\Rightarrow b=1$.
$(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=a^2b^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2=4\cdot1-1^2=3$.
So $3\lambda=4\sqrt3\Rightarrow\lambda=\frac{4\sqrt3}{3}$.

This equals none of $\frac12,\ 2,\ \frac14$, so the answer is (D). (Check: $\vec r=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)-2\vec a+10\vec b$ gives $\vec r\cdot\vec a=-8+10=2$ and $\vec r\cdot\vec b=-2+10=8$, so such an $\vec r$ exists.)

alternate_solutions.idea: Fix coordinates: put $\vec a$ along the $x$-axis and $\vec b$ in the $xy$-plane.
solution: Take $\vec a=(2,0,0)$ and $\vec b=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2},0\right)$; then $|\vec b|=1$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=1$ (angle $60^\circ$).
$\vec a\times\vec b=(0,0,\sqrt3)$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=3$.
$\vec r+2\vec a-10\vec b=\lambda(0,0,\sqrt3)$ gives $\vec r=(1,5\sqrt3,\lambda\sqrt3)$; check $\vec r\cdot\vec a=2$ and $\vec r\cdot\vec b=\frac12+\frac{15}{2}=8$ as given.
$(\vec r+2\vec a-10\vec b)\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=\lambda\sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3=3\lambda=4\sqrt3$.
So $\lambda=\frac{4\sqrt3}{3}$, not among (A), (B), (C): option (D).

useful_results: If $\vec v=\lambda\vec n$ then $\lambda=\dfrac{\vec v\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|^2}$ (dot with the vector itself).
$|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$; with $|\vec a|=2,\ |\vec b|=1,\ \vec a\cdot\vec b=1$ this is $3$.
In 'none of these' options, compute the exact value first and only then compare; do not force a match.

concepts: Maximum of a sum of squared lengths of unit-vector combinations
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are unit vectors, then the value of $|\vec a-2\vec b|^2+|\vec b-2\vec c|^2+|\vec c-2\vec a|^2$ does not exceed:
questions.key_idea: The expression equals $15-4(\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec b\cdot\vec c+\vec c\cdot\vec a)$, and $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2\ge0$ bounds the bracket below by $-\frac32$.
solution: $|\vec a-2\vec b|^2+|\vec b-2\vec c|^2+|\vec c-2\vec a|^2=5a^2+5b^2+5c^2-4(\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec b\cdot\vec c+\vec c\cdot\vec a)$.
For unit vectors this is $15-4(\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec b\cdot\vec c+\vec c\cdot\vec a)$.
Since $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2\ge0$, we get $3+2(\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec b\cdot\vec c+\vec c\cdot\vec a)\ge0$, i.e. $\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec b\cdot\vec c+\vec c\cdot\vec a\ge-\frac32$.
Hence the expression is $\le15-4\left(-\frac32\right)=21$.
Equality holds when $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$ (three unit vectors at $120^\circ$), so the maximum is exactly $21$ and the value does not exceed $21$: option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Rewrite the whole sum as a constant minus a square so the maximum and the equality case appear together.
solution: With $S=\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec b\cdot\vec c+\vec c\cdot\vec a$ and $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2=3+2S$ we have $S=\frac{|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2-3}{2}$.
The sum equals $15-4S=15-2|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2+6=21-2|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2$.
A non-negative square is subtracted, so the value is at most $21$, attained when $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$.
So the sum never exceeds $21$ (and $18$, $12$, $9$ are exceeded for the equilateral choice): option (D).

useful_results: For unit vectors, $\sum(\vec a-k\vec b)^2$ type sums reduce to a constant plus a multiple of $S=\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec b\cdot\vec c+\vec c\cdot\vec a$, and $S\ge-\frac32$ always (equality iff $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$).
Similarly $S\le3$ with equality iff $\vec a=\vec b=\vec c$.
'Does not exceed $N$' questions: the answer is the smallest option that is at least the maximum, and the maximum must be checked to be attained.

concepts: Rectangle in vectors: diagonals and angle between them
questions.question: The adjacent side vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ of a rectangle $OACB$ are $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ respectively where $O$ is the origin. If $16|\vec a\times\vec b|=3(|\vec a|+|\vec b|)^2$ and $\theta$ be the acute angle between the diagonals $OC$ and $AB$ then the possible value of $\tan(\theta/2)$ is:
questions.key_idea: In a rectangle $|\vec a\times\vec b|=ab$ turns the condition into $3a^2-10ab+3b^2=0$, so one side is three times the other.
solution: For a rectangle $\vec a\perp\vec b$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|=ab\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=ab$.
$(3a-b)(a-3b)=0\Rightarrow b=3a$ or $a=3b$ (take $b=3a$; the other case is symmetric).
Diagonals: $\overrightarrow{OC}=\vec a+\vec b$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}=\vec b-\vec a$, so $\overrightarrow{OC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=b^2-a^2$.
$\cos\theta=\frac{b^2-a^2}{|\overrightarrow{OC}||\overrightarrow{AB}|}=\frac{b^2-a^2}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}=\frac{9a^2-a^2}{9a^2+a^2}=\frac45$ (acute).
$\tan\frac\theta2=\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\theta}{1+\cos\theta}}=\sqrt{\frac{1-4/5}{1+4/5}}=\sqrt{\frac19}=\frac13$, option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the geometry of a rectangle: the diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so the half-angle between them is the angle a diagonal makes with the longer side.
solution: As before $b=3a$ (sides in the ratio $3:1$).
The diagonals meet at the centre; each diagonal makes an angle $\varphi$ with the longer side with $\tan\varphi=\frac{\text{shorter}}{\text{longer}}=\frac{a}{b}=\frac13$.
The two diagonals are symmetric about the longer side, so the angle between them (containing the longer side) is $2\varphi$, which is the acute one.
Hence $\theta=2\varphi$ and $\tan\frac\theta2=\tan\varphi=\frac13$ (check: $\tan2\varphi=\frac{2/3}{1-1/9}=\frac34$, $\cos\theta=\frac45$).

useful_results: In a rectangle with sides $a\ (\le b)$, the acute angle $\theta$ between the diagonals satisfies $\tan\frac\theta2=\frac ab$ and $\cos\theta=\frac{b^2-a^2}{a^2+b^2}$.
$|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec a||\vec b|$ iff $\vec a\perp\vec b$; a condition like $k|\vec a||\vec b|=m(a+b)^2$ gives a homogeneous quadratic in $a,b$ that fixes the ratio $a:b$.
Acute angle between two lines: use $|\cos\theta|$, not $\cos\theta$.

concepts: Reciprocal system of vectors and scalar triple product
questions.question: If $\vec d=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)+\mu(\vec b\times\vec c)+\nu(\vec c\times\vec a)$, $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\frac18$ and $\vec d\cdot(\vec a+\vec b+\vec c)=8$, then $\lambda+\mu+\nu$ is:
questions.key_idea: Each cross product is perpendicular to two of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$, so dotting $\vec d$ with $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ isolates $\mu,\nu,\lambda$.
solution: $\vec d\cdot\vec c=\lambda[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]+\mu\cdot0+\nu\cdot0$, since $(\vec b\times\vec c)\cdot\vec c=(\vec c\times\vec a)\cdot\vec c=0$.
$\vec d\cdot\vec a=\mu[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
$\vec d\cdot\vec b=\nu[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
Adding: $\vec d\cdot(\vec a+\vec b+\vec c)=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c](\lambda+\mu+\nu)$.
$8=\frac18(\lambda+\mu+\nu)\Rightarrow\lambda+\mu+\nu=64$ (the PDF's last line prints $\beta$ for $\mu$, a typing slip).

alternate_solutions.idea: Choose a convenient triad with the same triple product: orthogonal vectors along the axes.
solution: Take $\vec a=\frac12\hat i$, $\vec b=\frac12\hat j$, $\vec c=\frac12\hat k$; then $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\frac18$ as required.
$\vec a\times\vec b=\frac14\hat k$, $\vec b\times\vec c=\frac14\hat i$, $\vec c\times\vec a=\frac14\hat j$, so $\vec d=\frac14(\mu,\nu,\lambda)$.
$\vec d\cdot(\vec a+\vec b+\vec c)=\frac12\cdot\frac14(\lambda+\mu+\nu)=\frac{\lambda+\mu+\nu}{8}=8$.
Hence $\lambda+\mu+\nu=64$ (valid for every triad, since the answer depends only on $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$).

useful_results: If $\vec d=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)+\mu(\vec b\times\vec c)+\nu(\vec c\times\vec a)$ then $\lambda=\dfrac{\vec d\cdot\vec c}{[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]},\ \mu=\dfrac{\vec d\cdot\vec a}{[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]},\ \nu=\dfrac{\vec d\cdot\vec b}{[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]}$.
For non-coplanar $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$, $\vec a\times\vec b,\ \vec b\times\vec c,\ \vec c\times\vec a$ form a basis (reciprocal system, up to the factor $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$).
Answers that depend only on $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ can be tested with an orthogonal triad of the same triple product.

concepts: Scalar triple product identities
Volume of a tetrahedron
questions.question: If $[\vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a]+[\vec a+\vec b\ \ \vec b+\vec c\ \ \vec c+\vec a]=8$, then the area of the tetrahedron $OABC$ with three of its sides along $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ can be:
questions.key_idea: $[\vec a\times\vec b\ \vec b\times\vec c\ \vec c\times\vec a]=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$ and $[\vec a+\vec b\ \vec b+\vec c\ \vec c+\vec a]=2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ give a quadratic in the triple product.
solution: Let $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=t$. Then $[\vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a]=t^2$.
$[\vec a+\vec b\ \ \vec b+\vec c\ \ \vec c+\vec a]=2t$.
The condition becomes $t^2+2t=8\Rightarrow t^2+2t-8=0\Rightarrow(t+4)(t-2)=0$, so $t=2$ or $-4$.
The volume of the tetrahedron $OABC$ is $\frac16|t|$.
So the volume is $\frac13$ (for $t=2$) or $\frac23$ (for $t=-4$). (The question says 'area' but means volume.)
Among the options, $\frac23$ is possible: option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Work backwards from the options: each option fixes $|t|=6V$, and only one is consistent with $t^2+2t=8$ for some sign of $t$.
solution: The volume is $V=\frac{|t|}{6}$, so the options give $|t|=4,\ 1,\ 5,\ \frac34$.
The condition $t^2+2t=8$ allows only $t=2$ or $t=-4$, i.e. $|t|=2$ or $4$.
Of the four values $|t|=4,1,5,\frac34$ only $|t|=4$ (with $t=-4$) occurs.
That corresponds to option (A), $V=\frac23$; the other possible volume $\frac13$ is not offered.

useful_results: $[\vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a]=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$ and $[\vec a+\vec b\ \ \vec b+\vec c\ \ \vec c+\vec a]=2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
More generally $[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]$ of combinations equals the determinant of the coefficient matrix times $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
Remember that $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ can be negative: the volume of $OABC$ is $\frac16|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]|$, parallelepiped $|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]|$.

concepts: Position vectors: sum of squared sides and the centroid
questions.question: Let $A,B,C$ be three points in the $x$-$y$ plane such that $OA=2$, $OB=2$, $OC=3$ and $AB^2+BC^2+CA^2=51$, then the distance between $O$ and $D$ (where $D$ is the mid-point of $AB$ and $O$ is the origin) is:
questions.key_idea: The squared sides force $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$, so $OD=\frac12|\vec a+\vec b|=\frac12 OC$.
solution: Let $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ be the position vectors of $A,B,C$ with $|\vec a|=|\vec b|=2$, $|\vec c|=3$.
$AB^2+BC^2+CA^2=2(|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2+|\vec c|^2)-2(\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec b\cdot\vec c+\vec c\cdot\vec a)=34-2S=51$, so $S=-\frac{17}{2}$.
$|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2=17+2S=0$, hence $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$.
$D$ is the mid-point of $AB$: $\overrightarrow{OD}=\frac{\vec a+\vec b}{2}=-\frac{\vec c}{2}$.
So $OD=\frac{OC}{2}=\frac32$, option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Leibniz formula: the sum of the squared sides equals $3\sum OA^2-9\,OG^2$ for the centroid $G$.
solution: For any point $O$ and triangle $ABC$ with centroid $G$: $AB^2+BC^2+CA^2=3(OA^2+OB^2+OC^2)-9\,OG^2$.
Here $3(4+4+9)-9\,OG^2=51\Rightarrow51-9\,OG^2=51\Rightarrow OG=0$, so $O$ is the centroid.
The centroid lies on the median $CD$ and divides it $CO:OD=2:1$.
Hence $OD=\frac12\,OC=\frac32$.

useful_results: $AB^2+BC^2+CA^2=3\left(OA^2+OB^2+OC^2\right)-9\,OG^2$ (Leibniz); it equals $3\sum OA^2$ exactly when $O$ is the centroid.
$\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$ iff $O$ is the centroid of $ABC$; then $\overrightarrow{OD}=-\tfrac12\vec c$ for the mid-point $D$ of $AB$.
$|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2=\sum|\vec a|^2+2S$; a value $0$ gives $S=-\tfrac12\sum|\vec a|^2$.

concepts: Locus under scaling of a point about the origin
Intersection of a line and a plane
questions.question: Points $A,B$ lie on $x+2y+z-10=0$ and $\frac{x-5}{2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-2}$ respectively. $C,D$ divide $OA,OB$ in the ratio $1:2$, $1:3$ respectively ($O$ is the origin). The locus of $C$ is $P$ and the locus of $D$ is $L$. The point of intersection of $P$ and $L$ is:
questions.key_idea: $C=\frac13A$ and $D=\frac14B$ are images under scaling about $O$: $P$ is the plane $x+2y+z=\frac{10}{3}$ and $L$ is the line through $\left(\frac54,\frac12,\frac14\right)$ with the same direction.
solution: $C$ divides $OA$ in $1:2$, so $\overrightarrow{OC}=\frac13\overrightarrow{OA}$; the locus of $C$ is $P:\ x+2y+z=\frac{10}{3}$.
$D$ divides $OB$ in $1:3$, so $\overrightarrow{OD}=\frac14\overrightarrow{OB}$; $B=(5+2t,\,2+t,\,1-2t)$ gives the locus $L:\ \frac{x-\frac54}{2}=\frac{y-\frac12}{1}=\frac{z-\frac14}{-2}$.
A general point of $L$ is $\left(2t+\frac54,\ t+\frac12,\ -2t+\frac14\right)$.
Put it in $P$: $\left(2t+\frac54\right)+2\left(t+\frac12\right)+\left(-2t+\frac14\right)=\frac{10}{3}$.
$2t+\frac{10}{4}=\frac{10}{3}\Rightarrow2t=\frac56\Rightarrow t=\frac{5}{12}$.
The point of intersection is $\left(\frac{25}{12},\frac{11}{12},-\frac{7}{12}\right)$: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Scale the picture back: a common point $X$ of $P$ and $L$ has $4X$ on the given line and $3X$ on the given plane.
solution: If $X$ lies on both loci then $X=\frac14B$ with $B$ on the line and $3X=A$ on the plane, so $B=4X$ and $A=3X$.
Thus $4X$ lies on the given line and $3X$ on $x+2y+z=10$, i.e. $X\cdot(1,2,1)=\frac{10}{3}$, so $4X\cdot(1,2,1)=\frac{40}{3}$.
Find the point of the given line $(5+2t,2+t,1-2t)$ with $(1,2,1)$-sum $\frac{40}{3}$: $10+2t=\frac{40}{3}\Rightarrow t=\frac53$.
That point is $4X=\left(\frac{25}{3},\frac{11}{3},-\frac73\right)$, so $X=\left(\frac{25}{12},\frac{11}{12},-\frac{7}{12}\right)$: option (B).

useful_results: If $A$ runs over a set $S$, the point $C=kA$ (dividing $OA$ in $k:(1-k)$) runs over the image of $S$ under the central scaling (homothety) with centre $O$ and ratio $k$: a plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=d$ goes to $\vec n\cdot\vec r=kd$ and a line keeps its direction.
Point dividing $OA$ in the ratio $m:n$ is $\frac{m}{m+n}A$.
To intersect a line and a plane, substitute the parametric point into the plane equation.

concepts: Vector equation with given magnitudes and dot products
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are three vectors with magnitude $2,3$ and $1$ respectively and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=\frac14$. If the following relation holds true for some $\lambda(\neq0)$, $\vec b-\lambda\vec a=3\vec c$, then the value of $\lambda$ is:
questions.key_idea: Dot the relation $\vec b-3\vec c=\lambda\vec a$ successively with $\vec a$, $\vec b$ and $\vec c$ and eliminate the unknown dot products.
solution: Write the relation as $\vec b-3\vec c=\lambda\vec a$. Dot with $\vec a$: $\vec a\cdot\vec b-3\vec a\cdot\vec c=\lambda|\vec a|^2$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec b-\frac34=4\lambda\Rightarrow\vec a\cdot\vec b=4\lambda+\frac34$ ......(1).
Dot with $\vec b$: $|\vec b|^2-3\vec b\cdot\vec c=\lambda\,\vec a\cdot\vec b$, i.e. $9-3\vec b\cdot\vec c=\lambda\left(4\lambda+\frac34\right)$ using (1).
$\Rightarrow3\vec b\cdot\vec c=9-\lambda\left(4\lambda+\frac34\right)$ ......(2).
Dot with $\vec c$: $\vec b\cdot\vec c-3|\vec c|^2=\lambda\,\vec a\cdot\vec c$, i.e. $\vec b\cdot\vec c-3=\frac{\lambda}{4}$.
Multiply by 3 and use (2): $9-\lambda\left(4\lambda+\frac34\right)-9=\frac{3\lambda}{4}$.
$\Rightarrow-\lambda\left(4\lambda+\frac34\right)=\frac{3\lambda}{4}\Rightarrow4\lambda+\frac34=-\frac34$ (as $\lambda\neq0$).
$\Rightarrow4\lambda=-\frac32\Rightarrow\lambda=-\frac38$, option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Square the relation $\vec b=\lambda\vec a+3\vec c$: $|\vec b|^2$ is known, so only $\vec a\cdot\vec c$ is needed.
solution: $\vec b=\lambda\vec a+3\vec c\Rightarrow|\vec b|^2=\lambda^2|\vec a|^2+9|\vec c|^2+6\lambda\,\vec a\cdot\vec c$.
Substitute $|\vec b|^2=9$, $|\vec a|^2=4$, $|\vec c|^2=1$, $\vec a\cdot\vec c=\frac14$: $9=4\lambda^2+9+\frac{3\lambda}{2}$.
$4\lambda^2+\frac32\lambda=0\Rightarrow\lambda\left(4\lambda+\frac32\right)=0$.
Since $\lambda\neq0$, $\lambda=-\frac38$ (option D).

useful_results: If $\vec b=\lambda\vec a+\mu\vec c$ and $|\vec b|$ is known, square it: $|\vec b|^2=\lambda^2|\vec a|^2+\mu^2|\vec c|^2+2\lambda\mu\,\vec a\cdot\vec c$ - one equation for one unknown, no need for $\vec a\cdot\vec b$ or $\vec b\cdot\vec c$.
When a vector relation involves three vectors and given pairwise data, squaring (not dotting with all three) is usually the shortest path.
Remember to discard the trivial root ($\lambda=0$) that a condition like $\lambda\neq0$ excludes.

concepts: Vector equation with an inequality on a dot product
questions.question: The vectors $\vec x$ and $\vec y$ satisfy the equation $p\vec x+q\vec y=\vec a$ (where $p,q$ are scalar constants and $\vec a$ is a known vector). It is given that $\vec x\cdot\vec y\ge\frac{|\vec a|^2}{4pq}$, then $\frac{|\vec x|}{|\vec y|}$ is equal to $(pq>0)$:
questions.key_idea: $|p\vec x-q\vec y|^2=|\vec a|^2-4pq\,\vec x\cdot\vec y\le0$, which forces $p\vec x=q\vec y$.
solution: $p\vec x+q\vec y=\vec a$. Let $p\vec x-q\vec y=R\hat n$ with $R=|p\vec x-q\vec y|\ge0$.
$|p\vec x-q\vec y|^2=|p\vec x+q\vec y|^2-4pq\,\vec x\cdot\vec y=|\vec a|^2-4pq\,\vec x\cdot\vec y\ge0$.
But $\vec x\cdot\vec y\ge\frac{|\vec a|^2}{4pq}$ and $pq>0$ give $4pq\,\vec x\cdot\vec y\ge|\vec a|^2$, so $|p\vec x-q\vec y|^2\le0$.
Therefore $|p\vec x-q\vec y|=0\Rightarrow p\vec x=q\vec y$.
Then $\vec a=p\vec x+q\vec y=2p\vec x\Rightarrow\vec x=\frac{\vec a}{2p}$ and $\vec y=\frac{\vec a}{2q}$.
$\frac{|\vec x|}{|\vec y|}=\frac{|\vec a|/2|p|}{|\vec a|/2|q|}=\frac{|q|}{|p|}=\frac qp$ (since $pq>0$ means $p,q$ have the same sign), option (D).
questions.correction_note: PDF wrote 'x = a/(2p), y = a/(2p)' for the second vector; from p x = q y and p x + q y = a we get q y = a/2, i.e. y = a/(2q). The ratio |x|/|y| = q/p is correct as printed.
useful_results: $|\vec u+\vec v|^2-|\vec u-\vec v|^2=4\,\vec u\cdot\vec v$ (parallelogram identity): an inequality on $\vec u\cdot\vec v$ in the opposite direction to $|\vec u-\vec v|^2\ge0$ forces equality, $\vec u=\vec v$.
$p\vec x=q\vec y$ with $p\vec x+q\vec y=\vec a$ means both parts equal $\frac{\vec a}{2}$ (they are the two halves of the diagonal).
A 'given inequality + a square that is always $\ge0$' pattern usually means the extreme (equality) case is the only possibility.

concepts: Vectors equally inclined to three mutually perpendicular unit vectors
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$ are three mutually perpendicular unit vectors and $\vec d$ is a unit vector which makes equal angle with $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$, then $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c+\vec d|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Expand the square: $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c+\vec d|^2=4+2\vec d\cdot(\vec a+\vec b+\vec c)$, and equal angles with $|\vec d|=1$ give $\cos\theta=\pm\frac1{\sqrt3}$.
solution: $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c+\vec d|^2=\sum|\vec a|^2+|\vec d|^2+2\vec d\cdot(\vec a+\vec b+\vec c)=4+2\vec d\cdot(\vec a+\vec b+\vec c)$ (the mutual dot products of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ vanish).
$\vec d$ makes the same angle $\theta$ with each: $\vec d\cdot\vec a=\vec d\cdot\vec b=\vec d\cdot\vec c=\cos\theta$.
Write $\vec d=\lambda\vec a+\mu\vec b+\nu\vec c$; then $\lambda=\mu=\nu=\cos\theta$.
$\lambda^2+\mu^2+\nu^2=|\vec d|^2=1\Rightarrow3\cos^2\theta=1\Rightarrow\cos\theta=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$.
$\vec d\cdot(\vec a+\vec b+\vec c)=3\cos\theta=\pm\sqrt3$.
$|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c+\vec d|^2=4\pm2\sqrt3$, option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Choose the axes along $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$: then $\vec d=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1,1,1)$ is visible at once.
solution: Take $\vec a=\hat i$, $\vec b=\hat j$, $\vec c=\hat k$ (mutually perpendicular unit vectors can be taken as the coordinate axes).
Equal angles with the axes and $|\vec d|=1$ give direction cosines $\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ each: $\vec d=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1,1,1)$.
$\vec a+\vec b+\vec c+\vec d=(1,1,1)\left(1\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$.
Its squared length is $3\left(1\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)^2=3\pm2\sqrt3+1=4\pm2\sqrt3$.

useful_results: A unit vector equally inclined to the three axes has direction cosines $\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ (the cube diagonals).
$|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|=\sqrt3$ for three mutually perpendicular unit vectors; adding a unit vector $\vec d$ along or against it gives $\sqrt3\pm1$.
For orthonormal $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$: $\vec d=(\vec d\cdot\vec a)\vec a+(\vec d\cdot\vec b)\vec b+(\vec d\cdot\vec c)\vec c$ and $\sum(\vec d\cdot\vec a)^2=|\vec d|^2$.

concepts: Scalar triple product of vectors built from a Gram matrix
questions.question: Given vectors $\vec a=\sin\frac\pi6\hat i+\sin\frac\pi3\hat j$, $\vec b=\sin\frac\pi3\hat j+\sin\frac\pi6\hat k$ and $\vec c=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$. The volume of the parallelepiped with three conterminous edges as $\vec u=(\vec a\cdot\vec a)\vec a+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec b+(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec c$, $\vec v=(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec a+(\vec b\cdot\vec b)\vec b+(\vec b\cdot\vec c)\vec c$, $\vec w=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec a+(\vec b\cdot\vec c)\vec b+(\vec c\cdot\vec c)\vec c$ equals:
questions.key_idea: $[\vec u\ \vec v\ \vec w]$ is the Gram determinant times $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$, and the Gram determinant is $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$, so the volume is $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^3$.
solution: The coefficients of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ in $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ form the Gram matrix, so $[\vec u\ \vec v\ \vec w]=\left|\begin{matrix}\vec a\cdot\vec a&\vec a\cdot\vec b&\vec a\cdot\vec c\\\vec b\cdot\vec a&\vec b\cdot\vec b&\vec b\cdot\vec c\\\vec c\cdot\vec a&\vec c\cdot\vec b&\vec c\cdot\vec c\end{matrix}\right|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
The Gram determinant equals $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$, hence $[\vec u\ \vec v\ \vec w]=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^3$.
$\vec a=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2},0\right)$, $\vec b=\left(0,\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12\right)$, $\vec c=(1,2,3)$.

$[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\left|\begin{matrix}\frac12&\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&0\\0&\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\\1&2&3\end{matrix}\right|=\frac12\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}-1\right)-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\left(0-\frac12\right)$.
$=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}{4}=\sqrt3-\frac12=2\cos\frac\pi6-\sin\frac\pi6$.
Volume $=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^3=\left(2\cos\frac\pi6-\sin\frac\pi6\right)^3$, option (C).
questions.correction_note: PDF printed the third row of the determinant as (0, 2, 3); the components of c = i + 2j + 3k give the row (1, 2, 3). With (1, 2, 3) the determinant is sqrt3 - 1/2 = 2cos(pi/6) - sin(pi/6), which is option (C); the PDF's printed expansion (3sqrt3/4 - 1/2) is one term short.

alternate_solutions.idea: Evaluate $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ as $\vec c\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)$ instead of expanding the determinant.
solution: $\vec a\times\vec b=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac12-0,\ 0\cdot0-\frac12\cdot\frac12,\ \frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}-0\right)=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{4},-\frac14,\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)$.
$\vec c\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}-\frac24+\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}=\sqrt3-\frac12$.
$\sqrt3-\frac12=2\cos\frac\pi6-\sin\frac\pi6$, so the required volume $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^3=\left(2\cos\frac\pi6-\sin\frac\pi6\right)^3$ (option C).

useful_results: If $\vec u=\sum G_{1j}\vec e_j$, $\vec v=\sum G_{2j}\vec e_j$, $\vec w=\sum G_{3j}\vec e_j$ with $G$ the Gram matrix of $\vec e_1,\vec e_2,\vec e_3$, then $[\vec u\ \vec v\ \vec w]=\det G\cdot[\vec e_1\ \vec e_2\ \vec e_3]=[\vec e_1\ \vec e_2\ \vec e_3]^3$.
Gram determinant: $\det\left(\vec e_i\cdot\vec e_j\right)=[\vec e_1\ \vec e_2\ \vec e_3]^2$.
Combinations $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$: $[\vec u\ \vec v\ \vec w]=\det(\text{coefficient matrix})\,[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
Check: here $\sqrt3-\frac12\approx1.232$, cube $\approx1.870$.

concepts: Parallelogram law for unit vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ be two unit vectors. The maximum value of $\frac{|\vec a+\vec b|^2-|\vec a-\vec b|^2}{|\vec a+\vec b|^2+|\vec a-\vec b|^2}$ is:
questions.key_idea: For unit vectors the ratio simplifies to $\cos\theta$.
solution: Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec b$.
$|\vec a+\vec b|^2=2+2\cos\theta=4\cos^2\frac\theta2$.
$|\vec a-\vec b|^2=2-2\cos\theta=4\sin^2\frac\theta2$.
$\therefore\frac{|\vec a+\vec b|^2-|\vec a-\vec b|^2}{|\vec a+\vec b|^2+|\vec a-\vec b|^2}=\frac{4\cos\theta}{4}=\cos\theta$.
Clearly the maximum value is $1$, attained when $\theta=0$ (i.e. $\vec a=\vec b$), option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the parallelogram law: the sum of the two squares is $2(|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2)=4$ and the difference is $4\,\vec a\cdot\vec b$.
solution: $|\vec a+\vec b|^2+|\vec a-\vec b|^2=2(|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2)=4$ (parallelogram law).
$|\vec a+\vec b|^2-|\vec a-\vec b|^2=4\,\vec a\cdot\vec b$.
So the ratio is $\vec a\cdot\vec b\le|\vec a||\vec b|=1$ (Cauchy-Schwarz), with equality for $\vec a=\vec b$.
Maximum value $=1$: option (B).

useful_results: $|\vec a+\vec b|^2+|\vec a-\vec b|^2=2(|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2)$ and $|\vec a+\vec b|^2-|\vec a-\vec b|^2=4\,\vec a\cdot\vec b$.
Hence $\frac{|\vec a+\vec b|^2-|\vec a-\vec b|^2}{|\vec a+\vec b|^2+|\vec a-\vec b|^2}=\frac{2\,\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2}$, which equals $\cos\theta$ for equal-length vectors.
Maximum of $\vec a\cdot\vec b$ for fixed lengths is $|\vec a||\vec b|$ (when parallel).

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Vector equation involving a cross product and scalar triple product
questions.question: If $\vec q,\vec r$ are unit vectors such that $\vec p=\vec q\times\vec p+\vec r$, then:
options: maximum value of $[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]=\frac12$
minimum value of $[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]=0$
minimum value of $[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]=-1$
questions.key_idea: Dot the relation with $\vec q$ for (A); then square it twice (once as $|\vec p-\vec q\times\vec p|^2=1$, once as $|\vec p|^2$) to express $|\vec p|^2$ and $[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]$ through $\sin^2\theta$.
solution: Dot the relation $\vec p=\vec q\times\vec p+\vec r$ with $\vec q$: $\vec p\cdot\vec q=(\vec q\times\vec p)\cdot\vec q+\vec r\cdot\vec q=\vec r\cdot\vec q$, so (A) is true.
Write $\vec r=\vec p-\vec q\times\vec p$ and let $\theta$ be the angle between $\vec p$ and $\vec q$ ($\vec p\perp\vec q\times\vec p$).
Squaring: $|\vec r|^2=1=p^2+p^2\sin^2\theta$ (here $p=|\vec p|$), so $p^2=\frac{1}{1+\sin^2\theta}$.
Squaring $\vec p=\vec q\times\vec p+\vec r$ directly: $p^2=p^2\sin^2\theta+2[\vec q\ \vec p\ \vec r]+1$.
$2[\vec q\ \vec p\ \vec r]=p^2\cos^2\theta-1$, so $2[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]=1-p^2\cos^2\theta=1-\frac{1-\sin^2\theta}{1+\sin^2\theta}=\frac{2\sin^2\theta}{1+\sin^2\theta}$.
$[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]=1-\frac{1}{1+\sin^2\theta}=\frac{\sin^2\theta}{1+\sin^2\theta}$.
As $\sin^2\theta$ runs over $[0,1]$, this runs from $0$ (when $\sin\theta=0$) to $\frac12$ (when $\sin\theta=1$): minimum $0$, maximum $\frac12$.
So (B) maximum $=\frac12$ and (C) minimum $=0$ are true, while (D) minimum $=-1$ is false. Answer: A, B, C.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compute $[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]=\vec p\cdot(\vec q\times\vec r)$ directly by substituting $\vec r=\vec p-\vec q\times\vec p$ and expanding the double cross product.
solution: $\vec q\times\vec r=\vec q\times\vec p-\vec q\times(\vec q\times\vec p)=\vec q\times\vec p-\left[\vec q(\vec q\cdot\vec p)-\vec p\right]$ (as $|\vec q|=1$).
$[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]=\vec p\cdot(\vec q\times\vec r)=0-(\vec p\cdot\vec q)^2+|\vec p|^2=|\vec p|^2\sin^2\theta$.
With $|\vec p|^2=\frac{1}{1+\sin^2\theta}$ this is $\frac{\sin^2\theta}{1+\sin^2\theta}$, an increasing function of $\sin^2\theta\in[0,1]$, so it lies in $\left[0,\frac12\right]$.
Hence the minimum is $0$ and the maximum is $\frac12$ (so (C) and (B)), and $-1$ is impossible.

useful_results: $\vec p\cdot(\vec q\times\vec p)=0$ and $|\vec p-\vec q\times\vec p|^2=|\vec p|^2+|\vec q\times\vec p|^2$ (the two are perpendicular).
$\vec q\times(\vec q\times\vec p)=\vec q(\vec q\cdot\vec p)-\vec p$ for a unit $\vec q$: repeated cross products with a unit vector act as projection minus identity.
$f(s)=\frac{s}{1+s}$ is increasing on $s\ge0$, so range questions for expressions like $\frac{\sin^2\theta}{1+\sin^2\theta}$ reduce to the endpoint values of $s=\sin^2\theta\in[0,1]$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Gram determinant: volume and height of a parallelepiped
questions.question: Let $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ be three vectors such that $|\vec a|=|\vec b|=|\vec c|=2$ and $\vec a\wedge\vec b=\vec b\wedge\vec c=\vec c\wedge\vec a=\frac\pi3$, then:
options: volume of parallelepiped formed by $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ as three coterminous edges is $8\sqrt2$
volume of parallelepiped formed by $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ as three coterminous edges is $4\sqrt2$
height of parallelepiped formed by $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ as three coterminous edges is $\frac{2\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}$ whose base is a parallelogram with adjacent sides $\vec a,\vec b$
height of parallelepiped formed by $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ as three coterminous edges is $\frac{4\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}$ whose base is a parallelogram with adjacent sides $\vec a,\vec b$
questions.key_idea: The Gram determinant gives $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=32$; volume $=$ base area $\times$ height with the base on $\vec a,\vec b$.
solution: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=\left|\begin{matrix}\vec a\cdot\vec a&\vec a\cdot\vec b&\vec a\cdot\vec c\\\vec b\cdot\vec a&\vec b\cdot\vec b&\vec b\cdot\vec c\\\vec c\cdot\vec a&\vec c\cdot\vec b&\vec c\cdot\vec c\end{matrix}\right|=\left|\begin{matrix}4&2&2\\2&4&2\\2&2&4\end{matrix}\right|$ (since $\vec a\cdot\vec b=4\cos60^\circ=2$).
So the volume is $v=|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]|=4\sqrt2$: (B) is true and (A) $8\sqrt2$ is false.
Base area (parallelogram on $\vec a,\vec b$) $=|\vec a\times\vec b|=2\cdot2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=2\sqrt3$.
$v=(\text{base area})(\text{height})\Rightarrow4\sqrt2=2\sqrt3\cdot h$.
$h=\frac{2\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}$: (C) is true and (D) $\frac{4\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}$ is false. Answer: B, C.

alternate_solutions.idea: The tips $A,B,C$ and the origin are pairwise $2$ apart, so $OABC$ is a regular tetrahedron of edge $2$; a parallelepiped has $6$ times its volume.
solution: $|\vec a-\vec b|^2=4+4-2\cdot2\cdot2\cos60^\circ=4$, and similarly for the other pairs, so $OA=OB=OC=AB=BC=CA=2$: a regular tetrahedron of edge $2$.
Volume of a regular tetrahedron of edge $s$ is $\frac{s^3}{6\sqrt2}$, so $V_{OABC}=\frac{8}{6\sqrt2}$.
The parallelepiped on $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ has volume $6V_{OABC}=\frac{8}{\sqrt2}=4\sqrt2$.
Height over the face on $\vec a,\vec b$ (area $2\sqrt3$): $h=\frac{4\sqrt2}{2\sqrt3}=\frac{2\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}$, so (B) and (C) hold.

useful_results: Equal edges $a$ with equal pairwise angles $60^\circ$ give a regular tetrahedron $OABC$ of edge $a$; the parallelepiped on the three edges has volume $6\cdot\frac{a^3}{6\sqrt2}=\frac{a^3}{\sqrt2}$.
Gram determinant for equal lengths $a$ and angle $\varphi$: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=a^6(1-3\cos^2\varphi+2\cos^3\varphi)$; for $\varphi=60^\circ$ this is $\frac{a^6}{2}$ ($=32$ for $a=2$).
Height of a parallelepiped over the face on $\vec a,\vec b$ is $\frac{|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]|}{|\vec a\times\vec b|}$.

questions.question: The volume of the parallelepiped whose coterminous edges are represented by the vectors $2\vec b\times\vec c$, $3\vec c\times\vec a$ and $4\vec a\times\vec b$ where $\vec a=(1+\sin\theta)\hat j+\sin2\theta\,\hat k$, $\vec b=\sin\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\hat i+\cos\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\hat j+\sin\left(2\theta+\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\hat k$, $\vec c=\sin\left(\theta-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\hat i+\cos\left(\theta-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\hat j+\sin\left(2\theta-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\hat k$ is $18$ cubic units, then the values of $\theta$, in the interval $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$, is/are:
questions.answer: No option satisfies the data as printed (the root is $\theta\approx1.076$ rad). Paper's key: (A, B, D).
questions.key_idea: Volume $=24[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$ (not $24[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$), so $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=\frac34$ and the determinant reduces to a trigonometric equation.
solution: Volume $=[\,4\vec a\times\vec b,\ 2\vec b\times\vec c,\ 3\vec c\times\vec a\,]=24[\vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a]=24[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=18$, so $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=\frac34$ and $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\left|\begin{matrix}0&1+\sin\theta&\sin2\theta\\\sin\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)&\cos\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)&\sin\left(2\theta+\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\\\sin\left(\theta-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)&\cos\left(\theta-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)&\sin\left(2\theta-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\end{matrix}\right|$.

Expand along the first row: $-(1+\sin\theta)\left[\sin\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\sin\left(2\theta-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)-\sin\left(2\theta+\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)\sin\left(\theta-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\right]+\sin2\theta\left[\sin\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\cos\left(\theta-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)-\cos\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\sin\left(\theta-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\right]$.

Second bracket: $\sin\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}3\right)\cos\left(\theta-\frac{2\pi}3\right)-\cos\left(\theta+\frac{2\pi}3\right)\sin\left(\theta-\frac{2\pi}3\right)=\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
First bracket (product to sum): $\frac12\left[\cos\left(3\theta+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)-\cos\left(3\theta-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\right]=-\sin3\theta\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin3\theta$.
Hence $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}(1+\sin\theta)\sin3\theta-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sin2\theta=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\left[\sin3\theta(1+\sin\theta)-\sin2\theta\right]$.
So $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ gives $\sin3\theta(1+\sin\theta)-\sin2\theta=\pm1$ ......(*).
Test the options in (*): $\theta=\frac\pi9$ gives $0.519$; $\frac{2\pi}{9}$ gives $0.438$; $\frac\pi3$ gives $-0.866$; $\frac{4\pi}{9}$ gives $-2.061$. None equals $\pm1$.
Solving (*) numerically on $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$ gives only $\theta\approx1.076$ rad ($\approx61.7^\circ$), which is not an option. The key (A, B, D) cannot be derived from the data as printed.
questions.correction_note: PDF wrote the volume as 24[a b c] = 18 (should be 24[a b c]^2 = 18, since [a x b, b x c, c x a] = [a b c]^2) and stops at sin3t(1+sin t) - sin2t = +-1 without solving it. Solving that equation (checked numerically) gives a single root t = 1.076 rad in (0, pi/2), none of the options; the printed key A, B, D (pi/9, 2pi/9, 4pi/9, i.e. sin3t = +-sqrt3/2) does not follow from the printed vectors. Probably the vector a in the original differs. Left flagged for the teacher.
useful_results: $[\vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a\ \ \vec a\times\vec b]=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$, so the volume of a parallelepiped on $k_1\,\vec b\times\vec c,\ k_2\,\vec c\times\vec a,\ k_3\,\vec a\times\vec b$ is $k_1k_2k_3[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$.

Rows $(\sin\varphi,\cos\varphi,\sin2\varphi)$ with $\varphi$ equally spaced by $\frac{2\pi}{3}$ appear in determinants that collapse through $\sin A\cos B-\cos A\sin B=\sin(A-B)$ and product-to-sum rules.
Always substitute the proposed options back into the reduced equation: it is the fastest way to detect an inconsistent key.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Dot product as scalar multiples of vectors
Coplanarity and perpendicularity of vectors
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are non-zero, non-collinear vectors such that a vector $\vec p=ab\cos(2\pi-(\vec a\wedge\vec b))\vec c$ and a vector $\vec q=ac\cos(\pi-(\vec a\wedge\vec c))\vec b$ then $\vec p+\vec q$ is:
questions.key_idea: $ab\cos(\ldots)$ turns each coefficient into a dot product: $\vec p=(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$ and $\vec q=-(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b$.
solution: $\vec p=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos(2\pi-\vec a\wedge\vec b)\,\vec c=|\vec a||\vec b|\cos(\vec a\wedge\vec b)\,\vec c=(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$.
$\vec q=|\vec a||\vec c|\cos(\pi-\vec a\wedge\vec c)\,\vec b=-|\vec a||\vec c|\cos(\vec a\wedge\vec c)\,\vec b=-(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b$.
$\vec p+\vec q=(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c-(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b$ (this equals $-\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)$).
$\vec a\cdot(\vec p+\vec q)=(\vec a\cdot\vec b)(\vec a\cdot\vec c)-(\vec a\cdot\vec c)(\vec a\cdot\vec b)=0$, so $\vec p+\vec q\perp\vec a$: (B) is true.
$\vec p+\vec q$ is a linear combination of $\vec b$ and $\vec c$, so it is coplanar with $\vec b$ and $\vec c$: (C) is true.
Being perpendicular to $\vec a$ (and in general non-zero) it is not parallel to $\vec a$, so (A) is false; in general it is not in the plane of $\vec a,\vec c$, so (D) is false. Answer: B, C.
questions.correction_note: PDF wrote p = (a x b).c and q = (a x c).b using a CROSS product for ab cos(...) (a scalar multiple of the dot product), then used [a a b] = [a a c] = 0. ab cos(a^b) is a . b, so p = (a.b)c and q = -(a.c)b; a.(p+q) = 0 follows from the dot products cancelling. Final answer (B, C) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test with explicit vectors that are non-collinear: this confirms (B), (C) and kills (A), (D).
solution: Take $\vec a=\hat i$, $\vec b=\hat i+\hat j$, $\vec c=\hat i+\hat k$: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=1$, $\vec a\cdot\vec c=1$.
$\vec p+\vec q=(1)\vec c-(1)\vec b=(\hat i+\hat k)-(\hat i+\hat j)=\hat k-\hat j$.
$(\hat k-\hat j)\cdot\hat i=0$ so it is perpendicular to $\vec a$ (B); it is $\vec c-\vec b$, hence coplanar with $\vec b,\vec c$ (C).
It is not a multiple of $\hat i$ (A false); the plane of $\vec a,\vec c$ is spanned by $\hat i,\hat k$, but $\hat k-\hat j$ has a $\hat j$ component (D false).

useful_results: $|\vec a||\vec b|\cos\theta=\vec a\cdot\vec b$ and $\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\theta$, $\cos(2\pi-\theta)=\cos\theta$: convert such coefficients to dot products first.
$(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c-(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b=\vec a\times(\vec c\times\vec b)$ (BAC-CAB): it is always perpendicular to $\vec a$ and lies in the plane of $\vec b,\vec c$.
Any vector $\vec a\times\vec w$ is perpendicular to $\vec a$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Collinearity of three points in vector form
questions.question: Three points $A,B$ and $C$ with position vectors $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$ are collinear if:
options: $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=\vec 0$
$\exists$ a unique value of $\lambda$ for which the point $C(\vec c)$ satisfies the vector equation $\vec r=\vec a+\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)$
the area of the $\triangle ABC$ vanishes
$\exists$ scalars $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ not all zero simultaneously such that $\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c=\vec 0$, where $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$
questions.key_idea: Collinearity can be stated as $(\vec b-\vec a)\times(\vec c-\vec a)=\vec 0$, $\vec c=\vec a+\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)$, zero area, or an affine dependence $\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c=\vec 0$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$.
solution: If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are position vectors of collinear points, then $\vec c-\vec a=\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)$ for some scalar $\lambda$ (this is (B), the line through $A,B$ passes through $C$ for a unique $\lambda$).
Then $(\vec b-\vec a)\times(\vec c-\vec a)=\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)\times(\vec b-\vec a)=\vec 0$.
Expanding, $(\vec b-\vec a)\times(\vec c-\vec a)=\vec b\times\vec c-\vec b\times\vec a-\vec a\times\vec c=\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a$, so (A) holds.
Area of $\triangle ABC=\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a|=0$: (C) holds.

From $\vec c=\vec a+\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)$: $(\lambda-1)\vec a-\lambda\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$ with $\alpha=\lambda-1,\ \beta=-\lambda,\ \gamma=1$, and $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$ and not all zero: (D) holds.
All four statements are consequences of (and equivalent to) collinearity: the answer is A, B, C, D.

alternate_solutions.idea: Check all four statements on one collinear and one non-collinear example.
solution: Collinear: $\vec a=\vec 0$, $\vec b=\hat i$, $\vec c=2\hat i$: cross terms are $0$, $\lambda=2$, area $0$, and $\alpha=1,\beta=-2,\gamma=1$ gives $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$ and $\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c=0$.

Non-collinear: $\vec a=\vec 0$, $\vec b=\hat i$, $\vec c=\hat j$: $\vec b\times\vec c=\hat k\neq\vec 0$, no $\lambda$ gives $\hat j=\lambda\hat i$, area $\frac12$, and $\beta\hat i+\gamma\hat j=\vec 0$ forces $\beta=\gamma=0$, then $\alpha=0$.
So each statement holds exactly in the collinear case: all four are correct conditions.

useful_results: $A,B,C$ collinear $\iff(\vec b-\vec a)\times(\vec c-\vec a)=\vec 0\iff\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=\vec 0\iff$ area of $\triangle ABC=0$.

Affine dependence: $\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c=\vec 0$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$ (not all zero) holds iff $A,B,C$ are collinear; without the condition $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$ it only says the three position vectors are linearly dependent.
Four points $A,B,C,D$ are coplanar iff $\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c+\delta\vec d=\vec 0$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=0$ (not all zero).
