questions.question: Let $\vec a,\vec b$ be two unit vectors and $\vec r$ be a vector such that $\vec r=x\vec a+y\vec b+z(\vec a+\vec b)$. If $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\frac12$, $\vec r\cdot\vec a=2$, $\vec r\cdot\vec b=1$ and $|\vec r|=\vec r\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=2$, then:
questions.answer: As printed, the data are inconsistent. Paper's key: (A, C, D).
questions.key_idea: $\vec r$ lies in the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$, so $\vec r\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$ and cannot equal $2$.
solution: $\vec r=x\vec a+y\vec b+z(\vec a+\vec b)=(x+z)\vec a+(y+z)\vec b$ lies in the plane of $\vec a,\vec b$.
$\vec r\cdot\vec a=2$: $x+\frac y2+\frac{3z}{2}=2$ ......(1). $\ \vec r\cdot\vec b=1$: $\frac x2+y+\frac{3z}{2}=1$ ......(2).
Put $u=x+z$ and $w=y+z$: (1) and (2) read $u+\frac w2=2$ and $\frac u2+w=1$, so $u=2,\ w=0$ and $\vec r=2\vec a$.
Then $|\vec r|=2$ holds automatically (the PDF reaches $x=2-z,\ y=-z,\ z(z-4)=0$ from $|\vec r|^2=4$; $x,y,z$ are not unique because $\vec a,\vec b,\vec a+\vec b$ are dependent).

But $\vec r\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=2\vec a\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0\neq2$: the condition $|\vec r|=\vec r\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=2$ cannot hold for a vector in the plane of $\vec a$ and $\vec b$.

If the third vector were $\vec a\times\vec b$ instead, then $\vec r\cdot\vec a=2,\ \vec r\cdot\vec b=1$ give $x=2,\ y=0$ and $|\vec r|=2$ gives $z=0$, so again $\vec r\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0\neq2$.
Hence the data are inconsistent in either reading and none of (A) $x=1$, (B) $y=1$, (C) $z=1$, (D) $x^2+y^2+z^2=2$ can be derived; the PDF's key (A, C, D) is reported here as given.
useful_results: If $\vec r$ is a combination of $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ (including $\vec a+\vec b$), then $\vec r\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$.
Coefficients in $x\vec a+y\vec b+z(\vec a+\vec b)$ are not unique: only $x+z$ and $y+z$ are determined.
To split a vector in the basis $\vec a,\vec b,\vec a\times\vec b$ use $\vec r\cdot\vec a,\ \vec r\cdot\vec b$ and $\vec r\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=z|\vec a\times\vec b|^2$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Pyramid on a regular hexagonal base: altitude and foot of perpendicular
questions.question: A pyramid with vertex at the point $P$, whose position vector is $4\hat i+2\hat j+2\sqrt3\hat k$ has a regular hexagonal base $ABCDEF$. Position vectors of points $A$ and $B$ are $\hat i$ and $\hat i+2\hat j$ respectively. Centre of the base has the position vector $\hat i+\hat j+\sqrt3\hat k$. Altitude drawn from $P$ on the base meets the diagonal $AD$ at point $G$ and volume of the pyramid is $6\sqrt3$ cubic units then all possible position vectors of $G$ are:
questions.answer: (A) $\hat i+2\hat j+2\sqrt3\hat k$ only. (The paper's key (B, C) is wrong.)
questions.key_idea: $A$, $B$ and the centre all have $x=1$, so the base lies in the plane $x=1$ and the foot of the altitude from $P$ is simply $(1,2,2\sqrt3)$.
solution: Let the centre be $O=(1,1,\sqrt3)$, $A=(1,0,0)$, $B=(1,2,0)$: $\overrightarrow{AB}=2\hat j$ so the side is $2$ and the hexagon has $6$ equilateral triangles of side $2$.
Area of one triangle $OAB=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot4=\sqrt3$, so the base area is $6\sqrt3$.
Volume $=\frac13\cdot6\sqrt3\cdot h=6\sqrt3\Rightarrow h=3$.
$A,B,O$ all have $x$-coordinate $1$: the base lies in the plane $x=1$ and $P=(4,2,2\sqrt3)$ is at distance $3$ from it, which agrees with $h=3$.
The foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $x=1$ is $G=(1,2,2\sqrt3)$.
Check that $G$ is on $AD$: $D=2O-A=(1,2,2\sqrt3)$, so $G=D$ and $AG=AD=4$ (also $AP=5$, $AG=\sqrt{25-9}=4$).

So there is only one position vector of $G$: $\hat i+2\hat j+2\sqrt3\hat k$, option (A). The PDF used $\overrightarrow{AO}=\hat i+\hat j+\sqrt3\hat k$ (the position vector of $O$) instead of $O-A=\hat j+\sqrt3\hat k$, which produced the incorrect set $\{3\hat i+2\hat j+2\sqrt3\hat k,\ -\hat i-2\hat j-2\sqrt3\hat k\}$ and the key (B, C).
questions.correction_note: PDF took AG = lambda*AO with AO = i + j + sqrt3 k (the position vector of the centre) instead of the vector from A to O, which is j + sqrt3 k. It then got G = 3i+2j+2sqrt3k or -i-2j-2sqrt3k (options C and B). The correct foot of the altitude is (1,2,2sqrt3) = D, option (A). Also the pyramid is fixed, so G is unique. The paper's key (B, C) is wrong.

alternate_solutions.idea: The base lies in the plane $x=1$, so the altitude from $P$ is parallel to the $x$-axis: just drop the $x$-coordinate of $P$ to $1$.
solution: $A=(1,0,0)$, $B=(1,2,0)$ and the centre $(1,1,\sqrt3)$ all satisfy $x=1$, so the base plane is $x=1$ with normal $\hat i$.
The altitude from $P=(4,2,2\sqrt3)$ is parallel to $\hat i$, so it meets the plane at $G=(1,2,2\sqrt3)$.
The distance $PG=3$ matches the height from the volume ($\frac13\cdot6\sqrt3\cdot h=6\sqrt3$).
So $G=\hat i+2\hat j+2\sqrt3\hat k$: only option (A).

useful_results: If $A,B,\ldots$ all share one coordinate (here $x=1$), the base plane is that coordinate plane and the foot of an altitude is obtained by replacing that coordinate in the apex.
Regular hexagon of side $s$: area $=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}s^2$; the long diagonal $AD$ passes through the centre $O$ with $D=2O-A$.
Volume of a pyramid $=\frac13(\text{base area})(\text{height})$; check the data by recomputing the distance from the apex to the base plane.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Cross product equality and coplanarity
Scalar triple product
questions.question: If $\vec a=\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec c=2\hat i+3\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec c\times\vec b=\vec d\times\vec b$ and $\vec d\cdot\vec a=8$ then which of the following is/are correct:
questions.key_idea: $\vec c\times\vec b=\vec d\times\vec b$ means $\vec c-\vec d\parallel\vec b$, so $\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ are coplanar and $\vec d=\vec c+\mu\vec b$.
solution: $\vec c\times\vec b=\vec d\times\vec b\Rightarrow(\vec c-\vec d)\times\vec b=\vec 0$.
So $\vec c-\vec d\parallel\vec b$, i.e. $\vec b,\vec c,\vec d$ are coplanar: $[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]=0$ and (C) is true; also $\vec c=\vec d+\lambda\vec b$.
$\vec b\cdot\vec c=2-3+1=0$, so $\vec c\cdot\vec c=\vec d\cdot\vec c+\lambda\,\vec b\cdot\vec c=\vec d\cdot\vec c$; hence $\vec d\cdot\vec c=|\vec c|^2=14$: (B) is true.
For (A): write $\vec d=\vec c+\mu\vec b$; $\vec d\cdot\vec a=\vec c\cdot\vec a+\mu\,\vec b\cdot\vec a=6+\mu=8\Rightarrow\mu=2$.
Then $\vec d\cdot\vec b=\vec c\cdot\vec b+2|\vec b|^2=0+6=6\neq4$, so (A) is false. Answer: B, C, D.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve for $\vec d$ explicitly, then test each option numerically.
solution: $(\vec c-\vec d)\parallel\vec b$ gives $\vec d=\vec c+\mu\vec b=(2+\mu,\ 3-\mu,\ 1+\mu)$.
$\vec d\cdot\vec a=(2+\mu)+(3-\mu)+(1+\mu)=6+\mu=8\Rightarrow\mu=2$, so $\vec d=(4,1,3)$.
$\vec d\cdot\vec b=4-1+3=6$ (A false); $\vec d\cdot\vec c=8+3+3=14$ (B true).
$[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]=0$ since $\vec d=\vec c+2\vec b$ (C true); $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=2$ (D true).

useful_results: $\vec u\times\vec b=\vec v\times\vec b\iff\vec u-\vec v\parallel\vec b$: equal cross products with a common vector determine a vector only up to a multiple of that vector.
Then $\vec u\cdot\vec b\ne\vec v\cdot\vec b$ in general, but $\vec u\cdot\vec w=\vec v\cdot\vec w$ for every $\vec w\perp\vec b$ (here $\vec w=\vec c$ because $\vec b\perp\vec c$).
Four vectors where one is a combination of the others have a zero triple product: $[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]=0$ when $\vec d=\vec c+\mu\vec b$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Vector product with equal angles and Gram determinant
Counting integral points inside a sphere
questions.question: Let $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ be three vectors each of magnitude $\sqrt3$ and the angle between each pair of them is $\pi/3$. If $\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=x\vec a+y\vec b+z\vec c$ where $x,y,z$ are scalars, then:
options: Volume of parallelepiped formed by $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ is $\frac{3\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}$
Number of integral co-ordinates $(x,y,z)$ satisfying $x^2+y^2+z^2\le12$ is $125$
questions.key_idea: Dot the given relation with $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ to get three linear equations in $x,y,z$ using $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\frac32$ and $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$ from the Gram determinant.
solution: $|\vec a|=|\vec b|=|\vec c|=\sqrt3$ and each angle is $60^\circ$, so $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec b\cdot\vec c=\vec c\cdot\vec a=\frac32$.
Dot the relation with $\vec a$: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=3x+\frac{3y}{2}+\frac{3z}{2}$ (the PDF prints $3x+\frac y2+\frac z2$, a typo that does not change the later result).
Dot with $\vec b$: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\frac32x+3y+\frac32z$. Dot with $\vec c$: $0=\frac32x+\frac32y+3z$.
The first two give $x=y$; the third gives $z=-x$. So $x=y=-z$.
$[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=\left|\begin{matrix}3&\frac32&\frac32\\\frac32&3&\frac32\\\frac32&\frac32&3\end{matrix}\right|=\frac{27}{2}$, so the volume is $\frac{3\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}$: (A) is true.
With $x=y=-z$ the first equation is $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=3x$, so $x=\frac{3\sqrt3}{3\sqrt2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}$: (B) is true.
$x^2+y^2+z^2=3x^2=\frac92<\sqrt{21}\approx4.58$: (C) is true.
(D): the number of integral points with $x^2+y^2+z^2\le12$ is $179$ (not $125$; $125$ would be the cube $-2\le x,y,z\le2$), so (D) is false. Answer: A, B, C.
questions.correction_note: The paper's key says (A, C) but the PDF's own working shows x = sqrt3/sqrt2, so (B) is also true; answer is (A, B, C). Also the PDF's first dot-product equation prints 3x + y/2 + z/2 instead of 3x + 3y/2 + 3z/2 (harmless because y = x, z = -x). (D) was not examined in the PDF: the integral points with x^2+y^2+z^2 <= 12 number 179, so (D) is false.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the reciprocal basis: $\vec b\times\vec c=V\vec a^*$ and $\vec c\times\vec a=V\vec b^*$ with $V=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$, and the inverse of the Gram matrix.
solution: The Gram matrix is $G=\frac32(I+J)$ ($J$ = all-ones matrix), with inverse $G^{-1}=\frac23\left(I-\frac J4\right)$: diagonal $\frac12$, off-diagonal $-\frac16$.

Reciprocal vectors: $\vec a^*=\frac12\vec a-\frac16\vec b-\frac16\vec c$ and $\vec b^*=-\frac16\vec a+\frac12\vec b-\frac16\vec c$, with $\vec b\times\vec c=V\vec a^*$ and $\vec c\times\vec a=V\vec b^*$.
$\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=V\left(\frac13\vec a+\frac13\vec b-\frac13\vec c\right)$, so $x=y=\frac V3$ and $z=-\frac V3$ with $V=\frac{3\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}$.
Hence $x=\frac{\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}$, and $x^2+y^2+z^2=3\cdot\frac32=\frac92$, the same as before.

useful_results: For vectors $\vec e_1,\vec e_2,\vec e_3$ with Gram matrix $G$: $\vec e_2\times\vec e_3=V\vec e_1^*$ (reciprocal basis), $V^2=\det G$, and $\vec e_i^*=\sum_j(G^{-1})_{ij}\vec e_j$.
Three equal vectors of length $a$ with $60^\circ$ between each pair: $V=\frac{a^3}{\sqrt2}$ (here $a=\sqrt3$ gives $\frac{3\sqrt3}{\sqrt2}$).
Number of integer points with $x^2+y^2+z^2\le12$: $179$; with $\le3$: $27$; (a good check of a counted answer is to enumerate by $x$).

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Cross product relation implying coplanarity
questions.question: Let $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$ be three distinct non-zero vectors such that $\vec a\times\vec b=-\vec b\times\vec c$ then which of the following is/are correct:
options: $|(\vec a+\vec c)\cdot\vec b|=|\vec a+\vec c||\vec b|$
$(\vec a+\vec b)\cdot[(\vec b+\vec c)\times(\vec c+\vec a)]=2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c=\vec 0$ means $(\vec a-\vec c)\times\vec b=\vec 0$, so $\vec a=\vec c+\lambda\vec b$.
solution: $\vec a\times\vec b=-\vec b\times\vec c\Rightarrow\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c=\vec 0$.
$\Rightarrow(\vec a-\vec c)\times\vec b=\vec 0\Rightarrow\vec a-\vec c=\lambda\vec b$.
$\Rightarrow\vec a=\lambda\vec b+\vec c$, so $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are coplanar. (D) is true (with $\mu=1$).
Coplanar vectors have $\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=0$: (B) is true.
$[\vec a+\vec b\ \ \vec b+\vec c\ \ \vec c+\vec a]=2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0$, i.e. $(\vec a+\vec b)\cdot[(\vec b+\vec c)\times(\vec c+\vec a)]=2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ holds: (C) is true.

(A): $|(\vec a+\vec c)\cdot\vec b|=|\vec a+\vec c||\vec b|$ would need $\vec a+\vec c=\lambda\vec b+2\vec c$ to be parallel to $\vec b$, which fails unless $\vec c\parallel\vec b$ (e.g. $\vec b=\hat i,\ \vec c=\hat j,\ \vec a=2\hat i+\hat j$: LHS $=2$, RHS $=\sqrt8$). So (A) is false. Answer: B, C, D.

alternate_solutions.idea: Confirm with one explicit triple and read off the truth of each statement.
solution: Take $\vec b=\hat i$, $\vec c=\hat j$ and $\vec a=2\hat i+\hat j=2\vec b+\vec c$ (so $\lambda=2$).
$\vec a\times\vec b=(2\hat i+\hat j)\times\hat i=-\hat k$ and $-\vec b\times\vec c=-\hat i\times\hat j=-\hat k$: the given condition holds.
$\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ all lie in the $xy$-plane: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=0$ (B) and the triple product in (C) is $0=2\cdot0$ (C); $\vec a=2\vec b+1\vec c$ (D).
$(\vec a+\vec c)\cdot\vec b=(2\hat i+2\hat j)\cdot\hat i=2$ but $|\vec a+\vec c||\vec b|=2\sqrt2$: (A) fails.

useful_results: $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=(\vec a-\vec c)\times(\vec b-\vec c)$; here $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c=\vec 0$ is the shorter relation $(\vec a-\vec c)\times\vec b=\vec 0$, meaning $\vec a-\vec c\parallel\vec b$.
$[\vec a+\vec b\ \ \vec b+\vec c\ \ \vec c+\vec a]=2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ always, so (C) is an identity.
$|\vec u\cdot\vec v|=|\vec u||\vec v|$ holds iff $\vec u\parallel\vec v$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Planes through feet of perpendiculars and their line of intersection
Plane through the intersection of two planes
questions.question: From point $A(-1,1,-1)$, the perpendicular is drawn to a plane $P_1$ whose foot is $(1,-1,1)$. From point $B(3,-1,-1)$, the perpendicular is drawn to a plane $P_2$ whose foot is $(1,2,1)$. $P_3$ is a plane containing the line of intersection of $P_1$ and $P_2$ and passing through the mid point of the line joining $A$ and $B$. Then which of the following statement (s) is/are correct:
options: Direction ratios of line of intersection of $P_1$ and $P_2$ are $5,4,-1$.
Equation of line of intersection of $P_1$ and $P_2$ is $\frac{x-15}{5}=\frac{y-12}{4}=\frac{z-0}{-1}$.
The length of perpendicular from $(0,0,0)$ to plane $P_3$ is $\frac{2}{\sqrt{18}}$.
questions.key_idea: The normal of each plane is the vector from the point to its foot; the line of intersection has direction $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$, and $P_3=P_1+\lambda P_2$ through the mid-point.
solution: Normal of $P_1$: foot $-A=(2,-2,2)$, so $P_1:\ (2x-1)-2(y+1)+2(z-1)=0\Rightarrow x-y+z=3$.
Direction of the line of intersection: $(1,-1,1)\times(2,-3,-2)=(5,4,-1)$, so (A) is true (direction ratios $5,4,-1$).
Mid-point of $AB$ is $(1,0,-1)$. A plane through the intersection: $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$, i.e. $(x-y+z-3)+\lambda(2x-3y-2z+6)=0$.
Put $(1,0,-1)$: $(1-1-3)+\lambda(2+2+6)=0\Rightarrow\lambda=\frac{3}{10}$.
$10(x-y+z-3)+3(2x-3y-2z+6)=0\Rightarrow16x-19y+4z-12=0$, so (B) is true.
Put $z=0$ in $P_1,P_2$: $x-y=3,\ 2x-3y=-6$, giving $x=15,\ y=12$. So the line is $\frac{x-15}{5}=\frac{y-12}{4}=\frac{z-0}{-1}$ and (C) is true.
(D): distance of $(0,0,0)$ from $P_3$ is $\frac{12}{\sqrt{16^2+19^2+4^2}}=\frac{12}{\sqrt{633}}\ne\frac{2}{\sqrt{18}}$, so (D) is false. Answer: A, B, C.

alternate_solutions.idea: Build $P_3$ directly from the line and the mid-point: its normal is perpendicular to the line direction and to the vector from a point of the line to the mid-point.
solution: The line passes through $(15,12,0)$ with direction $\vec d=(5,4,-1)$; the mid-point is $M=(1,0,-1)$.
Vector in $P_3$: $\overrightarrow{M\,(15,12,0)}=(14,12,1)$.
Plane through $M$: $16(x-1)-19y+4(z+1)=0\Rightarrow16x-19y+4z=12$, the same as (B).

useful_results: Line of intersection of planes with normals $\vec n_1,\vec n_2$ has direction $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$.
Every plane through the line $P_1=0=P_2$ is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ (one parameter, fixed by one extra condition).

The perpendicular from a point $A$ to a plane meeting it at the foot $F$ gives the normal $\overrightarrow{AF}$ and the plane $\overrightarrow{AF}\cdot(\vec r-\vec F)=0$ (no need for the plane's equation).

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Identity in trigonometric functions and parallel/perpendicular vectors
questions.question: $a_1,a_2,a_3\in R-\{0\}$ and $a_1+a_2\cos2x+a_3\sin^2x=0\ \forall x\in R$, then which of the following is/are true:
options: $\vec a=a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j+a_3\hat k$ and $\vec b=4\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$ are perpendicular.
$\vec a=a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j+a_3\hat k$ and $\vec b=-\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$ are parallel.
If $\vec a=a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j+a_3\hat k$ is of length $\sqrt6$ units, then $(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ can be $(1,-1,-2)$.
If $2a_1+3a_2+6a_3=26$ then $|a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j+a_3\hat k|=2\sqrt6$ units.
questions.key_idea: An identity in $x$ forces the coefficient of $\sin^2x$ and the constant term to vanish: $a_1+a_2=0$ and $a_3=2a_2$, so $\vec a=\lambda(-1,1,2)$.
solution: Using $\cos2x=1-2\sin^2x$: $(a_1+a_2)+\sin^2x(a_3-2a_2)=0$ for all $x$.
$(a_1,a_2,a_3)=(-\lambda,\lambda,2\lambda)$.
(A) $\vec a\cdot\vec b=-4\lambda+2\lambda+2\lambda=0$, so $\vec a\perp\vec b$ for $\vec b=4\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$: true.
(B) $\vec a=\lambda(-\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k)=\lambda\vec b$ for $\vec b=-\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$: parallel, true.
(C) $|\vec a|=\sqrt6\Rightarrow|\lambda|\sqrt6=\sqrt6\Rightarrow\lambda=\pm1$; $\lambda=-1$ gives $(1,-1,-2)$: possible, true.
(D) $2a_1+3a_2+6a_3=\lambda(-2+3+12)=13\lambda=26\Rightarrow\lambda=2$, so $|\vec a|=2\sqrt6$: true. Answer: A, B, C, D.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute two convenient values of $x$ instead of comparing coefficients.
solution: $x=0$: $a_1+a_2\cdot1+a_3\cdot0=0\Rightarrow a_1=-a_2$.
$x=\frac\pi2$: $a_1+a_2\cos\pi+a_3\cdot1=0\Rightarrow a_1-a_2+a_3=0\Rightarrow a_3=a_2-a_1=2a_2$.
So $(a_1,a_2,a_3)=a_2(-1,1,2)$, the same family as before (and every $x$ then satisfies the identity).
The four statements then follow as above: all four are true.

useful_results: If $A+B\,s=0$ for all $s=\sin^2x$ in a set with more than one value, then $A=B=0$ (comparing coefficients of independent functions).
Two substitutions of $x$ (e.g. $0$ and $\frac\pi2$) are enough to get the coefficients, and they must be verified in the original identity.
Vectors $\vec a=\lambda\vec b$ are parallel; $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$ perpendicular; fixing $|\vec a|$ or a linear combination fixes $\lambda$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Tetrahedron: altitude and foot of the altitude on a median
questions.question: The position vector of the vertices $A,B$ & $C$ of a tetrahedron $ABCD$ are $(1,1,1)$, $(1,0,0)$ & $(3,0,0)$ respectively. The altitude from the vertex $D$ to the opposite face $ABC$ meets the median through $A$ of $\triangle ABC$ at point $E$. If $AD=4$ units and volume of tetrahedron $=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}$, then the correct statement(s) among the following is/are:
options: There is only one possible position for point $E$
There are two possible positions for point $E$
Vector $\hat j-\hat k$ is normal to the plane $ABC$
questions.key_idea: Volume $=\frac13(\text{area of }ABC)\cdot h$ gives $h=2$; then $AE^2=AD^2-h^2=12$ places $E$ on the median at distance $2\sqrt3$ from $A$ on either side.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=(0,-1,-1)$, $\overrightarrow{AC}=(2,-1,-1)$, so $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=(0,-2,2)$ and the area of $\triangle ABC=\frac12\cdot2\sqrt2=\sqrt2$.
Volume $\frac13\cdot\sqrt2\cdot h=\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}\Rightarrow h=2$: (A) is true.
Normal to the plane $ABC$ is $\propto(0,-2,2)\propto\hat j-\hat k$: (D) is true.
Let $E$ divide the median $AM$ ($M=(2,0,0)$ the mid-point of $BC$) in $AE:EM=\lambda:1$: $E=\left(\frac{2\lambda+1}{\lambda+1},\frac{1}{\lambda+1},\frac{1}{\lambda+1}\right)$.
$DE\perp$ plane and $DE=2$, so $AE^2+ED^2=AD^2\Rightarrow AE^2=16-4=12$, $AE=2\sqrt3$. Also $AM=\sqrt3$, $AE=\left|\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}\right|\sqrt3$.
$\left|\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}\right|=2\Rightarrow\lambda=-2$ or $\lambda=-\frac23$.
$\lambda=-2$ gives $E=(3,-1,-1)$; $\lambda=-\frac23$ gives $E=(-1,3,3)$. There are two possible positions of $E$: (C) is true and (B) is false. Answer: A, C, D.
questions.correction_note: PDF's displayed determinant for the area has rows (1,1,1) and (2,-1,-1), which are not AB and AC; the correct rows are AB = (0,-1,-1), AC = (2,-1,-1), giving AB x AC = (0,-2,2), area sqrt2 and h = 2 (the PDF's later 'h|j-k| = 2 sqrt2' line is consistent with this). The rest of the PDF working is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $E$ directly: it lies on line $AM$ at distance $2\sqrt3$ from $A$, so move $\pm2\sqrt3$ along the unit vector of $\overrightarrow{AM}$.
solution: $h=2$ and $AD=4$ give $AE=\sqrt{16-4}=2\sqrt3$ (right triangle $AED$ with $DE\perp$ plane).
$\overrightarrow{AM}=(2,0,0)-(1,1,1)=(1,-1,-1)$, of length $\sqrt3$; its unit vector is $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1,-1,-1)$.
Both positions are possible (on opposite sides of $A$): two positions for $E$.

useful_results: Volume of a tetrahedron $=\frac13(\text{base area})\,h$; base area $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$ and the normal is $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$.
The foot $E$ of the altitude from $D$ satisfies $AE^2=AD^2-h^2$ (Pythagoras); if $E$ is known to lie on a line through $A$, the point is $A\pm AE\cdot\hat u$ - usually two solutions.
A point on a segment dividing it in $\lambda:1$ from the start allows negative $\lambda$ (external division) when the point lies beyond the ends.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Scalar triple product of vectors built from cross products
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$ are three non-coplanar vectors, then $[\vec a\times(\vec b+\vec c)\ \ \ \vec b\times(\vec c-2\vec a)\ \ \ \vec c\times(\vec a+3\vec b)]$ is equal to:
options: $-5[\vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a]$
$7[\vec c\times\vec a\ \ \vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c]$
questions.key_idea: With $X=\vec a\times\vec b,\ Y=\vec b\times\vec c,\ Z=\vec c\times\vec a$ each factor is a combination of $X,Y,Z$, so the triple product is $\det(\text{coefficients})\,[X\ Y\ Z]$.
solution: Let $X=\vec a\times\vec b$, $Y=\vec b\times\vec c$, $Z=\vec c\times\vec a$.
$\vec a\times(\vec b+\vec c)=\vec a\times\vec b+\vec a\times\vec c=X-Z$.
$\vec b\times(\vec c-2\vec a)=\vec b\times\vec c-2\,\vec b\times\vec a=Y+2X$.
$\vec c\times(\vec a+3\vec b)=\vec c\times\vec a+3\,\vec c\times\vec b=Z-3Y$.
$[X-Z\ \ \ 2X+Y\ \ \ Z-3Y]=\left|\begin{matrix}1&0&-1\\2&1&0\\0&-3&1\end{matrix}\right|[X\ Y\ Z]$.
The determinant is $1(1-0)-0+(-1)(-6-0)=7$.
So the value is $7[\vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a]=7[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$: (B) is true, and (A), $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$, is false.
$[\vec c\times\vec a\ \ \vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c]=[Z\ X\ Y]=[X\ Y\ Z]$ (cyclic), so (D) is true; (C), $-5[\ldots]$, is false. Answer: B, D.

alternate_solutions.idea: Pick $\vec a=\hat i,\ \vec b=\hat j,\ \vec c=\hat k$ (non-coplanar) and evaluate the determinant of the three explicit vectors.
solution: $\vec a\times(\vec b+\vec c)=\hat i\times(\hat j+\hat k)=\hat k-\hat j=(0,-1,1)$.
$\vec b\times(\vec c-2\vec a)=\hat j\times(\hat k-2\hat i)=\hat i+2\hat k=(1,0,2)$.
$\vec c\times(\vec a+3\vec b)=\hat k\times(\hat i+3\hat j)=\hat j-3\hat i=(-3,1,0)$.

$\left|\begin{matrix}0&-1&1\\1&0&2\\-3&1&0\end{matrix}\right|=0-(-1)(0+6)+1(1-0)=7$, while $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=1$: the value is $7[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$ ((B) and (D); (A) gives $1$, (C) gives $-5$).

useful_results: $[\vec a\times\vec b\ \ \vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a]=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2$ and the triple product is invariant under cyclic permutation.
If $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ are linear combinations of $\vec e_1,\vec e_2,\vec e_3$ with coefficient matrix $M$, then $[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]=\det M\,[\vec e_1\ \vec e_2\ \vec e_3]$.
Cross products $\vec a\times(\vec b+\vec c)$ etc. are combinations of $X,Y,Z$ because $\vec a\times\vec c=-Z$, $\vec b\times\vec a=-X$, $\vec c\times\vec b=-Y$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Perpendicular unit vectors and combinations of vectors
Properties of rhombus diagonals in vectors
questions.question: If unit vectors $\hat i$ and $\hat j$ are at right angles to each other and $\vec p=3\hat i+4\hat j,\ \vec q=5\hat i,\ 4\vec r=\vec p+\vec q$ and $2\vec s=\vec p-\vec q$, then:
options: $|\vec r+k\vec s|=|\vec r-k\vec s|$ for all real $k$
$\vec r+\vec s$ is perpendicular to $\vec r-\vec s$
questions.key_idea: Compute $\vec r=2\hat i+\hat j$ and $\vec s=-\hat i+2\hat j$; then $\vec r\cdot\vec s=0$, $|\vec r|=|\vec s|$.
solution: $\hat i\cdot\hat j=0$, $\vec p=3\hat i+4\hat j$, $\vec q=5\hat i$.
$4\vec r=\vec p+\vec q=8\hat i+4\hat j\Rightarrow\vec r=2\hat i+\hat j$; $\ 2\vec s=\vec p-\vec q=-2\hat i+4\hat j\Rightarrow\vec s=-\hat i+2\hat j$.
(A): $|\vec r+k\vec s|=|(2-k)\hat i+(1+2k)\hat j|=\sqrt{5+5k^2}$ and $|\vec r-k\vec s|=|(2+k)\hat i+(1-2k)\hat j|=\sqrt{5+5k^2}$: equal for all $k$, true.
(B): $\vec r\cdot\vec s=-2+2=0$, so $\vec r\perp\vec s$: true.
(C): $\vec r+\vec s=\hat i+3\hat j$ and $\vec r-\vec s=3\hat i-\hat j$; $(\vec r+\vec s)\cdot(\vec r-\vec s)=3-3=0$: true.
(D): $|\vec r|=\sqrt5=|\vec s|$ but $|\vec p|=5=|\vec q|$, so $|\vec r|=|\vec s|=|\vec p|=|\vec q|$ is false. Answer: A, B, C.

alternate_solutions.idea: Work with $\vec p,\vec q$ only: $|\vec p|=|\vec q|=5$, so the diagonals $\vec p\pm\vec q$ of the rhombus are perpendicular.
solution: $\vec r=\frac{\vec p+\vec q}{4}$ and $\vec s=\frac{\vec p-\vec q}{2}$, so $\vec r\cdot\vec s=\frac{|\vec p|^2-|\vec q|^2}{8}=\frac{25-25}{8}=0$: (B).
$|\vec r+k\vec s|^2-|\vec r-k\vec s|^2=4k\,\vec r\cdot\vec s=0$ for all $k$: (A).

$|\vec r|^2=\frac{|\vec p+\vec q|^2}{16}=\frac{50+30}{16}=5$ and $|\vec s|^2=\frac{|\vec p-\vec q|^2}{4}=\frac{50-30}{4}=5$ (with $\vec p\cdot\vec q=15$), so $|\vec r|=|\vec s|$ and $(\vec r+\vec s)\cdot(\vec r-\vec s)=|\vec r|^2-|\vec s|^2=0$: (C).
$|\vec r|=\sqrt5\ne5=|\vec p|$: (D) false.

useful_results: $|\vec u+k\vec v|=|\vec u-k\vec v|$ for all $k$ iff $\vec u\cdot\vec v=0$.
$(\vec u+\vec v)\cdot(\vec u-\vec v)=|\vec u|^2-|\vec v|^2$: perpendicular iff equal lengths (rhombus diagonals).
Equal-length $\vec p,\vec q$: $\vec p+\vec q\perp\vec p-\vec q$ always (diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular).

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Collinearity of vector functions of x
Unique root of cos x = x
questions.question: The vectors $\vec a(x)=(\cos x)\hat i+(\sin x)\hat j,\ \vec b(x)=x\hat i+(\sin x)\hat j$ are collinear for:
questions.key_idea: Collinearity gives $\sin x(\cos x-x)=0$; on $(0,\frac\pi2)$ this is $\cos x=x$, which has exactly one root, between $\frac\pi6$ and $\frac\pi3$.
solution: $\vec a(x)$ and $\vec b(x)$ are collinear iff $\cos x\sin x-x\sin x=0$, i.e. $\sin x(\cos x-x)=0$; for $0<x<\frac\pi2$, $\sin x\ne0$, so the condition is $\cos x=x$.
Let $f(x)=x-\cos x$. Then $f'(x)=1+\sin x\ge0$, so $f$ is increasing and has at most one zero.
$f\left(\frac\pi6\right)=\frac\pi6-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}<0$ and $f\left(\frac\pi3\right)=\frac\pi3-\frac12>0$.
So $f(x)<0$ for $x<\frac\pi6$ and $f(x)>0$ for $x\ge\frac\pi3$: $\cos x=x$ has exactly one solution, and it lies in $\left(\frac\pi6,\frac\pi3\right)$.
Hence (B) is true, (C) is true (no value in $\left(0,\frac\pi6\right)$), (A) and (D) are false. Answer: B, C.

alternate_solutions.idea: Sketch $y=\cos x$ (decreasing from $1$ to $0$) and $y=x$ (increasing) on $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$: they cross exactly once.
solution: On $\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$, $\cos x$ is strictly decreasing from $1$ to $0$, while $y=x$ is strictly increasing from $0$ to $\frac\pi2$.
A decreasing and an increasing function cross at most once; at $x=0$ the line is below the curve and at $x=\frac\pi2$ above, so they cross exactly once.
At $x=\frac\pi6$: $\cos x=0.866>0.524$ (curve above line) and at $x=\frac\pi3$: $\cos x=0.5<1.047$ (curve below line).
So the crossing lies in $\left(\frac\pi6,\frac\pi3\right)$: (B) and (C).

useful_results: $\vec u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $\vec v=(v_1,v_2)$ are collinear iff $u_1v_2-u_2v_1=0$ (components in a plane).
The equation $\cos x=x$ has a unique real root $x\approx0.739$ (the Dottie number); an increasing vs a decreasing function meet at most once.
To locate a root between two values, check the sign change of $f(x)=x-\cos x$ at the end points.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Linear independence of vectors and solving linear equations
questions.question: If $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ are three non-coplanar vectors satisfying $x(-\vec p+2\vec q+3\vec r)+y(2\vec p+3\vec q-4\vec r)+z(\vec p-4\vec q+5\vec r)=-4\vec p-21\vec q+38\vec r$, then choose the correct option (s):
questions.key_idea: Non-coplanar $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ are linearly independent, so the coefficients of $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ on both sides must be equal, giving three linear equations in $x,y,z$.
solution: Compare the coefficients of $\vec p$: $-x+2y+z=-4$ ......(1).
Compare the coefficients of $\vec q$: $2x+3y-4z=-21$ ......(2).
Compare the coefficients of $\vec r$: $3x-4y+5z=38$ ......(3).
Put in (3): $3x-4y+5x-10y-20=38\Rightarrow8x-14y=58\Rightarrow4x-7y=29$ ......(5).

alternate_solutions.idea: Cramer's rule on the three coefficient equations.
solution: $D=\left|\begin{matrix}-1&2&1\\2&3&-4\\3&-4&5\end{matrix}\right|=-60$.

$D_x=\left|\begin{matrix}-4&2&1\\-21&3&-4\\38&-4&5\end{matrix}\right|=-120$, $D_y=\left|\begin{matrix}-1&-4&1\\2&-21&-4\\3&38&5\end{matrix}\right|=180$, $D_z=\left|\begin{matrix}-1&2&-4\\2&3&-21\\3&-4&38\end{matrix}\right|=-240$.
The same values as the elimination; options (A) and (D) hold, (B) and (C) fail.

useful_results: If $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ are non-coplanar, $\alpha\vec p+\beta\vec q+\gamma\vec r=\vec 0$ forces $\alpha=\beta=\gamma=0$; so a vector equation becomes three scalar equations.
Compare coefficients of independent vectors whenever an equation holds between combinations of $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$.
Always check a solution by substituting it back into at least one of the original equations.

concepts: Projection and image (reflection) of a line in a plane
Distance of a point from a line and a plane from the origin
questions.question: Given a line $L$ and a plane $\Pi$: $L=\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac z3$, $\Pi=x+y+z=3$. Let lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively be projection and image of line $L$ in plane $\Pi$. Let planes $\Pi_1,\Pi_2$ respectively be planes containing $L$ and parallel, perpendicular to $\Pi$. Then shortest distance of:
questions.answer: (A, B, D) as per the paper's key. (B) and (D) verified; (C) false; (A) cannot be derived as printed.
questions.key_idea: The point $L\cap\Pi$ lies on $L_1$ and $L_2$; $L_1$ has direction $\vec d-\frac{\vec d\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$, $L_2$ has direction $\vec d-2\frac{\vec d\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$, and $\Pi_2$ has normal $\vec d\times\vec n$.
solution: $L$ passes through $(-2,-1,0)$ with direction $\vec d=(2,-1,3)$; $\Pi$ has normal $\vec n=(1,1,1)$, $\vec d\cdot\vec n=4$.
$L$ meets $\Pi$ where $(2t-2)+(-t-1)+3t=3\Rightarrow4t=6\Rightarrow t=\frac32$: $Q=\left(1,-\frac52,\frac92\right)$.

Projection $L_1$: direction $\vec d-\frac43\vec n=\left(\frac23,-\frac73,\frac53\right)\parallel(2,-7,5)$ through $Q$. For $(-9,6,-3)$: $\vec w=(-10,\frac{17}{2},-\frac{15}{2})$, $\vec w\times(2,-7,5)=(-10,35,53)$, distance$^2=\frac{4134}{78}=53$: (B) is true ($\sqrt{53}$).

$\Pi_2$ (contains $L$, perpendicular to $\Pi$): normal $\vec d\times\vec n=(-4,1,3)$, so $-4(x+2)+(y+1)+3z=0\Rightarrow4x-y-3z+7=0$; distance from origin $\frac{7}{\sqrt{26}}=\sqrt{\frac{49}{26}}$: (D) is true.

Image $L_2$: direction $\vec d-\frac83\vec n=\left(-\frac23,-\frac{11}3,\frac13\right)\parallel(-2,-11,1)$ through $Q$. The distance of the origin is $\sqrt{\frac{2565}{126}}=\sqrt{\frac{285}{14}}\ne\sqrt{\frac{285}{7}}$: (C) is false.

(A): no plane containing $L$ is parallel to $\Pi$ because $\vec d\cdot\vec n=4\ne0$, so $\Pi_1$ is not defined as printed. The key's value $\sqrt3$ equals the distance $\frac{3}{\sqrt3}$ of $\Pi$ itself from the origin, so (A) can only be read that way. The PDF gives no working; the key (A, B, D) is reported with this caveat.
useful_results: Projection of a line (direction $\vec d$) on a plane with normal $\vec n$: direction $\vec d-\frac{\vec d\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$; image (reflection) direction $\vec d-2\frac{\vec d\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$; both pass through $L\cap\Pi$.
The plane through a line $L$ perpendicular to a plane $\Pi$ has normal $\vec d\times\vec n$ and contains the projection of $L$ onto $\Pi$.
Distance of a point $P$ from the line through $Q$ with direction $\vec e$: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{QP}\times\vec e|}{|\vec e|}$.

concepts: Orthocentre of a triangle in 3D
questions.paragraph: The vertices of $\triangle ABC$ are $A(2,0,0)$, $B(0,1,0)$, $C(0,0,2)$. Its orthocentre is $H$ and circumcentre is $S$. $P$ is a point equidistant from $A,B,C$ and the origin $O$.
questions.question: The $z$-coordinate of $H$ is:
questions.key_idea: $AB=BC=\sqrt5$, so the altitude from $B$ is the median $BM$; $H=B+r\overrightarrow{BM}$ and $\overrightarrow{AH}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0$ fixes $r$.
solution: $AB=\sqrt{4+1}=\sqrt5=BC$, so $B$ is the apex of an isosceles triangle and the altitude from $B$ goes to the mid-point $M=(1,0,1)$ of $AC$.
$H$ lies on $BM$: position vector of $H=\hat j+r(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)$ (since $\overrightarrow{BM}=(1,-1,1)$).
$\overrightarrow{AH}=(r-2)\hat i+(1-r)\hat j+r\hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=-\hat j+2\hat k$.
$\overrightarrow{AH}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0\Rightarrow-(1-r)+2r=0\Rightarrow r-1+2r=0\Rightarrow r=\frac13$.
$H=\left(\frac13,\frac23,\frac13\right)$, so the $z$-coordinate of $H$ is $\frac13$: option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve for $H=(x,y,z)$ from two perpendicularity conditions and the plane of the triangle.
solution: The plane $ABC$ is $\frac x2+y+\frac z2=1$, i.e. $x+2y+z=2$.
$\overrightarrow{BH}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=0$: $(x,y-1,z)\cdot(-2,0,2)=0\Rightarrow z=x$.
$\overrightarrow{AH}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0$: $(x-2,y,z)\cdot(0,-1,2)=0\Rightarrow-y+2z=0\Rightarrow y=2z$.
Plane: $z+4z+z=2\Rightarrow z=\frac13$; so $H=\left(\frac13,\frac23,\frac13\right)$ and the $z$-coordinate is $\frac13$.

useful_results: In a triangle with $AB=BC$ the orthocentre, centroid and circumcentre all lie on the median from $B$ (the axis of symmetry).

Orthocentre $H$ satisfies $\overrightarrow{AH}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=0$, $\overrightarrow{BH}\cdot\overrightarrow{CA}=0$ (two of the three altitude conditions) and lies in the plane of the triangle.
Euler line: $\vec H=3\vec G-2\vec S$ ($G$ centroid, $S$ circumcentre).

concepts: Circumcentre of a triangle in 3D (Euler line)
questions.paragraph: The vertices of $\triangle ABC$ are $A(2,0,0)$, $B(0,1,0)$, $C(0,0,2)$. Its orthocentre is $H$ and circumcentre is $S$. $P$ is a point equidistant from $A,B,C$ and the origin $O$.
questions.question: The $y$-coordinate of $S$ is:
questions.key_idea: Euler line: $H=3G-2S$, so $S=\frac{3G-H}{2}$.
solution: Position vector of $H=\frac{\hat i}{3}+\frac{2\hat j}{3}+\frac{\hat k}{3}$.
Position vector of the centroid $G=\frac{2\hat i}{3}+\frac{\hat j}{3}+\frac{2\hat k}{3}$.
$H$, $G$, $S$ are collinear with $\vec H=3\vec G-2\vec S$, so position vector of $S=\frac{3\vec G-\vec H}{2}$.
$3\vec G-\vec H=\left(2-\frac13,\ 1-\frac23,\ 2-\frac13\right)=\left(\frac53,\frac13,\frac53\right)$, so $S=\left(\frac56,\frac16,\frac56\right)$.
The $y$-coordinate of $S$ is $\frac16$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the circumcentre directly: $S$ is equidistant from $A,B,C$ and lies in the plane of the triangle.
solution: $SA=SB$: $(x-2)^2+y^2+z^2=x^2+(y-1)^2+z^2\Rightarrow-4x+4=-2y+1\Rightarrow4x-2y=3$.
$SB=SC$: $x^2+(y-1)^2+z^2=x^2+y^2+(z-2)^2\Rightarrow-2y+1=-4z+4\Rightarrow4z-2y=3$, hence $x=z$.
Plane $ABC$: $x+2y+z=2\Rightarrow2x+2y=2\Rightarrow y=1-x$.
$4x-2(1-x)=3\Rightarrow6x=5\Rightarrow x=\frac56$ and $y=\frac16$ (so $S=\left(\frac56,\frac16,\frac56\right)$, the same value).

useful_results: Euler line of a triangle: $H$, $G$, $S$ collinear with $HG=2\,GS$, i.e. $\vec H+2\vec S=3\vec G$.
The circumcentre is the point of the plane equidistant from the three vertices: solve $SA^2=SB^2=SC^2$ together with the plane equation.
Equidistance from two points gives a plane (perpendicular bisector); two such planes and the triangle's plane meet in $S$.

concepts: Circumcentre of a tetrahedron with mutually perpendicular edges
questions.paragraph: The vertices of $\triangle ABC$ are $A(2,0,0)$, $B(0,1,0)$, $C(0,0,2)$. Its orthocentre is $H$ and circumcentre is $S$. $P$ is a point equidistant from $A,B,C$ and the origin $O$.
questions.question: $PA$:
questions.key_idea: $P$ is equidistant from $O,A,B,C$: the centre of the box with edges $OA,OB,OC$.
solution: Let $P=(a,b,c)$; $PA=PB=PC=OP$.
$PB^2=OP^2$: $a^2+(b-1)^2+c^2=a^2+b^2+c^2\Rightarrow b=\frac12$.
So $P=\left(1,\frac12,1\right)$ and $PA=\sqrt{(1-2)^2+\frac14+1}=\sqrt{\frac94}=\frac32$: option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: $OA,OB,OC$ are mutually perpendicular: $P$ is the centre of the rectangular box with these edges, and $PA=\frac12\times$ space diagonal.
solution: $OA=2,\ OB=1,\ OC=2$ along the three axes: $O,A,B,C$ are four vertices of the box $[0,2]\times[0,1]\times[0,2]$.
The sphere through $O,A,B,C$ has the diagonal of the box as a diameter, so its centre is the centre of the box $(1,\frac12,1)$.
Radius $=\frac12\sqrt{2^2+1^2+2^2}=\frac32$, so $PA=\frac32$.

useful_results: If $OA,OB,OC$ are mutually perpendicular with lengths $a,b,c$, the circumcentre of $OABC$ is $\left(\frac a2,\frac b2,\frac c2\right)$ and the circumradius is $\frac12\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$.
A point equidistant from the origin and $(a,0,0)$ has $x=\frac a2$: equidistance from $O$ and a point on an axis fixes that coordinate.
Circumradius of a right-corner tetrahedron: half the body diagonal of the enclosing box.

concepts: Solving simultaneous vector equations with cross products
questions.question: Vector $\vec x$ is:
options: $\frac{r}{|\vec a\times\vec b|}\left[\vec a\times\vec b-\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\right]$
$\frac{r}{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}\left[\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\right]$
questions.answer: (B) (the printed denominator should be $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2$)
questions.key_idea: First $\vec y=\frac{\vec a\times\vec b}{r}$; then cross (i) with $\vec y$: $(\vec x\times\vec y)\times\vec y=\vec y-|\vec y|^2\vec x$.
solution: From (i) and (ii): $\vec a\times\vec b=(\vec x\times\vec y)\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z]\,\vec y$ (the term $[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec y]\vec z$ vanishes).
$[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z]=\vec x\cdot(\vec y\times\vec z)=\vec x\cdot\vec b=r$ by (ii) and (iii), so $\vec y=\frac{\vec a\times\vec b}{r}$ and $|\vec y|^2=\frac{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}{r^2}$.
Cross (i) with $\vec y$ on the right: $(\vec x\times\vec y)\times\vec y=\vec a\times\vec y$.
Left side: $(\vec x\times\vec y)\times\vec y=\vec y(\vec x\cdot\vec y)-\vec x(\vec y\cdot\vec y)=\vec y-|\vec y|^2\vec x$ (using (iv)).

Right side: $\vec a\times\vec y=\frac{\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)}{r}$. So $|\vec y|^2\vec x=\vec y-\frac{\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)}{r}=\frac{\vec a\times\vec b-\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)}{r}$.

$\vec x=\frac{r^2}{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}\cdot\frac{\vec a\times\vec b-\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)}{r}=\frac{r}{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}\left[\vec a\times\vec b-\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\right]$.
This is option (B) (its printed denominator $|\vec a\times\vec b|$ lacks the square; a numerical test with random $\vec a,\vec b$ confirms the squared form is the correct one and (A), (C) are not).

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the options on an explicit instance: $\vec a=\hat i$, $\vec b=\hat j$, $r=1$, for which the system can be solved by inspection.
solution: $\vec y\perp\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec x\times\vec y=\hat i$, $\vec y\times\vec z=\hat j$: take $\vec y=\hat k$ (from $\vec y=\frac{\vec a\times\vec b}{r}=\hat i\times\hat j=\hat k$).
$\vec x\times\hat k=\hat i$ with $\vec x\cdot\hat k=1$ (iv) and $\vec x\cdot\hat j=1$ (iii): $\vec x=\hat j+\hat k$ (check: $(\hat j+\hat k)\times\hat k=\hat i$).
Option (B) with the squared denominator: $\frac{1}{1}\left[\hat k-\hat i\times\hat k\right]=\hat k+\hat j=\hat j+\hat k$ ✓.
Option (A) gives $\hat i\times\hat k=-\hat j$ and option (C) gives $\hat k+\hat j\times\hat k=\hat k+\hat i$: both differ from $\hat j+\hat k$. So (B) is the vector $\vec x$.

useful_results: $(\vec p\times\vec q)\times(\vec r\times\vec s)=[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec s]\vec r-[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]\vec s$.
$(\vec u\times\vec v)\times\vec w=\vec v(\vec u\cdot\vec w)-\vec u(\vec v\cdot\vec w)$ - the standard way to recover a vector from its cross product with a known vector plus one dot product.
Given $\vec x\times\vec y=\vec a$ and $\vec x\cdot\vec y=k$, $\vec x$ is determined: $\vec x=\frac{\vec y\,k-\vec a\times\vec y}{|\vec y|^2}$ (for $\vec y\ne\vec 0$).

concepts: Vector triple product identities
questions.paragraph: If $\vec x\times\vec y=\vec a$ ......(i), $\vec y\times\vec z=\vec b$ ......(ii), $\vec x\cdot\vec b=r$ ......(iii), $\vec x\cdot\vec y=1$ ......(iv) and $\vec y\cdot\vec z=1$ ......(v), where $\vec a,\vec b$ are non-zero non-collinear vectors, then.
questions.question: Vector $\vec y$ is:
questions.key_idea: $(\vec x\times\vec y)\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z]\vec y$ and $[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z]=\vec x\cdot\vec b=r$.
solution: From (i) and (ii): $(\vec x\times\vec y)\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=\vec a\times\vec b$.
Use $(\vec p\times\vec q)\times(\vec r\times\vec s)=[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec s]\vec r-[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]\vec s$ with $\vec p=\vec x,\ \vec q=\vec y,\ \vec r=\vec y,\ \vec s=\vec z$.
$=[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z]\vec y-[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec y]\vec z=[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z]\vec y$.
$[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z]=\vec x\cdot(\vec y\times\vec z)=\vec x\cdot\vec b=r$ by (ii), (iii).
So $r\,\vec y=\vec a\times\vec b$ and $\vec y=\frac{\vec a\times\vec b}{r}$: option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand $(\vec x\times\vec y)\times\vec w$ with $\vec w=\vec y\times\vec z$ by the rule $(\vec u\times\vec v)\times\vec w=\vec v(\vec u\cdot\vec w)-\vec u(\vec v\cdot\vec w)$.
solution: $\vec a\times\vec b=(\vec x\times\vec y)\times\vec b$ with $\vec b=\vec y\times\vec z$.
$(\vec x\times\vec y)\times\vec b=\vec y(\vec x\cdot\vec b)-\vec x(\vec y\cdot\vec b)$.
$\vec y\cdot\vec b=\vec y\cdot(\vec y\times\vec z)=0$ and $\vec x\cdot\vec b=r$ by (iii).
So $\vec a\times\vec b=r\,\vec y$, giving $\vec y=\frac{\vec a\times\vec b}{r}$ (option A).

useful_results: If $\vec y$ appears in two cross products $\vec x\times\vec y=\vec a$ and $\vec y\times\vec z=\vec b$, then $\vec y\parallel\vec a\times\vec b$.
$(\vec x\times\vec y)\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z]\,\vec y$ (the product of two cross products sharing $\vec y$ is a multiple of $\vec y$).
$[\vec x\ \vec y\ \vec z]$ can be read as $\vec x\cdot\vec b$ or $\vec a\cdot\vec z$.

concepts: Vector triple product identities
Solving simultaneous vector equations
questions.paragraph: If $\vec x\times\vec y=\vec a$ ......(i), $\vec y\times\vec z=\vec b$ ......(ii), $\vec x\cdot\vec b=r$ ......(iii), $\vec x\cdot\vec y=1$ ......(iv) and $\vec y\cdot\vec z=1$ ......(v), where $\vec a,\vec b$ are non-zero non-collinear vectors, then.
questions.question: $\vec z$ is:
options: $\frac{r}{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}\left[\vec a+\vec b+(\vec a\times\vec b)\right]$
$\frac{r}{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}\left[\vec a+\vec b-\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\right]$
$\frac{r}{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}\left[\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\right]$
questions.key_idea: Cross (ii) with $\vec y$ from the left: $\vec y\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=\vec y-|\vec y|^2\vec z$ (using (v)), which equals $\vec y\times\vec b$.
solution: From (i), (ii): $\vec y=\frac{\vec a\times\vec b}{r}$ and $|\vec y|^2=\frac{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}{r^2}$.
Cross (ii) with $\vec y$ from the left: $\vec y\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=\vec y\times\vec b$.
Left side: $\vec y\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=\vec y(\vec y\cdot\vec z)-\vec z(\vec y\cdot\vec y)=\vec y-|\vec y|^2\vec z$ (using (v)).
Right side: $\vec y\times\vec b=\frac{(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec b}{r}=-\frac{\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec b)}{r}$.
So $|\vec y|^2\vec z=\vec y+\frac{\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec b)}{r}=\frac{(\vec a\times\vec b)+\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec b)}{r}$.

$\vec z=\frac{r^2}{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}\cdot\frac{(\vec a\times\vec b)+\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec b)}{r}=\frac{r}{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}\left[\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\right]$: option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Check each option on the explicit instance $\vec a=\hat i$, $\vec b=\hat j$, $r=1$, where the system is solved by inspection.
solution: As in the previous part, $\vec y=\hat k$ and $\vec x=\hat j+\hat k$.
$\vec y\times\vec z=\hat j$ and $\vec y\cdot\vec z=1$ with $\vec y=\hat k$: $\vec z=\hat k+\hat i$ (check: $\hat k\times(\hat k+\hat i)=\hat j$ and $\hat k\cdot(\hat k+\hat i)=1$).

Option (C): $\frac{1}{1}\left[\hat k+\hat j\times\hat k\right]=\hat k+\hat i$ ✓; option (A) gives $\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$ and option (B) gives $\hat i+\hat j+\hat j$ (as $\hat i\times\hat k=-\hat j$): both wrong.
So (C) is the correct vector $\vec z$.

useful_results: $\vec y\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=\vec y(\vec y\cdot\vec z)-|\vec y|^2\vec z$: a vector $\vec z$ is recovered from $\vec y\times\vec z$ and $\vec y\cdot\vec z$.
Given $\vec y\times\vec z=\vec b$ and $\vec y\cdot\vec z=k$: $\vec z=\frac{k\,\vec y+\vec b\times\vec y}{|\vec y|^2}$.
The same device with $\vec x\times\vec y$ gives $\vec x$ in the previous question; the three vectors form the reciprocal-type system built from $\vec a,\vec b,\vec a\times\vec b$.

concepts: Locus of a point: double cone (angle with an axis)
questions.paragraph: A conic section is obtained by the intersection of two inverted cones (having same vertex) with a plane. If a plane passes through the vertex, then its intersection with the cones either represents a pair of straight lines or a point depending upon whether it intersects the cones or not. If plane does not pass through vertex, then section may be hyperbola or circle depending upon whether plane is parallel to axis of the cone or perpendicular to it. If it has any other inclination, then intersection of plane and cone gives an ellipse. If a variable point $P$ moves such that the line passing through $P$ and $Q(0,0,2)$ makes an angle $60^\circ$ with $z$-axis, then
questions.question: The locus of $P$ is:
questions.key_idea: The direction cosine of $\overrightarrow{QP}$ with the $z$-axis satisfies $\cos^2 60^\circ=\frac14$.
solution: $P(x,y,z)$ lies on a line through $Q(0,0,2)$ making $60^\circ$ with the $z$-axis, so $\overrightarrow{QP}=x\hat i+y\hat j+(z-2)\hat k$ has $\cos60^\circ$ with $\hat k$.
$\frac{z-2}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+(z-2)^2}}=\cos60^\circ=\frac12$ (squaring covers both nappes, i.e. the angle $60^\circ$ or $120^\circ$ with the axis).
$x^2+y^2-3(z-2)^2=0$: option (C) (a double cone with vertex $Q$ and semi-vertical angle $60^\circ$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Parametrise the line through $Q$: direction cosines $(l,m,n)$ with $n=\cos60^\circ=\frac12$, and eliminate the parameter.
solution: A point of the line is $P=Q+t(l,m,n)$: $x=tl,\ y=tm,\ z-2=tn$ with $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$ and $n=\frac12$.
Hence $x^2+y^2-3(z-2)^2=0$ (option C).

useful_results: Locus of lines through a fixed point $Q$ making a fixed angle $\alpha$ with a fixed line (axis along $\hat k$): $x^2+y^2=\tan^2\alpha\,(z-z_Q)^2$.
A double cone with vertex $Q$, axis $z$ and semi-vertical angle $\alpha$ has $x^2+y^2=\tan^2\alpha\,(z-z_Q)^2$; here $\tan^2 60^\circ=3$.
Squaring a direction-cosine equation includes both nappes of the cone.

concepts: Section of a cone by a plane through its vertex
questions.paragraph: A conic section is obtained by the intersection of two inverted cones (having same vertex) with a plane. If a plane passes through the vertex, then its intersection with the cones either represents a pair of straight lines or a point depending upon whether it intersects the cones or not. If plane does not pass through vertex, then section may be hyperbola or circle depending upon whether plane is parallel to axis of the cone or perpendicular to it. If it has any other inclination, then intersection of plane and cone gives an ellipse. If a variable point $P$ moves such that the line passing through $P$ and $Q(0,0,2)$ makes an angle $60^\circ$ with $z$-axis, then
questions.question: The locus of intersection of locus of $P$ and the plane $x+y+z=2$ is:
questions.key_idea: The plane passes through the vertex $Q(0,0,2)$, so the section is a pair of lines or a point; substitute $z-2=-(x+y)$ to see which.
solution: The plane $x+y+z=2$ passes through the vertex $Q(0,0,2)$ ($0+0+2=2$).
On the plane $z-2=-(x+y)$. Substitute in the cone $x^2+y^2=3(z-2)^2$: $x^2+y^2=3(x+y)^2$.
$2x^2+6xy+2y^2=0\Rightarrow x^2+3xy+y^2=0$.
Discriminant $9-4=5>0$, so this is a pair of distinct real lines through $Q$.

(Criterion: a plane through the vertex cuts the cone in two lines if the angle between the plane and the axis, $\varphi$ with $\sin\varphi=\frac{|\hat n\cdot\hat k|}{|\hat n|}=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, i.e. $\varphi\approx35.3^\circ$, is less than the semi-vertical angle $60^\circ$.) Hence the locus is a pair of straight lines: option (A).
questions.correction_note: PDF compared the angle alpha with cos(alpha)=1/sqrt3 (angle between the plane's NORMAL and the axis, about 54.7 degrees) with 60 degrees. The criterion needs the angle between the PLANE and the axis (35.3 degrees); both happen to be below 60 degrees, so the answer (A) is right. Verified by direct substitution (x^2+3xy+y^2=0, two real lines).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the angle criterion: a plane through the vertex meets the cone in two lines iff the plane's inclination to the axis is less than the semi-vertical angle.
solution: The normal of $x+y+z=2$ is $(1,1,1)$, making an angle $\beta$ with the axis $\hat k$ where $\cos\beta=\frac1{\sqrt3}$ ($\beta\approx54.7^\circ$).
The plane itself therefore makes the angle $\varphi=90^\circ-\beta\approx35.3^\circ$ with the axis.
The semi-vertical angle of the cone is $60^\circ$ and $\varphi<60^\circ$, so the plane (through the vertex) cuts both nappes in two real lines.
Hence the locus is a pair of straight lines.

useful_results: A plane through the vertex of a double cone: pair of distinct lines if (angle of the plane with the axis) < semi-vertical angle; a single line if equal; the vertex only if it is greater.

If the plane does not pass through the vertex: ellipse (plane meets the axis at an angle greater than the semi-vertical angle, meeting one nappe), parabola (parallel to a generator), hyperbola (smaller angle, meeting both nappes).
Direct check: substitute the plane into the cone's equation and test the discriminant of the resulting homogeneous quadratic.

concepts: Section of a cone by a plane parallel to its axis: hyperbola
questions.paragraph: A conic section is obtained by the intersection of two inverted cones (having same vertex) with a plane. If a plane passes through the vertex, then its intersection with the cones either represents a pair of straight lines or a point depending upon whether it intersects the cones or not. If plane does not pass through vertex, then section may be hyperbola or circle depending upon whether plane is parallel to axis of the cone or perpendicular to it. If it has any other inclination, then intersection of plane and cone gives an ellipse. If a variable point $P$ moves such that the line passing through $P$ and $Q(0,0,2)$ makes an angle $60^\circ$ with $z$-axis, then
questions.question: The locus of intersection of locus of $P$ with $x+y=2$ is:
questions.key_idea: The plane $x+y=2$ is parallel to the $z$-axis and misses the vertex, so the section is a hyperbola.
solution: The plane $x+y=2$ is parallel to the axis ($z$-axis) of the cone, and it does not pass through the vertex $(0,0,2)$.
A plane parallel to the axis (not through the vertex) cuts both nappes in a hyperbola.
$3(z-2)^2-2(x-1)^2=2$ is a hyperbola: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the general rule instead of substitution: the plane makes angle $0^\circ$ with the axis, smaller than the semi-vertical angle $60^\circ$, and misses the vertex.
solution: The normal of $x+y=2$ is $(1,1,0)\perp\hat k$, so the plane is parallel to the axis (inclination $0^\circ$).
Inclination to the axis ($0^\circ$) is less than the semi-vertical angle ($60^\circ$), so the plane cuts both nappes.
The plane does not contain the vertex ($0+0\ne2$), so the section is a non-degenerate conic with two branches: a hyperbola.

useful_results: A plane parallel to the axis of a double cone (and not through the vertex) cuts it in a hyperbola; perpendicular to the axis: a circle.
Perpendicular distance from the vertex to the plane tells whether the plane passes through the vertex ($0$ gives a degenerate section).
Substituting a plane into the cone's equation and completing squares identifies the conic from the sign of the squared terms.

concepts: Vector triple product and magnitude relations
questions.question: Three vectors $\vec\alpha,\vec\beta,\vec\gamma$ having magnitude $2,3$ and $5^{1/3}$ respectively satisfying $\vec\gamma\times\left((\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)\times\vec\gamma\right)=\vec\beta$, then $\sin(\vec\alpha\wedge\vec\gamma)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $\vec\gamma\perp(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)\times\vec\gamma$ and $\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma\perp\vec\gamma$, so magnitudes multiply without angles.
solution: $|\vec\alpha|=2$, $|\vec\beta|=3$, $|\vec\gamma|=5^{1/3}$.

$\vec\gamma\times\left((\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)\times\vec\gamma\right)=\vec\beta$: the vector $(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)\times\vec\gamma$ is perpendicular to $\vec\gamma$, so taking magnitudes gives $5^{1/3}\left|(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)\times\vec\gamma\right|=3$.
$(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)\perp\vec\gamma$, so $\left|(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)\times\vec\gamma\right|=|\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma|\cdot5^{1/3}$.
Hence $|\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma|\cdot5^{2/3}=3$.
$|\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma|=2\cdot5^{1/3}\sin(\vec\alpha\wedge\vec\gamma)$, so $2\cdot5^{1/3}\cdot5^{2/3}\sin(\vec\alpha\wedge\vec\gamma)=3$.
$10\sin(\vec\alpha\wedge\vec\gamma)=3\Rightarrow\sin(\vec\alpha\wedge\vec\gamma)=\frac{3}{10}=0.30$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand the triple product: $(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)\times\vec\gamma=\vec\gamma(\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\gamma)-\vec\alpha|\vec\gamma|^2$, so $\vec\beta=|\vec\gamma|^2(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)$.
solution: $(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)\times\vec\gamma=\vec\gamma(\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\gamma)-\vec\alpha(\vec\gamma\cdot\vec\gamma)$.
$\vec\gamma\times\left[\vec\gamma(\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\gamma)-\vec\alpha|\vec\gamma|^2\right]=-|\vec\gamma|^2(\vec\gamma\times\vec\alpha)=|\vec\gamma|^2(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)$.
So $\vec\beta=|\vec\gamma|^2(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)$ and $|\vec\beta|=|\vec\gamma|^3|\vec\alpha|\sin\theta=5\cdot2\sin\theta$.
$3=10\sin\theta\Rightarrow\sin\theta=0.30$.

useful_results: $\vec\gamma\times\left((\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)\times\vec\gamma\right)=|\vec\gamma|^2(\vec\alpha\times\vec\gamma)$: two cross products with the same vector $\vec\gamma$ act as multiplication by $|\vec\gamma|^2$ on the part of $\vec\alpha$ perpendicular to $\vec\gamma$ (and a rotation by $90^\circ$ in each step).
$|\vec u\times\vec v|=|\vec u||\vec v|$ when $\vec u\perp\vec v$.
$\vec u\times(\vec u\times\vec w)=\vec u(\vec u\cdot\vec w)-\vec w|\vec u|^2=-|\vec u|^2\vec w_\perp$: repeated crossing rotates by $90^\circ$ and scales by $|\vec u|$ each time.

concepts: Plane through a line and a point
Intercepts and volume of a tetrahedron OABC
questions.question: Let $P$ be a plane containing the line $z=2,\ x=-y$ and passing through a point $M(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ where $\alpha>0,\beta>0,\gamma>0$. The distance of $M$ from $yz$ plane, $zx$ plane and $xy$ plane are $1,2$ and $3$ respectively. Plane $P$ meets co-ordinate axes at points $A,B$ and $C$ respectively. Find the volume of tetrahedron $OABC$ ($O$ is the origin).
questions.key_idea: $M=(1,2,3)$; the plane contains the line direction $(1,-1,0)$ and the vector from a point of the line to $M$.
solution: The distances from $yz,zx,xy$ planes are $\alpha=1$, $\beta=2$, $\gamma=3$, so $M=(1,2,3)$.
The line $z=2,\ x=-y$ is $\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-2}{0}$: it passes through $(1,-1,2)$ with direction $(1,-1,0)$.
Direction of the join of $(1,-1,2)$ and $M$: $(0,3,1)$ (the PDF uses $(0,-3,-1)$).
Plane through $M(1,2,3)$: $-(x-1)-(y-2)+3(z-3)=0\Rightarrow-x-y+3z-6=0\Rightarrow x+y-3z=-6$.
Volume $=\frac16|[\overrightarrow{OA}\ \overrightarrow{OB}\ \overrightarrow{OC}]|=\frac16\left|\begin{matrix}-6&0&0\\0&-6&0\\0&0&2\end{matrix}\right|=\frac16\times6\times6\times2=12$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the intercept form $\frac xa+\frac yb+\frac zc=1$ and make it contain the line.
solution: The line $z=2,\ x+y=0$ lies in the plane iff for $z=2$ the equation $\frac xa+\frac yb=1-\frac2c$ is the same as $x+y=0$.
That needs $1-\frac2c=0$, i.e. $c=2$, and $\frac1a=\frac1b$, i.e. $a=b$.
$M(1,2,3)$ on the plane: $\frac1a+\frac2a+\frac32=1\Rightarrow\frac3a=-\frac12\Rightarrow a=b=-6$.
Volume $=\frac16|abc|=\frac16\cdot36\cdot2=12$.

useful_results: A plane with intercepts $a,b,c$ ($\frac xa+\frac yb+\frac zc=1$) cuts off a tetrahedron of volume $\frac16|abc|$.
The plane through a line (point $P_0$, direction $\vec d$) and a point $M$ has normal $\vec d\times\overrightarrow{P_0M}$.
A line $z=c_0,\ x+y=0$ lies in $\frac xa+\frac yb+\frac zc=1$ iff $c=c_0$ and $a=b$: use this to avoid computing a cross product.

concepts: Distance of a point from a line measured parallel to a plane and from a plane measured along a line
questions.question: Let $\pi:\ x+y-z-4=0$ be the equation of a plane and $A$ be the point with position vector $\hat i+2\hat j-3\hat k$. $L$ is a line which passes through the point $(1,2,3)$ with direction ratios $3,-1$ and $4$. If the distance of the point $A$ from the line $L$ measured parallel to the plane $\pi$ is $d_1$ and the distance of the point $A$ from the plane $\pi$ measured parallel to the line $L$ is $d_2$, then find the value of $\sqrt{d_1^2-d_2^2}$.
questions.key_idea: For $d_1$ find the point $P$ of $L$ with $\overrightarrow{AP}\parallel\pi$; for $d_2$ move from $A$ along the direction of $L$ until the plane is met.
solution: Plane $\pi$ has normal $\vec n=(1,1,-1)$. $A=(1,2,-3)$; line $L:\frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{4}=\lambda$.
A point of $L$: $P(3\lambda+1,\ -\lambda+2,\ 4\lambda+3)$. Direction ratios of $\overrightarrow{AP}$: $(3\lambda,\ -\lambda,\ 4\lambda+6)$.
$\overrightarrow{AP}$ is parallel to $\pi$: $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\vec n=0\Rightarrow3\lambda-\lambda-(4\lambda+6)=0\Rightarrow-2\lambda-6=0\Rightarrow\lambda=-3$.
$d_1=AP=\sqrt{9\lambda^2+\lambda^2+(4\lambda+6)^2}=\sqrt{81+9+36}=\sqrt{126}$.
Line through $A$ parallel to $L$: $x=3\lambda+1,\ y=2-\lambda,\ z=4\lambda-3$. It meets $\pi$ where $(3\lambda+1)+(2-\lambda)-(4\lambda-3)-4=0$.
$\Rightarrow-2\lambda+2=0\Rightarrow\lambda=1$ (the PDF reaches $\lambda=1$ through $2\lambda-4\lambda+6=4$).
$d_2=\sqrt{(3\lambda)^2+(-\lambda)^2+(4\lambda)^2}=\sqrt{26\lambda^2}=\sqrt{26}$.
questions.correction_note: PDF line '3 lambda + 1 - lambda + 2 + 2 - (4 lambda - 3) = 4' is mis-transcribed (taken literally it gives lambda = 2); the correct equation of the intersection with the plane is (3 lambda+1) + (2 - lambda) - (4 lambda - 3) - 4 = 0, i.e. -2 lambda + 2 = 0, lambda = 1, which is what the PDF's following lines use. d2 = sqrt26 and the answer 10 are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Intersect $L$ with the plane through $A$ parallel to $\pi$ for $d_1$, and divide the perpendicular distance of $A$ from $\pi$ by the cosine of the angle between $L$ and the normal for $d_2$.
solution: The plane through $A$ parallel to $\pi$ is $x+y-z=1+2+3=6$. $L$ meets it where $(3\lambda+1)+(2-\lambda)-(4\lambda+3)=6\Rightarrow-2\lambda=6$, so $\lambda=-3$ and $P=(-8,5,-9)$.
Both $A$ and $P$ lie in that plane, so $AP$ is parallel to $\pi$: $d_1^2=|AP|^2=81+9+36=126$.
The distance of $A$ from $\pi$ is $\frac{|1+2+3-4|}{\sqrt3}=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$, and $\cos\varphi=\frac{|\vec d\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{26}\sqrt3}$ between $L$ and the normal.

useful_results: Distance of $A$ from a line $L$ measured parallel to a plane: intersect $L$ with the plane through $A$ parallel to the given plane.
Distance of $A$ from a plane measured along a direction $\vec d$: $\frac{\text{perpendicular distance}}{|\cos\varphi|}=\frac{|\vec n\cdot A-p|\,|\vec d|}{|\vec n\cdot\vec d|}$.
Both are 'oblique distances': set up the line through $A$ in the required direction, then find the intersection parameter.

concepts: Circles bisecting circumference and AM-GM
Plane through the line of intersection of two planes
questions.question: If the circle $x^2+y^2+4x+22y+a=0$ bisects the circumference of the circle $x^2+y^2-2x+8y-b=0$ (where $a,b>0$), then the maximum value of $(ab)$ is $\lambda$. The plane denoted by $\Pi_1:\ 4x+7y+4z+81=0$ is rotated through a right angle about its line of intersection with the plane $\Pi_2:\ 5x+3y+10z=\sqrt\lambda$. If the plane in its new position be denoted by $\Pi$, and the distance of this plane from the origin is $\sqrt k$ where $k\in N$, then find $k$.
questions.key_idea: The common chord passes through the centre $(1,-4)$ giving $a+b=50$; then AM-GM gives $ab\le625$; the rotated plane is $\Pi_1+\mu\Pi_2$ with $\mu$ fixed by perpendicularity to $\Pi_1$.
solution: The common chord $S_1-S_2=0$ is $6x+14y+a+b=0$ and must pass through the centre $(1,-4)$ of the second circle: $6-56+a+b=0\Rightarrow a+b=50$.
By AM-GM, $\frac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab}$, so $ab\le25^2=625$; the maximum is $\lambda=625$ and $\sqrt\lambda=25$.
$\Pi_2:\ 5x+3y+10z-25=0$. A plane through the line of intersection: $(4x+7y+4z+81)+\mu(5x+3y+10z-25)=0$, i.e. $(5\mu+4)x+(3\mu+7)y+(10\mu+4)z+81-25\mu=0$.
Perpendicular to $\Pi_1$: $4(5\mu+4)+7(3\mu+7)+4(10\mu+4)=0\Rightarrow81\mu+81=0\Rightarrow\mu=-1$.
New plane: $-x+4y-6z+106=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the new plane from its normal: perpendicular to $\Pi_1$ and containing the line, so its normal is $\vec n_1\times\vec d$ with $\vec d=\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$ the line direction.
solution: $\vec n_1=(4,7,4)$, $\vec n_2=(5,3,10)$, line direction $\vec d=\vec n_1\times\vec n_2=(58,-20,-23)$.
Normal of the rotated plane: $\vec n_1\times\vec d=(-81,324,-486)=-81(1,-4,6)$.
A point on the line (set $z=0$): $4x+7y=-81$, $5x+3y=25\Rightarrow y=-\frac{505}{23},\ x=\frac{418}{23}$.
Plane: $x-4y+6z=\frac{418+2020}{23}=106$; distance from origin $=\frac{106}{\sqrt{53}}=\sqrt{212}$, so $k=212$.

useful_results: Any plane through the line of intersection of $P_1=0$ and $P_2=0$ is $P_1+\mu P_2=0$; imposing perpendicularity to $P_1$ is one linear equation in $\mu$.
The plane through a line perpendicular to a given plane has normal $\vec n_1\times\vec d$ ($\vec d$ = direction of the line).
AM-GM: $a+b=S$ with $a,b>0$ gives $ab\le\frac{S^2}{4}$.

concepts: Vector triple product of mutually perpendicular vectors
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$ are mutually perpendicular vectors such that $|\vec a|=\sqrt6$, $|\vec b|=\sqrt2$, $|\vec c|=\sqrt3$ and a vector $\vec v=(\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b))\times\vec c+(\vec b\times(\vec b\times\vec c))\times\vec a+(\vec c\times(\vec c\times\vec a))\times\vec b$ where magnitude of $\vec v$ is $M$ then $\frac{M^2}{100}$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: For perpendicular $\vec a,\vec b$: $\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=-|\vec a|^2\vec b$, so each term becomes a multiple of a cross product of two of the vectors, and those cross products are mutually perpendicular.
solution: $(\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b))\times\vec c=\left(\left(\vec a\cdot\vec b\right)\vec a-(\vec a\cdot\vec a)\vec b\right)\times\vec c=-|\vec a|^2\,\vec b\times\vec c=-6(\vec b\times\vec c)$.
Similarly $(\vec b\times(\vec b\times\vec c))\times\vec a=-|\vec b|^2\,\vec c\times\vec a=-2(\vec c\times\vec a)$.
And $(\vec c\times(\vec c\times\vec a))\times\vec b=-|\vec c|^2\,\vec a\times\vec b=-3(\vec a\times\vec b)$.
$\vec v=-\left[3(\vec a\times\vec b)+6(\vec b\times\vec c)+2(\vec c\times\vec a)\right]$.
Since $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are mutually perpendicular, $\vec a\times\vec b,\ \vec b\times\vec c,\ \vec c\times\vec a$ are also mutually perpendicular (parallel to $\vec c,\vec a,\vec b$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Choose axes along $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ and compute $\vec v$ in components.
solution: Take $\vec a=(\sqrt6,0,0)$, $\vec b=(0,\sqrt2,0)$, $\vec c=(0,0,\sqrt3)$.
$\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=-6\vec b=(0,-6\sqrt2,0)$, and crossing with $\vec c$ gives $(-6\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt3,0,0)=(-6\sqrt6,0,0)$.
$\vec b\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=-2\vec c$, crossing with $\vec a$: $(0,-2\sqrt3\sqrt6,0)=(0,-6\sqrt2,0)$.
$\vec c\times(\vec c\times\vec a)=-3\vec a$, crossing with $\vec b$: $(0,0,-3\sqrt6\sqrt2)=(0,0,-6\sqrt3)$.

useful_results: $\vec a\times(\vec a\times\vec b)=-|\vec a|^2\vec b$ when $\vec a\perp\vec b$ (in general $\vec a(\vec a\cdot\vec b)-|\vec a|^2\vec b$).

For mutually perpendicular $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$: $\vec a\times\vec b=\pm|\vec a||\vec b|\hat c$ etc., so $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2$ and the three cross products are mutually perpendicular.
If $\vec v=\sum\lambda_i\vec e_i$ with $\vec e_i$ mutually perpendicular then $|\vec v|^2=\sum\lambda_i^2|\vec e_i|^2$.

concepts: Image of a point in a line
Median of a triangle
questions.question: Consider a line passing through the point $P(3,4,5)$ & having direction ratios $(2,-2,1)$. If image of point $Q(1,-1,8)$ w.r.t. given line is $Q'$, then length of median of $\triangle PQQ'$ through vertex $P$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: $\triangle PQQ'$ is isosceles with $PQ=PQ'$, and the median from $P$ is the projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ on the line.
solution: The image $Q'$ is the reflection of $Q$ in the line, so with $M$ the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ (the mid-point of $QQ'$), $PQ=PQ'$ and the median through $P$ is $PM$.
$\overrightarrow{PQ}=(1-3,\,-1-4,\,8-5)=(-2,-5,3)$ (the PDF writes $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(2,5,-3)$, i.e. $\overrightarrow{QP}$; the length is unaffected).
$PM$ is the projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ on the direction $(2,-2,1)$, of unit vector $\frac13(2,-2,1)$.
The required length of the median is $3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use Pythagoras in the right triangle $PMQ$: $PM^2=PQ^2-QM^2$, where $QM$ is the distance of $Q$ from the line.
solution: The distance of $Q$ from the line: $QM=\frac{|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times(2,-2,1)|}{|(2,-2,1)|}=\frac{|(1,8,14)|}{3}=\frac{\sqrt{261}}{3}=\sqrt{29}$.
$PM^2=38-29=9\Rightarrow PM=3$.

useful_results: The median of the isosceles triangle $PQQ'$ from the apex $P$ is also the altitude: $PM\perp QQ'$ and $M$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ to the line.

Length of the projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ on a line with direction $\vec d$: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$; distance of $Q$ from the line: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$ (they satisfy $PQ^2=\text{proj}^2+\text{dist}^2$).
The image $Q'=2M-Q$ is not needed here.

concepts: Perpendicular lines in 3D with parameters
Cosine rule and AM-GM
questions.question: If lines $bx=1-cy,\ bz=1$ and $bx=2+ay,\ bz=3+cy$ are perpendicular, where $a,b,c$ are sides of $\triangle ABC$, then minimum value of $\cos B$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: Perpendicularity gives $b^2=ac$; then $\cos B=\frac{a^2+c^2-ac}{2ac}\ge\frac12$.
solution: Line 1: $x=\frac1b-\frac cby,\ z=\frac1b$, i.e. $\frac{x-\frac1b}{c}=\frac{y-\frac1b}{-b}=\frac{z-\frac1b}{0}$ (direction $(c,-b,0)$).
Line 2: $\frac{x-\frac2a}{a}=\frac{y-\frac1b}{b}=\frac{z-\frac3c}{c}$ (as in the PDF; direction $(a,b,c)$).
The lines are perpendicular: $ac-b^2+0=0\Rightarrow b^2=ac$.
$\cos B=\frac{a^2+c^2-b^2}{2ac}=\frac{a^2+c^2-ac}{2ac}=\frac12\left(\frac ac+\frac ca\right)-\frac12$.
Since $\frac ac+\frac ca\ge2$ (for $a,c>0$), $\cos B\ge\frac12(2)-\frac12=\frac12$.
Equality holds when $a=c$ (then $b=a$: an equilateral triangle), so the minimum value of $\cos B$ is $\frac12=0.5$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complete the square in the numerator: $a^2+c^2-ac=(a-c)^2+ac$.
solution: From $b^2=ac$: $\cos B=\frac{a^2+c^2-ac}{2ac}$.
$a^2+c^2-ac=(a-c)^2+ac$, so $\cos B=\frac12+\frac{(a-c)^2}{2ac}$.
The second term is $\ge0$ and is $0$ iff $a=c$; hence the minimum of $\cos B$ is $\frac12$ (equilateral triangle).

useful_results: Direction ratios of $bx+cy=1,\ z=\frac1b$ (a line in the plane $z=\frac1b$): $(c,-b,0)$; direction of $\frac{x-x_0}{a}=\frac{y-y_0}{b}=\frac{z-z_0}{c}$ is $(a,b,c)$.
If $b^2=ac$ (sides in G.P.), $\cos B=\frac12\left(\frac ac+\frac ca\right)-\frac12\ge\frac12$, i.e. $B\le60^\circ$.
Two lines with direction vectors $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ are perpendicular iff $\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2=0$ (whether or not they intersect).

concepts: Vector equation with cross product and projections
questions.question: Let $|\vec a|=4$, $|\vec b|=1$ and $\vec b\times\vec\alpha+\vec a=\vec\alpha$. If projection of $\vec\alpha$ along $\vec b$ is $3$ then projection of $\vec\alpha$ along $\vec a$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: Dot with $\vec b$ gives $\vec a\cdot\vec b=3$; crossing with $\vec b$ and eliminating $\vec b\times\vec\alpha$ solves $\vec\alpha$ completely.
solution: Dot $\vec b\times\vec\alpha+\vec a=\vec\alpha$ with $\vec b$: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec\alpha\cdot\vec b$ (as $\vec b\cdot(\vec b\times\vec\alpha)=0$).
Projection of $\vec\alpha$ on $\vec b$ is $\vec\alpha\cdot\hat b=\vec\alpha\cdot\vec b=3$ ($|\vec b|=1$), so $\vec\alpha\cdot\vec b=\vec a\cdot\vec b=3$.
Cross the relation with $\vec b$ on the left: $\vec b\times(\vec b\times\vec\alpha)+\vec b\times\vec a=\vec b\times\vec\alpha$.
$(\vec b\cdot\vec\alpha)\vec b-|\vec b|^2\vec\alpha+\vec b\times\vec a=\vec b\times\vec\alpha\Rightarrow3\vec b-\vec\alpha+\vec b\times\vec a=\vec b\times\vec\alpha$.
Use $\vec b\times\vec\alpha=\vec\alpha-\vec a$: $3\vec b-\vec\alpha+\vec b\times\vec a=\vec\alpha-\vec a$.
$\Rightarrow2\vec\alpha=3\vec b+\vec a+\vec b\times\vec a\Rightarrow\vec\alpha=\frac12\left(3\vec b+\vec a+\vec b\times\vec a\right)$.
Projection of $\vec\alpha$ along $\vec a$: $\vec\alpha\cdot\hat a=\frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac12\left(3\vec b\cdot\vec a+|\vec a|^2+0\right)=\frac18(9+16)=\frac{25}{8}=3.125$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Fix coordinates with $\vec b=\hat k$ and write $\vec\alpha$ in components.
solution: Take $\vec b=(0,0,1)$ and $\vec a=(a_1,a_2,3)$ with $a_1^2+a_2^2=7$ (since $\vec a\cdot\vec b=3$ and $|\vec a|=4$).
Let $\vec\alpha=(x,y,3)$. Then $\vec b\times\vec\alpha=(-y,x,0)$ and the relation reads $(x+y,\ y-x,\ 3)=(a_1,a_2,3)$.
So $x=\frac{a_1-a_2}{2}$, $y=\frac{a_1+a_2}{2}$ and $\vec\alpha\cdot\vec a=xa_1+ya_2+9=\frac{a_1^2+a_2^2}{2}+9=\frac72+9=\frac{25}{2}$.
Projection along $\vec a$: $\frac{25/2}{4}=\frac{25}{8}=3.125$.

useful_results: For a unit vector $\vec b$: $\vec b\times(\vec b\times\vec\alpha)=(\vec b\cdot\vec\alpha)\vec b-\vec\alpha$; crossing an equation with $\vec b$ turns $\vec b\times\vec\alpha$ terms into $\vec\alpha$ terms.
$\vec\alpha-\vec b\times\vec\alpha=\vec a$ has the solution $\vec\alpha=\frac12\left(\vec a+\vec b\times\vec a+(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec b\right)$ for a unit $\vec b$ (here $\vec a\cdot\vec b=3$).
Projection of $\vec u$ along $\vec v$ is $\frac{\vec u\cdot\vec v}{|\vec v|}$; the PDF key $3.12$ is $3.125$ truncated to two decimals.

concepts: Dot product in triangles with a mid-point
questions.question: If $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle AEF$ are such that $EB=BF$ ($B$ the mid-point of $EF$), $AB=EF=1$, $BC=6$, $AC=\sqrt{33}$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AE}+\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AF}=2$, then the value of $\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\overrightarrow{BF}$ is (given figure).
questions.key_idea: $B$ is the mid-point of $EF$, so $\overrightarrow{AE}+\overrightarrow{AF}=2\overrightarrow{AB}$; with $\overrightarrow{AC}=\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}$ the given condition becomes $\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AF}=0$.
solution: The PDF's figure is missing; assume $E,B,F$ are collinear with $B$ the mid-point of $EF$, so $\overrightarrow{AE}+\overrightarrow{AF}=2\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $|\overrightarrow{BF}|=\frac12$.

$\overrightarrow{AC}=\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}$, so $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AE}+\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AF}=\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\overrightarrow{AE}+\overrightarrow{AF})+\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AF}$.
$=2|\overrightarrow{AB}|^2+\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AF}=2+\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AF}$.
The given value $2$ gives $\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AF}=0$.

$\overrightarrow{BF}=\overrightarrow{AF}-\overrightarrow{AB}$, so $\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\overrightarrow{BF}=0-\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=-\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}$.
$AC^2=|\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}|^2=1+36+2\,\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=33\Rightarrow\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=-2$.
Hence $\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\overrightarrow{BF}=2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand with $\overrightarrow{BF}=\vec u$, $\overrightarrow{BE}=-\vec u$ without combining terms in advance.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AE}=\overrightarrow{AB}-\vec u$ and $\overrightarrow{AF}=\overrightarrow{AB}+\vec u$ with $|\vec u|=\frac12$.

$\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AE}=1-\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\vec u$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\overrightarrow{AF}=(\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC})\cdot(\overrightarrow{AB}+\vec u)=1+\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\vec u+\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}+\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\vec u$.

Sum $=2+\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}+\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\vec u=2\Rightarrow\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\vec u=-\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=2$ (using $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=-2$ from $AC^2=33$).
So $\overrightarrow{BC}\cdot\overrightarrow{BF}=2$.

useful_results: If $B$ is the mid-point of $EF$ then $\overrightarrow{AE}+\overrightarrow{AF}=2\overrightarrow{AB}$ for every point $A$.
$\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=\frac{AC^2-AB^2-BC^2}{2}$ (cosine rule in vector form).
Splitting $\overrightarrow{AC}=\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC}$ often turns a sum of dot products into one involving a single unknown dot product.

concepts: Tetrahedron with mutually perpendicular edges: altitude from the right-angle vertex
questions.question: In a tetrahedron $LMNO$ edges $ML$, $MN$ and $MO$ are mutually perpendicular and length of altitudes drawn from $O,L$ and $N$ to opposite faces are $1,2$ and $3$ units, then length of altitude drawn from $M$ to face $LNO$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: $ML,MN,MO$ are the altitudes from $L,N,O$: with $M$ as the origin the face $LNO$ has intercepts $2,3,1$.
solution: Take $M$ as the origin and $ML,MN,MO$ along the axes. The altitude from $O$ to face $LMN$ is $MO=1$; from $L$ to face $MNO$ is $ML=2$; from $N$ to face $MLO$ is $MN=3$.

So $L=(2,0,0)$, $N=(0,3,0)$, $O=(0,0,1)$ and the face $LNO$ is $\frac x2+\frac y3+z=1$ (the PDF writes it with the intercepts in another order, $x+\frac y2+\frac z3=1$, which gives the same distance).
The altitude from $M$ is the distance of the origin from this plane: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac14+\frac19+1}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{49}{36}}}=\frac67$.
$\frac67=0.857\ldots$ (the paper's key prints $0.85$, the value truncated to two decimals; rounded it would be $0.86$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Volume method: $V=\frac13(\text{area of }LNO)\cdot h_M$ and $V=\frac16\cdot ML\cdot MN\cdot MO$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{LN}=(-2,3,0)$, $\overrightarrow{LO}=(-2,0,1)$: $\overrightarrow{LN}\times\overrightarrow{LO}=(3,2,6)$, magnitude $7$, so the area of $\triangle LNO$ is $\frac72$.
$1=\frac13\cdot\frac72\cdot h\Rightarrow h=\frac{6}{7}\approx0.857$.

useful_results: For a tetrahedron with mutually perpendicular edges $p,q,r$ at $M$, the altitude from $M$ is $h$ with $\frac1{h^2}=\frac1{p^2}+\frac1{q^2}+\frac1{r^2}$.
Here $\frac1{h^2}=\frac14+\frac19+1=\frac{49}{36}$, so $h=\frac67$.
The altitude from each of $L,N,O$ equals the corresponding perpendicular edge from $M$.

concepts: Determinant of dot products of vectors and area of a triangle
questions.question: If $\vec a_1=a\hat i+b\hat j$, $\vec a_2=\vec a_1-(2\hat i+\sqrt5\hat j)$ and $\vec a_3=\vec a_1+(2\hat i-\sqrt5\hat j)$, then $\left|\begin{matrix}1+\vec a_1\cdot\vec a_1&1+\vec a_1\cdot\vec a_2&1+\vec a_1\cdot\vec a_3\\1+\vec a_2\cdot\vec a_1&1+\vec a_2\cdot\vec a_2&1+\vec a_2\cdot\vec a_3\\1+\vec a_3\cdot\vec a_1&1+\vec a_3\cdot\vec a_2&1+\vec a_3\cdot\vec a_3\end{matrix}\right|$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The matrix is $MM^T$ with $M$ the rows $(1,\vec a_i)$, so the determinant is $\left(\det M\right)^2=(2\Delta)^2$ where $\Delta$ is the area of the triangle with vertices $\vec a_1,\vec a_2,\vec a_3$.
solution: Area of the triangle with these vertices: $\Delta=\frac12\left|\begin{matrix}1&a&b\\1&a-2&b-\sqrt5\\1&a+2&b-\sqrt5\end{matrix}\right|$.
The sides are $|\vec a_1-\vec a_2|=\sqrt{4+5}=3$, $|\vec a_1-\vec a_3|=3$, $|\vec a_2-\vec a_3|=4$: an isosceles triangle with base $4$ and height $\sqrt{9-4}=\sqrt5$.
$\Delta=\frac12\cdot4\cdot\sqrt5=2\sqrt5$.
The given determinant equals $\left|\begin{matrix}1&a&b\\1&a-2&b-\sqrt5\\1&a+2&b-\sqrt5\end{matrix}\right|^2=(2\Delta)^2$, because the matrix of entries $1+\vec a_i\cdot\vec a_j$ is $MM^T$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The determinant does not depend on $(a,b)$ (it is a squared area), so take $\vec a_1=\vec 0$ and evaluate the $3\times3$ determinant directly.
solution: $\vec a_2\cdot\vec a_2=9$, $\vec a_3\cdot\vec a_3=9$, $\vec a_2\cdot\vec a_3=-4+5=1$, and every dot product with $\vec a_1$ is $0$.
The matrix is $\left(\begin{matrix}1&1&1\\1&10&2\\1&2&10\end{matrix}\right)$ with determinant $1(100-4)-1(10-2)+1(2-10)=96-8-8=80$.

useful_results: $\det\left(1+\vec a_i\cdot\vec a_j\right)_{3\times3}=\left(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&\vec a_i\end{bmatrix}\right)^2=(2\,\text{Area})^2=4\Delta^2$ for points in a plane.
The area of a triangle with vertices $(x_i,y_i)$ is $\frac12\left|\det\begin{bmatrix}1&x_i&y_i\end{bmatrix}\right|$; a matrix of the form $MM^T$ has determinant $(\det M)^2$.
A translation-invariant quantity can be evaluated by moving one vertex to the origin.

concepts: Volume of a tetrahedron by the Gram determinant
questions.question: The volume of a tetrahedron $OABC$ formed by the vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}=\vec a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\vec b$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\vec c$ where $|\vec a|=3$, $|\vec b|=4$, $|\vec c|=6$, angle between the vector pairs $\{\vec a,\vec b\}$; $\{\vec b,\vec c\}$ and $\{\vec c,\vec a\}$ be $\frac\pi3$, $\cos^{-1}\frac14$ and $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{-1}{18}\right)$ respectively is $V$. If the value of $V^2$ can be written as $\frac{pq}{r^2}$ where $p,q,r$ are prime numbers then evaluate $\frac{p+q}{r}$.
questions.key_idea: $V=\frac16\sqrt{\det(\text{Gram matrix})}$ with entries $\vec a\cdot\vec b=6$, $\vec b\cdot\vec c=6$, $\vec c\cdot\vec a=-1$.
