solution: $\vec a\cdot\vec a=9$, $\vec b\cdot\vec b=16$, $\vec c\cdot\vec c=36$; $\vec a\cdot\vec b=3\cdot4\cdot\frac12=6$, $\vec b\cdot\vec c=4\cdot6\cdot\frac14=6$, $\vec c\cdot\vec a=6\cdot3\cdot\left(-\frac1{18}\right)=-1$. (The PDF prints the second pair as $\{\vec b,\vec a\}$, a typing slip for $\{\vec b,\vec c\}$.)
$[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=\left|\begin{matrix}9&6&-1\\6&16&6\\-1&6&36\end{matrix}\right|$.
Volume of the tetrahedron $V=\frac16|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]|$, so $V^2=\frac{3476}{36}=\frac{869}{9}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the closed formula $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=a^2b^2c^2\left(1+2\cos\alpha\cos\beta\cos\gamma-\cos^2\alpha-\cos^2\beta-\cos^2\gamma\right)$.
solution: $\cos\alpha=\frac12$, $\cos\beta=\frac14$, $\cos\gamma=-\frac1{18}$ and $a^2b^2c^2=9\cdot16\cdot36=5184$.
$[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=5184\cdot\frac{869}{1296}=3476$, the same as before; $V^2=\frac{3476}{36}=\frac{869}{9}=\frac{11\cdot79}{3^2}$.

useful_results: Gram formula: $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]^2=a^2b^2c^2\left(1+2\cos\alpha\cos\beta\cos\gamma-\cos^2\alpha-\cos^2\beta-\cos^2\gamma\right)$, with $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ the three pairwise angles.
Volume of tetrahedron $OABC=\frac16|[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]|$; $V^2=\frac{\det G}{36}$.
Factor integers into primes before matching a form $\frac{pq}{r^2}$: $869=11\cdot79$.

concepts: Inscribed sphere of a tetrahedron (volume and face areas)
questions.question: A sphere is inscribed in a tetrahedron whose vertices are $A=(6,0,0)$, $B=(0,4,0)$, $C=(0,0,2)$ and $D=(0,0,0)$. If the radius of sphere is $\frac mn$ (where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime), then $(m+n)$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: $V=\frac13 r\,(S_1+S_2+S_3+S_4)$, so $r=\frac{3V}{\text{total surface area}}$.
solution: If $S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4$ are the areas of the four faces, then $\frac13r(S_1+S_2+S_3+S_4)=V$ (the tetrahedron splits into four pyramids of height $r$ with the centre as apex).
Faces: $S_1=\frac12\cdot6\cdot4=12$ ($DAB$), $S_2=\frac12\cdot4\cdot2=4$ ($DBC$), $S_3=\frac12\cdot6\cdot2=6$ ($DAC$).
$\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=(-6,4,0)\times(-6,0,2)=(8,12,24)$, of magnitude $28$, so $S_4=\frac12\cdot28=14$ ($ABC$).
$V=\frac16\cdot6\cdot4\cdot2=8$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The incentre is $(r,r,r)$ (equidistant from the three coordinate planes); make its distance to the slanted face also $r$.
solution: The face $ABC$ is $\frac x6+\frac y4+\frac z2=1$, i.e. $2x+3y+6z=12$.
The incentre $(r,r,r)$ is inside, so the distance to this face is $\frac{12-2r-3r-6r}{\sqrt{4+9+36}}=\frac{12-11r}{7}$.
Setting this equal to $r$: $12-11r=7r\Rightarrow r=\frac{12}{18}=\frac23$.

useful_results: Inradius of a tetrahedron: $r=\frac{3V}{S}$ where $S$ is the total surface area (the 3D analogue of $r=\frac{\Delta}{s}$).
For a right-corner tetrahedron with legs $a,b,c$: $r=\frac{abc}{ab+bc+ca+\sqrt{a^2b^2+b^2c^2+c^2a^2}}$; here $\frac{48}{44+28}=\frac23$.
The incentre of such a tetrahedron is $(r,r,r)$ because it is equidistant from the three coordinate planes.

concepts: Cauchy-Schwarz equality case for vectors
questions.question: If $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ & $x,y,z$ are non-zero real numbers such that $(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z)+\sqrt{(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2)(x^2+y^2+z^2)}=0$, then the value of $\sqrt{\frac{\alpha y}{\beta x}}+\sqrt{\frac{\beta z}{\gamma y}}$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The condition says $\vec p\cdot\vec q=-|\vec p||\vec q|$ with $\vec p=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, $\vec q=(x,y,z)$: the vectors are anti-parallel.
solution: Let $\vec p=\alpha\hat i+\beta\hat j+\gamma\hat k$ and $\vec q=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$.
The given condition is $\vec p\cdot\vec q+|\vec p||\vec q|=0$, i.e. $\vec p\cdot\vec q=-|\vec p||\vec q|$.
$\cos\theta=-1\Rightarrow\theta=\pi$: $\vec p$ and $\vec q$ are anti-parallel.
So $\frac\alpha x=\frac\beta y=\frac\gamma z=k$ (say), i.e. $\alpha=kx,\ \beta=ky,\ \gamma=kz$ (with $k<0$).
$\frac{\alpha y}{\beta x}=\frac{kxy}{kyx}=1$ and $\frac{\beta z}{\gamma y}=\frac{kyz}{kzy}=1$.
$\sqrt1+\sqrt1=2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Square the condition and use Lagrange's identity: the sum of three squares must vanish.
solution: The condition gives $(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z)^2=(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2)(x^2+y^2+z^2)$.
Lagrange's identity: $(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2)(x^2+y^2+z^2)-(\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma z)^2=(\alpha y-\beta x)^2+(\beta z-\gamma y)^2+(\gamma x-\alpha z)^2$.
So $\alpha y=\beta x$, $\beta z=\gamma y$, $\gamma x=\alpha z$.
Hence $\frac{\alpha y}{\beta x}=1$ and $\frac{\beta z}{\gamma y}=1$, and the value is $1+1=2$.

useful_results: $\vec p\cdot\vec q=|\vec p||\vec q|$ iff parallel (same direction); $\vec p\cdot\vec q=-|\vec p||\vec q|$ iff anti-parallel; the corresponding component ratios are all equal.
Lagrange's identity: $(a^2+b^2+c^2)(x^2+y^2+z^2)-(ax+by+cz)^2=(ay-bx)^2+(bz-cy)^2+(cx-az)^2$.
Cauchy-Schwarz equality $\iff\frac ax=\frac by=\frac cz$.

concepts: Projection of a line on a plane
Area of a triangle in 3D
questions.question: Let $L_1$ be the projection line of a line $L:\ \frac{x-1}{4}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac z3$ on the plane $\Pi:\ 3x-4z-2=0$. $P$ and $Q$ are the points on $L_1$ corresponding to $A=(1,-1,0)$ and $B=(5,0,3)$ on the line $L$ which divides $AB$ externally in the ratio $31:5$ then area of $\triangle PQR=\sqrt{\frac pq}$ where $p,q\in N$. Find the least value of $|4p-q|$.
questions.key_idea: $L\parallel\Pi$ (since $(4,1,3)\cdot(3,0,-4)=0$), so $L_1\parallel L$, $PQ=AB$, and every point $R$ of $L$ is at the same distance $\frac15$ from the plane.
solution: Direction of $L$ is $(4,1,3)$ and the normal of $\Pi$ is $(3,0,-4)$: $12+0-12=0$, so $L\parallel\Pi$. Hence the projection $L_1$ is parallel to $L$, and $P,Q$ (the feet of the perpendiculars from $A,B$) satisfy $PQ=AB$.
$R$ is a point on $L$ (it divides $AB$ externally in $31:5$). All points of $L$ are at the same distance from $\Pi$: $AP=\frac{|3(1)-4(0)-2|}{\sqrt{9+16}}=\frac15$.
The foot of the perpendicular from $R$ to $\Pi$ lies on $L_1$, so the distance of $R$ from the line $PQ$ is $\frac15$.
Area of $\triangle PQR=\frac12\cdot PQ\cdot\frac15=\frac12\cdot\sqrt{26}\cdot\frac15=\frac{\sqrt{26}}{10}=\sqrt{\frac{26}{100}}=\sqrt{\frac{13}{50}}$.
$\frac pq=\frac{13}{50}$, i.e. $p=13k,\ q=50k$ for $k\in N$, so $|4p-q|=|52k-50k|=2k$, whose least value is $2$ (for $k=1$).
questions.correction_note: PDF writes the area as (1/2) x sqrt26 x (1/5) sqrt(26/100), which equals 13/50 (not sqrt(13/50)); the factor AP = (1/5) sqrt(26/100) is wrong (AP is the distance 1/5 of A from the plane). With AP = 1/5 the area is sqrt26/10 = sqrt(13/50), which is what the PDF's next line states. Answer 2 unchanged. R's position is irrelevant because L is parallel to the plane.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compute the area with coordinates: find $P$ and $Q$ as feet of perpendiculars and take $R=A$ (any point of $L$ gives the same area).
solution: $P=A-\frac{3\cdot1-4\cdot0-2}{25}(3,0,-4)=\left(\frac{22}{25},-1,\frac{4}{25}\right)$, so $\overrightarrow{AP}=\left(-\frac3{25},0,\frac4{25}\right)$ and $|AP|=\frac15$.
$\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{AB}=(4,1,3)$ (since $L\parallel\Pi$, $PQ$ is a translate of $AB$).
With $R=A$: $\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PA}=(4,1,3)\times\left(\frac3{25},0,-\frac4{25}\right)$ has magnitude $\frac{\sqrt{26}}{5}$.
Area $=\frac12\cdot\frac{\sqrt{26}}5=\frac{\sqrt{26}}{10}=\sqrt{\frac{13}{50}}$, so $p:q=13:50$ and the least $|4p-q|=2$.

useful_results: A line parallel to a plane projects onto a parallel line of the same length; every point of the line is at the same distance from the plane (check $\vec d\cdot\vec n=0$).

The triangle formed by a segment of the line, its projection and a point of the line has area $\frac12(\text{length of the segment})(\text{distance of the line from the plane})$ (a right-angle trapezoid/triangle relation).
For $\sqrt{p/q}$ with unreduced $p,q$, $p=13k,\ q=50k$ are all allowed; then $|4p-q|=2k$ is minimised at $k=1$.

concepts: Counting positive integer solutions of a linear equation
questions.question: Number of points having positive integral co-ordinate lying on the plane $x+2y+3z=15$ is $n$, then $\frac n2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Fix $z$ and count the positive solutions of $x+2y=15-3z$.
solution: $z\ge5$ gives $x+2y\le0$: impossible.

alternate_solutions.idea: Shift to non-negative variables and count partitions: positive solutions of $x+2y+3z=15$ correspond to partitions of $9$ into parts $1,2,3$.
solution: The number of non-negative solutions of $x'+2y'+3z'=9$ equals the number of partitions of $9$ into parts of size at most $3$ ($z'$ threes, $y'$ twos, $x'$ ones).
$n=12$, $\frac n2=6$ (also the coefficient of $t^9$ in $\frac{1}{(1-t)(1-t^2)(1-t^3)}$ is $12$).

useful_results: The number of non-negative solutions of $x_1+2x_2+3x_3=m$ is the number of partitions of $m$ into parts $\le3$, the coefficient of $t^m$ in $\frac1{(1-t)(1-t^2)(1-t^3)}$ (nearest integer to $\frac{(m+3)^2}{12}$).
For positive-integer solutions first subtract the minimum: $x'+2y'+3z'=15-6=9$.
For $m=9$: $\left(\frac{12^2}{12}\right)=12$, matching the count.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines in a cuboid
questions.question: Let $OA,OB,OC$ be coterminous edges of a cuboid. If $l,m,n$ be the shortest distances between the sides $OA,OB,OC$ and their respective skew body diagonals to them, respectively, then find $\frac{\left(\frac1{l^2}+\frac1{m^2}+\frac1{n^2}\right)}{\left(\frac1{OA^2}+\frac1{OB^2}+\frac1{OC^2}\right)}$.
questions.key_idea: For the edge $OA$ (the $x$-axis) and a skew body diagonal, the distance is $\frac{bc}{\sqrt{b^2+c^2}}$, so $\frac1{l^2}=\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}$.
solution: Let the cuboid have $O=(0,0,0)$, $A=(a,0,0)$, $B=(0,b,0)$, $C=(0,0,c)$. The body diagonals skew to $OA$ are $(0,b,0)\to(a,0,c)$ and $(0,0,c)\to(a,b,0)$.
Take the diagonal through $(0,b,0)$ with direction $(a,-b,c)$. The common perpendicular to $OA$ is along $\hat i\times(a,-b,c)=(0,-c,-b)$.
Similarly $\frac1{m^2}=\frac1{c^2}+\frac1{a^2}$ and $\frac1{n^2}=\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}$.
$\frac1{l^2}+\frac1{m^2}+\frac1{n^2}=2\left(\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}\right)$.
The required ratio is $\frac{2\left(\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}\right)}{\frac1{a^2}+\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}}=2$ (with $OA=a,\ OB=b,\ OC=c$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Project along the edge: the distance between the line $OA$ and a skew line is the distance, in the plane perpendicular to $OA$, between the point $O$ and the projection of the diagonal.
solution: The edge $OA$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, so project everything on the $yz$-plane: $OA$ becomes the single point $O'=(0,0)$.
The diagonal from $(0,b,0)$ to $(a,0,c)$ projects to the line through $(b,0)$ and $(0,c)$: $\frac yb+\frac zc=1$ in the $yz$-plane.
The distance from the origin to this line is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}}}=l$, so $\frac1{l^2}=\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}$.
Cyclically, the sum is $2\sum\frac1{a^2}$ and the ratio is $2$.

useful_results: The shortest distance between an edge of a rectangular box ($a\times b\times c$) and a skew face/body diagonal not meeting it is $\frac{bc}{\sqrt{b^2+c^2}}$ (product over the other two edges divided by the diagonal of their face); $\frac{1}{l^2}=\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}$.
Distance between a line parallel to an axis and a skew line = distance in the projection along that axis.
Intercept form: the distance from the origin to $\frac yb+\frac zc=1$ is $\left(\frac1{b^2}+\frac1{c^2}\right)^{-1/2}$.

concepts: Counting solutions of $a+b+c=0$ with bounded integers
questions.question: If $\vec V_1=\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec V_2=a\hat i+b\hat j+c\hat k$ where $a,b,c\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$. If $p$ is the number of non zero vectors $\vec V_2$ which are perpendicular to $\vec V_1$. Then sum of digits of $p$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: $\vec V_1\cdot\vec V_2=0$ means $a+b+c=0$; count the non-zero ordered triples from $\{-2,\dots,2\}$.
solution: $\vec V_1\cdot\vec V_2=a+b+c=0$ with $a,b,c\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$ and $\vec V_2\ne\vec 0$.
(i) $\{1,-1,0\}$: all three different, $3!=6$ vectors.
(ii) $\{2,-2,0\}$: all three different, $3!=6$ vectors.
(iii) $\{1,1,-2\}$: two equal, $\frac{3!}{2!}=3$ vectors.
(iv) $\{-1,-1,2\}$: two equal, $\frac{3!}{2!}=3$ vectors.
Total $p=6+6+3+3=18$, whose digits sum to $1+8=9$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Stars and bars with inclusion-exclusion: shift by $2$ so that $a'+b'+c'=6$ with $0\le a',b',c'\le4$.
solution: Without the upper bound: $\binom{8}{2}=28$.
Subtract the cases where some variable is $\ge5$: $3\times\binom{3}{2}=9$ (two variables cannot both be $\ge5$).
Valid triples: $28-9=19$; remove the zero vector $(a',b',c')=(2,2,2)$: $19-1=18$. So $p=18$ and the digit sum is $9$.

useful_results: Perpendicular to $\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$ means component sum zero; count with stars and bars after shifting the range to start at $0$.
Inclusion-exclusion for bounded variables: subtract $\binom{n-(m+1)+2}{2}$-type terms for each variable exceeding its bound.
Do not forget to exclude the zero vector.

concepts: Odd function property of a polynomial
Vector sum and magnitude
questions.question: Let $P$ and $Q$ be two points in $xy$-plane on the curve $y=x^7-2x^5+5x^3+8x+5$ such that $\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\hat i=2$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}\cdot\hat i=-2$ and the magnitude of $\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{OQ}=2M$, (where $O$ is origin) then find the value of $M$ ________.
solution: Let $P=(x_1,y_1)$ and $Q=(x_2,y_2)$. $\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\hat i=x_1=2$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}\cdot\hat i=x_2=-2$.
$\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{OQ}=(x_1+x_2)\hat i+(y_1+y_2)\hat j=(f(2)+f(-2))\hat j$.
$f(x)-5=x^7-2x^5+5x^3+8x$ is an odd function, so $f(2)+f(-2)=10$.
$|\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{OQ}|=10=2M\Rightarrow M=5$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Evaluate the polynomial directly at $\pm2$.
solution: $f(2)+f(-2)=10$, so $\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{OQ}=10\hat j$ and $2M=10$, $M=5$.

useful_results: For a polynomial with an odd part and a constant $c$, $f(x)+f(-x)=2c$ (the odd terms cancel).
$\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\hat i$ is the $x$-coordinate; sums of position vectors add coordinates.
Symmetry about a point: $y=g(x)+c$ with $g$ odd is symmetric about $(0,c)$.

concepts: Regular tetrahedron: opposite edges are perpendicular
Area of a triangle from vectors
questions.question: If area of a triangular face $BCD$ of a regular tetrahedron $ABCD$ is $4\sqrt3$ sq. units, then find area of a triangle whose two sides are represented by vectors $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{CD}$ ________.
questions.key_idea: In a regular tetrahedron opposite edges are perpendicular, so the triangle on $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{CD}$ is right-angled with legs equal to the edge.
solution: Let the edge be $a$. A face is an equilateral triangle: $\frac12a^2\sin60^\circ=4\sqrt3$ (the PDF prints the right-hand side as $\frac{4\sqrt3}{2}$, but the next line $a^2=16$ is what follows from $4\sqrt3$).
$\frac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2=4\sqrt3\Rightarrow a^2=16$, so $a=4$.
In a regular tetrahedron $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{CD}=0$: $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\overrightarrow{AD}-\overrightarrow{AC})=a^2\cos60^\circ-a^2\cos60^\circ=0$.
The triangle on $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{CD}$ has a right angle: area $=\frac12a^2\sin90^\circ=\frac{a^2}{2}=8$.
questions.correction_note: PDF line '1/2 a^2 sin60 = 4 sqrt3 / 2' has a stray '/2' on the right-hand side; the face area is 4 sqrt3, so (sqrt3/4) a^2 = 4 sqrt3 and a^2 = 16 (as the next PDF line states). The answer 8 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Embed the regular tetrahedron in a cube: its edges are face diagonals, and $AB,CD$ are diagonals of opposite faces, which are perpendicular.
solution: A regular tetrahedron of edge $a$ has vertices at alternate corners of a cube of side $s$, with $a=s\sqrt2$.
The face area is $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2=4\sqrt3\Rightarrow a^2=16\Rightarrow s^2=8$.
$AB$ and $CD$ are the diagonals $(s,s,0)$ and $(s,-s,0)$-type in opposite (parallel) faces: $(1,1,0)\cdot(1,-1,0)=0$, so they are perpendicular.
Area $=\frac12|AB||CD|=\frac12\cdot4\cdot4=8$.

useful_results: In a regular tetrahedron every pair of opposite edges is perpendicular ($\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{CD}=0$); also true in any 'orthocentric' tetrahedron.
Equilateral triangle of side $a$ has area $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2$; a right triangle with legs $a,a$ has area $\frac{a^2}{2}$.
A regular tetrahedron is inscribed in a cube of side $\frac{a}{\sqrt2}$; its volume is $\frac13$ of the cube's.

concepts: Maximum of a scalar triple product under a vector condition
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b$ are two unit vectors and $\vec c$ is such that $\vec c=\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b$, then the maximum value of $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ is $\frac pq$ where $p$ and $q$ are co-prime natural numbers, then find the value of $(p+q)$ ________.
questions.key_idea: $\vec c-\vec b=\vec a\times\vec c$; square it and use $\vec b\cdot\vec c=1-[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$ to bound the triple product.
solution: $\vec c=\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b\Rightarrow\vec c-\vec b=\vec a\times\vec c$, so $|\vec c-\vec b|^2=|\vec a\times\vec c|^2$.
With $\theta=\vec a\wedge\vec c$: $c^2+1-2\vec b\cdot\vec c=c^2\sin^2\theta$, so $2\,\vec b\cdot\vec c=c^2\cos^2\theta+1$.
Also $\vec b\cdot\vec c=\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b)=[\vec b\ \vec a\ \vec c]+1=1-[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
So $2-2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=c^2\cos^2\theta+1\Rightarrow2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=1-c^2\cos^2\theta\le1$.
$[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\le\frac12$, with equality when $\vec a\perp\vec c$ (take $|\vec c|=\frac1{\sqrt2}$, $\vec b=\vec c-\vec a\times\vec c$ has unit length, so the value is attained).
The maximum is $\frac12$, so $p=1,\ q=2$ and $p+q=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use coordinates with $\vec a=\hat k$ and solve $\vec c=\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b$ for $\vec b$.
solution: Take $\vec a=(0,0,1)$ and $\vec c=(x,y,z)$: $\vec a\times\vec c=(-y,x,0)$, so $\vec b=\vec c-\vec a\times\vec c=(x+y,\ y-x,\ z)$.
$[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=(b_xc_y-b_yc_x)=(x+y)y-(y-x)x=x^2+y^2$.
From $2(x^2+y^2)+z^2=1$: $x^2+y^2\le\frac12$ (equality when $z=0$). So the maximum is $\frac12$ and $p+q=3$.

useful_results: $\vec c=\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b\Rightarrow\vec b=\vec c-\vec a\times\vec c$: the unknown $\vec c$ can be parametrised by components with $\vec a=\hat k$.
$[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)$ equals the $z$-component of $\vec b\times\vec c$ when $\vec a=\hat k$.
Maximise a quantity by writing it as $\frac12(1-\text{a non-negative term})$.

concepts: Vector products of four vectors (identity for $(a\times b)\times(c\times d)$)
questions.question: If $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=2$, and $\vec d$ is unit vector then find the value of $\left|(\vec a\times\vec b)\times(\vec c\times\vec d)+(\vec b\times\vec c)\times(\vec a\times\vec d)+(\vec c\times\vec a)\times(\vec b\times\vec d)\right|$ ________.
questions.key_idea: Use $(\vec p\times\vec q)\times(\vec r\times\vec s)=[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec s]\vec r-[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]\vec s$ for each term; the three $[\cdot\cdot\vec d]$ pieces combine to $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\vec d$.
solution: Write $\vec d=\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c$. Then $\vec d\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=2\alpha$, $\vec d\cdot(\vec c\times\vec a)=2\beta$, $\vec d\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=2\gamma$.
Hence $[\vec d\ \vec b\ \vec c]\vec a+[\vec d\ \vec c\ \vec a]\vec b+[\vec d\ \vec a\ \vec b]\vec c=2(\alpha\vec a+\beta\vec b+\gamma\vec c)=2\vec d$.
$(\vec a\times\vec b)\times(\vec c\times\vec d)=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec d]\vec c-[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\vec d=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec d]\vec c-2\vec d$.
$(\vec b\times\vec c)\times(\vec a\times\vec d)=[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]\vec a-[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec a]\vec d=[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]\vec a-2\vec d$.
$(\vec c\times\vec a)\times(\vec b\times\vec d)=[\vec c\ \vec a\ \vec d]\vec b-[\vec c\ \vec a\ \vec b]\vec d=[\vec c\ \vec a\ \vec d]\vec b-2\vec d$.
Adding: $\left([\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec d]\vec c+[\vec b\ \vec c\ \vec d]\vec a+[\vec c\ \vec a\ \vec d]\vec b\right)-6\vec d=2\vec d-6\vec d=-4\vec d$.
$|-4\vec d|=4$ since $\vec d$ is a unit vector.

alternate_solutions.idea: The value does not depend on the particular $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$: take them along the axes with $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=2$ and a general unit $\vec d$.
solution: Let $\vec a=2\hat i,\ \vec b=\hat j,\ \vec c=\hat k$ ($[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]=2$) and $\vec d=(x,y,z)$ with $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$.
$(\vec a\times\vec b)\times(\vec c\times\vec d)=2\hat k\times(-y,x,0)=(-2x,-2y,0)$.
$(\vec b\times\vec c)\times(\vec a\times\vec d)=\hat i\times(0,-2z,2y)=(0,-2y,-2z)$; $\ (\vec c\times\vec a)\times(\vec b\times\vec d)=2\hat j\times(z,0,-x)=(-2x,0,-2z)$.
Sum $=(-4x,-4y,-4z)=-4\vec d$, of magnitude $4$.

useful_results: $(\vec p\times\vec q)\times(\vec r\times\vec s)=[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec s]\vec r-[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]\vec s$.
Any $\vec d=\frac{[\vec d\ \vec b\ \vec c]\vec a+[\vec d\ \vec c\ \vec a]\vec b+[\vec d\ \vec a\ \vec b]\vec c}{[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]}$ (resolution in a non-coplanar basis).
Summing a cyclic expression in $(\vec a,\vec b,\vec c)$ of this type gives $-2[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]\vec d$.

concepts: Angle between vectors and definite integration
Greatest integer function
questions.question: Let $\vec a=x^2\hat i-3\hat j+(x+3)\hat k$ and $\vec b=\hat i+3\hat j-(x-3)\hat k$ be two vectors such that $|\vec a|=|\vec b|$. If $\vec v_1=2\vec a+3\vec b$ and $\vec v_2=3\vec a-2\vec b$ and $I=\int_1^3(\vec v_1\wedge\vec v_2)\,dx$, then find the value of $[I]$ ________. [Note: $[k]$ denotes greatest integer function less than or equal to $k$.]
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$ and (as given) $|\vec a|=|\vec b|$, so $\vec v_1\cdot\vec v_2=6|\vec a|^2-6|\vec b|^2=0$ and the angle is $\frac\pi2$ throughout.
solution: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=x^2-9-(x+3)(x-3)=x^2-9-(x^2-9)=0$, so $\vec a\perp\vec b$ (the PDF writes '$|\vec a|\perp|\vec b|$', which is a typing slip).
$\vec v_1\cdot\vec v_2=(2\vec a+3\vec b)\cdot(3\vec a-2\vec b)=6|\vec a|^2-6|\vec b|^2-4\,\vec a\cdot\vec b+9\,\vec b\cdot\vec a=6\left(|\vec a|^2-|\vec b|^2\right)+5\,\vec a\cdot\vec b$.
With $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$ and the given $|\vec a|=|\vec b|$: $\vec v_1\cdot\vec v_2=0$, so $\vec v_1\wedge\vec v_2=\frac\pi2$.
$I=\int_1^3\frac\pi2\,dx=\frac\pi2(3-1)=\pi$.
$[I]=[\pi]=3$. (Remark: $|\vec a|=|\vec b|$ literally holds only at $x^4+12x-1=0$, i.e. $x\approx0.08$, outside $[1,3]$; the question intends it to hold throughout.)
questions.correction_note: PDF wrote 'a.b = 0 => a perp b and |a| perp |b|' (the second part is meaningless; the given condition is |a| = |b|, not a perpendicularity). Also the printed condition |a| = |b| is true only at x ~ 0.083 (root of x^4 + 12x - 1 = 0), so it cannot hold for every x in [1,3]; the answer 3 follows only under the intended reading that it holds throughout. Reported to the teacher.

alternate_solutions.idea: Picture $\vec a\perp\vec b$ with equal lengths as a $90^\circ$ rotation: $\vec v_2$ is $\vec v_1$ rotated by a right angle.
solution: Take $\vec a\to1$, $\vec b\to i$ in a plane (perpendicular, equal length): $\vec v_1=2+3i$.
$\vec v_2=3\vec a-2\vec b\to3-2i=-i(2+3i)$, i.e. $\vec v_2$ is $\vec v_1$ rotated by $-90^\circ$.
So $\vec v_1\wedge\vec v_2=\frac\pi2$ for every such pair, the integrand is the constant $\frac\pi2$, $I=\pi$ and $[I]=3$.

useful_results: For perpendicular vectors of equal length, $2\vec a+3\vec b$ and $3\vec a-2\vec b$ are perpendicular too ($(2+3i)\cdot(-i)=3-2i$ in complex form).
$(m\vec a+n\vec b)\cdot(n\vec a-m\vec b)=mn\left(|\vec a|^2-|\vec b|^2\right)+(n^2-m^2)\,\vec a\cdot\vec b$: it vanishes when $|\vec a|=|\vec b|$ and $\vec a\perp\vec b$.
$[\pi]=3$; greatest integer function of $\pi$.

concepts: Dot product of exponential vectors and inequality $a^3+b^3+c^3\ge3abc$
questions.question: $\vec p=3^{(\sin x+\tan x)}\hat i+3^{(\tan x-1)}\hat j-3^{\sin x}\hat k$ and $\vec q=3^{(\sin x-1)}\hat i+\left(3^{\sin x+\tan x}\right)\hat j+\left(3^{\tan x}\right)\hat k$. If sum of all values of $x$ in $[0,50\pi]$ for which $\vec p\cdot\vec q$ is minimum is $S$, then find the value of $\left(\frac{S}{255\pi}\right)$.
questions.key_idea: $3\,\vec p\cdot\vec q+1=A^3+B^3+1-3AB$ with $A=3^{(2\sin x+\tan x)/3}$, $B=3^{(\sin x+2\tan x)/3}$, which is $\ge0$ with equality iff $A=B=1$.
solution: $\vec p\cdot\vec q=3^{2\sin x+\tan x}+3^{\sin x+2\tan x-1}-3^{\sin x+\tan x}$.
$3\,\vec p\cdot\vec q=3^{2\sin x+\tan x}+3^{\sin x+2\tan x}-3\cdot3^{\sin x+\tan x}$.

$3\,\vec p\cdot\vec q+1=\left(3^{\frac{2\sin x+\tan x}{3}}\right)^3+\left(3^{\frac{\sin x+2\tan x}{3}}\right)^3+1^3-3\left(3^{\frac{2\sin x+\tan x}{3}}\right)\left(3^{\frac{\sin x+2\tan x}{3}}\right)\cdot1$.
For positive $a,b,c$: $a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc\ge0$ with equality iff $a=b=c$. So $3\,\vec p\cdot\vec q+1\ge0$, with equality iff $3^{\frac{2\sin x+\tan x}{3}}=3^{\frac{\sin x+2\tan x}{3}}=1$.
That requires $2\sin x+\tan x=0$ and $\sin x+2\tan x=0$, i.e. $\sin x=\tan x=0\Rightarrow x=n\pi$ (in $[0,50\pi]$: $n=0,1,\dots,50$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat $u=3^{(2\sin x+\tan x)/3}$ and $v=3^{(\sin x+2\tan x)/3}$ as free positive variables and minimise $f(u,v)=\frac{u^3+v^3}{3}-uv$ by calculus.
solution: With $u=3^{\frac{2\sin x+\tan x}{3}}$ and $v=3^{\frac{\sin x+2\tan x}{3}}$ the dot product is $\vec p\cdot\vec q=\frac{u^3+v^3}{3}-uv$ (note $3^{\sin x+\tan x}=uv$).
$\frac{\partial f}{\partial u}=u^2-v=0$ and $\frac{\partial f}{\partial v}=v^2-u=0$ give $u^4=u$, so $u=v=1$ for $u,v>0$.
$u=v=1$ means $2\sin x+\tan x=0$ and $\sin x+2\tan x=0$, i.e. $\sin x=\tan x=0$, $x=n\pi$ ($n=0,\dots,50$) with minimum value $\frac23-1=-\frac13$.

useful_results: $a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc=\frac12(a+b+c)\left[(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\right]\ge0$ for $a,b,c>0$, with equality iff $a=b=c$.
An expression of the form $X^3+Y^3+1-3XY$ is the signal for this inequality (here $X\cdot Y\cdot1$).
Sum of the multiples $n\pi$ for $n=0..N$ is $\pi\frac{N(N+1)}{2}$.

concepts: Rotation of a vector in a plane
Volume of a tetrahedron
questions.question: Let a vector $\vec V_1=\overrightarrow{OP}$, where $O$ is origin and $P$ is $(2,0,2)$. Vector $\vec V_1$ is rotated about origin by an angle of $\frac\pi3$ in a plane which is perpendicular to $XOZ$ plane to get vector $\vec V_2$, where $\vec V_2\cdot\hat j>0$. Again $\vec V_1$ is rotated about origin by right angle in $XOZ$ plane to get vector $\vec V_3$. If $V$ is volume of tetrahedron whose coterminous edges are $\vec V_1,\vec V_2$ and $\vec V_3$ then value of $\frac{3V}{\sqrt6}$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: $\vec V_2$ lies in the plane through $\vec V_1$ and $\hat j$ (the plane $x=z$, perpendicular to $XOZ$); fix it from $|\vec V_2|=|\vec V_1|$ and $\vec V_1\cdot\vec V_2=|\vec V_1|^2\cos60^\circ$.
solution: The plane perpendicular to $XOZ$ containing $O$ and $P$ is $x-z=0$. $\vec V_2$ is coplanar with $\vec V_1$ and $\hat j$: $\vec V_2=x\vec V_1+y\hat j=x(2\hat i+2\hat k)+y\hat j$.
$\vec V_2\cdot\vec V_1=|\vec V_2||\vec V_1|\cos\frac\pi3=4\Rightarrow4=x(2\hat i+2\hat k)\cdot(2\hat i+2\hat k)=8x\Rightarrow x=\frac12$.
(1) gives $y=\pm\sqrt6$; $\vec V_2\cdot\hat j>0$ gives $y=\sqrt6$ and $\vec V_2=\hat i+\sqrt6\hat j+\hat k$.
$\vec V_3$ is $\vec V_1$ rotated by $90^\circ$ in the $XOZ$ plane: $\vec V_3=\vec V_1+x\hat i$ with $\vec V_3\cdot\vec V_1=0\Rightarrow8+2x=0\Rightarrow x=-4$, so $\vec V_3=-2\hat i+2\hat k$.
$V=\frac16\left|\begin{matrix}2&0&2\\1&\sqrt6&1\\-2&0&2\end{matrix}\right|=\frac16\cdot8\sqrt6$.
$\frac{3V}{\sqrt6}=\frac{3}{\sqrt6}\cdot\frac{8\sqrt6}{6}=4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use an orthonormal frame $\hat e_1=\frac{\hat i+\hat k}{\sqrt2}$, $\hat j$, $\hat e_2=\frac{-\hat i+\hat k}{\sqrt2}$ in which the three vectors are simple.
solution: $\vec V_1=2\sqrt2\,\hat e_1$ and $\vec V_3=2\sqrt2\,\hat e_2$ (rotation by $90^\circ$ in the $XOZ$ plane).
$\vec V_2$ is $\vec V_1$ rotated by $60^\circ$ towards $\hat j$: $\vec V_2=2\sqrt2\left(\cos60^\circ\hat e_1+\sin60^\circ\hat j\right)=\sqrt2\,\hat e_1+\sqrt6\,\hat j$.
$\hat e_1,\hat j,\hat e_2$ are orthonormal, so $|[\vec V_1\ \vec V_2\ \vec V_3]|=(2\sqrt2)(\sqrt6)(2\sqrt2)=8\sqrt6$.
$V=\frac{8\sqrt6}{6}$ and $\frac{3V}{\sqrt6}=4$.

useful_results: Rotating a vector $\vec u$ by angle $\varphi$ in the plane of $\vec u$ and a perpendicular unit vector $\hat n$ gives $\vec u\cos\varphi+|\vec u|\hat n\sin\varphi$.
The triple product of vectors along an orthonormal frame with lengths $p,q,r$ is $\pm pqr$; choose a frame adapted to the problem.
Plane perpendicular to $XOZ$ through the $y$-axis direction: it contains $\hat j$ and the vector in $XOZ$ (here $x=z$).

concepts: Counting lattice points inside a tetrahedron
questions.question: Let $n$ represents the number of lattice points ($x,y,z$ all being integers) inside the tetrahedron (not on the surface) having vertices $(0,0,0)$, $(8,0,0)$, $(0,8,0)$ and $(0,0,8)$ then the value of $\left(\frac n7\right)$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: Interior points have $x,y,z\ge1$ and $x+y+z<8$; add a slack variable $w\ge1$ with $x+y+z+w=8$ and use stars and bars.
solution: The tetrahedron is $x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ z\ge0,\ x+y+z\le8$; an interior lattice point has $x,y,z\ge1$ and $x+y+z<8$.
Introduce $w=8-(x+y+z)\ge1$: $x+y+z+w=8$ with $x,y,z,w\ge1$.
The number of solutions in positive integers is $\binom{8-1}{4-1}=\binom73=35$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count layer by layer in $s=x+y+z$ and add with the hockey-stick identity.
solution: For a fixed $s=x+y+z$ the number of positive solutions is $\binom{s-1}{2}$, and $s$ runs from $3$ to $7$.
$\binom22+\binom32+\binom42+\binom52+\binom62=1+3+6+10+15=35$.
By the hockey-stick identity this equals $\binom73=35$, so $n=35$ and $\frac n7=5$.

useful_results: Positive integer solutions of $x_1+\dots+x_k=N$: $\binom{N-1}{k-1}$; non-negative: $\binom{N+k-1}{k-1}$.
Lattice points strictly inside the simplex $x,y,z>0,\ x+y+z<N$ number $\binom{N-1}{3}$.
A strict inequality is turned into an equation by a positive slack variable.

concepts: Locus of a point dividing a segment between two lines
Equation of a plane
questions.question: Consider two straight lines $L_1:\ \frac{x-2}{-1}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-4}{2}$ and $L_2:\ \frac{x-0}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-3}{-2}$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the variable on $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively and point $M$ divides $PQ$ in the ratio $2:3$ internally. If point $M$ moves in a plane $ax+bz=6$, then value of $a+b$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: $M=\frac{3P+2Q}{5}$ with $P,Q$ on two lines is a point of the plane through $\frac{3P_0+2Q_0}{5}$ spanned by the two directions.
solution: $P=(2-\lambda,\ 2+\lambda,\ 4+2\lambda)$ on $L_1$ and $Q=(\mu,\ -1+2\mu,\ 3-2\mu)$ on $L_2$.
$M$ divides $PQ$ in $2:3$: $M=\frac{3P+2Q}{5}=(u,v,w)$ with $5u=6-3\lambda+2\mu$, $\ 5v=4+3\lambda+4\mu$, $\ 5w=18+6\lambda-4\mu$.
Eliminate $\lambda$ and $\mu$: $2(5u)+5w=12-6\lambda+4\mu+18+6\lambda-4\mu=30$.
So $10u+5w=30\Rightarrow2u+w=6$: $M(u,v,w)$ moves on the plane $2x+z=6$ (the PDF's last line misprints this as $w+2\mu=6$).
Compare with $ax+bz=6$: $a=2,\ b=1$, so $a+b=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The locus of $M=\frac{3P+2Q}{5}$ is the plane through the point $M_0=\frac{3P_0+2Q_0}{5}$ spanned by the direction vectors of the two lines.
solution: Directions: $\vec d_1=(-1,1,2)$ and $\vec d_2=(1,2,-2)$, normal $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=(-6,0,-3)\parallel(2,0,1)$.
Plane: $2x+z=2\cdot\frac65+\frac{18}{5}=6$, i.e. $ax+bz=6$ with $a=2,b=1$.

useful_results: If $P$ runs over a line with direction $\vec d_1$ and $Q$ over a line with direction $\vec d_2$, then $\frac{mQ+nP}{m+n}$ runs over the plane through the weighted point of the base points with directions $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$.
The normal of that plane is $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ whatever the ratio; only the constant term depends on the ratio.
If the locus plane is $ax+bz=6$ (no $y$), the normal has zero $y$-component: a check on the computation.

concepts: Reciprocal system of vectors and determinants
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ be three non-coplanar unit vectors such that the angle between every pair of them is $60^\circ$. If $p_i,q_i,r_i;\ i=1,2,3$ are scalars satisfying $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=p_1\vec a+q_1\vec b+r_1\vec c$, $\ \vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=p_2\vec a+q_2\vec b+r_2\vec c$ and $\vec c\times\vec a+\vec a\times\vec b=p_3\vec a+q_3\vec b+r_3\vec c$ then $\left|\begin{matrix}p_1&q_1&r_1\\p_2&q_2&r_2\\p_3&q_3&r_3\end{matrix}\right|=\lambda\left|\begin{matrix}p_1+q_1&q_1&r_1\\p_2-r_2&q_2&r_2\\p_3+2q_3&q_3&r_3\end{matrix}\right|$. The value of $\lambda$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Write $\vec b\times\vec c=V\vec a^*$, $\vec c\times\vec a=V\vec b^*$, $\vec a\times\vec b=V\vec c^*$ with the reciprocal vectors from the inverse Gram matrix.
solution: Let $V=[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$. The Gram matrix is $G=\left(\begin{matrix}1&\frac12&\frac12\\\frac12&1&\frac12\\\frac12&\frac12&1\end{matrix}\right)$, $\det G=\frac12=V^2$, and $G^{-1}=\left(\begin{matrix}\frac32&-\frac12&-\frac12\\-\frac12&\frac32&-\frac12\\-\frac12&-\frac12&\frac32\end{matrix}\right)$.

Reciprocal vectors: $\vec a^*=\frac32\vec a-\frac12\vec b-\frac12\vec c$, $\ \vec b^*=-\frac12\vec a+\frac32\vec b-\frac12\vec c$, $\ \vec c^*=-\frac12\vec a-\frac12\vec b+\frac32\vec c$, with $\vec b\times\vec c=V\vec a^*$, $\ \vec c\times\vec a=V\vec b^*$, $\ \vec a\times\vec b=V\vec c^*$.
Row 1: $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=V(\vec a^*+\vec b^*+\vec c^*)=\frac V2(\vec a+\vec b+\vec c)$, so $(p_1,q_1,r_1)=V\left(\frac12,\frac12,\frac12\right)$.
Row 2: $\vec b\times\vec c+\vec c\times\vec a=V(\vec a^*+\vec b^*)=V(\vec a+\vec b-\vec c)$, so $(p_2,q_2,r_2)=V(1,1,-1)$.
Row 3: $\vec c\times\vec a+\vec a\times\vec b=V(\vec b^*+\vec c^*)=V(-\vec a+\vec b+\vec c)$, so $(p_3,q_3,r_3)=V(-1,1,1)$.
Left determinant: $V^3\left|\begin{matrix}\frac12&\frac12&\frac12\\1&1&-1\\-1&1&1\end{matrix}\right|=V^3\cdot\frac12\cdot4=2V^3$.
Right determinant: rows $V(1,\frac12,\frac12)$, $V(2,1,-1)$, $V(1,1,1)$ give $V^3\left[1(1+1)-\frac12(2+1)+\frac12(2-1)\right]=V^3(2-\frac32+\frac12)=V^3$.
$\lambda=\frac{2V^3}{V^3}=2$ (a numerical check with explicit unit vectors at $60^\circ$ gives $0.7071$ and $0.3536$, ratio $2$). The paper's key value $1$ does not follow from the printed data.

Computed with the reciprocal basis and cross-checked numerically with explicit unit vectors at 60 degrees: the two determinants are 2V^3 and V^3, so lambda = 2. The printed key (1) does not match. For three unit vectors at $60^\circ$: $V^2=\det G=\frac12$ and $\vec a^*+\vec b^*+\vec c^*=\frac12(\vec a+\vec b+\vec c)$.

concepts: Vector method for collinearity of three points on the sides of a parallelogram
questions.question: A straight line cuts the sides $AB$, $AC$ and $AD$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ at points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ respectively. If $\overrightarrow{AP}=\lambda_1\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\overrightarrow{AR}=\lambda_2\overrightarrow{AD}$, $\overrightarrow{AQ}=\frac{\lambda_3}{2}\overrightarrow{AC}$, where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ are scalars then prove that $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ are in H.P.
questions.answer: Proved: $\frac{2}{\lambda_3}=\frac1{\lambda_1}+\frac1{\lambda_2}$, i.e. $\lambda_1,\lambda_3,\lambda_2$ are in H.P. (with $\lambda_3$ the middle term).
questions.key_idea: Take $A$ as origin and $\vec b=\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\vec d=\overrightarrow{AD}$ as independent vectors; $P,Q,R$ collinear gives a relation between the coefficients.
solution: Take $A$ as the origin, $\overrightarrow{AB}=\vec b$, $\overrightarrow{AD}=\vec d$ (independent), so $\overrightarrow{AC}=\vec b+\vec d$.
$P=\lambda_1\vec b$, $\ R=\lambda_2\vec d$, $\ Q=\frac{\lambda_3}{2}(\vec b+\vec d)$.
$P,Q,R$ are collinear, so $Q=(1-t)P+tR$ for some scalar $t$: $\frac{\lambda_3}{2}\vec b+\frac{\lambda_3}{2}\vec d=(1-t)\lambda_1\vec b+t\lambda_2\vec d$.
Equating coefficients of the independent vectors $\vec b,\vec d$: $\frac{\lambda_3}{2}=(1-t)\lambda_1$ and $\frac{\lambda_3}{2}=t\lambda_2$.
Hence $1-t=\frac{\lambda_3}{2\lambda_1}$ and $t=\frac{\lambda_3}{2\lambda_2}$; adding, $1=\frac{\lambda_3}{2}\left(\frac1{\lambda_1}+\frac1{\lambda_2}\right)$.

$\Rightarrow\frac{2}{\lambda_3}=\frac1{\lambda_1}+\frac1{\lambda_2}$: the reciprocals $\frac1{\lambda_1},\frac1{\lambda_3},\frac1{\lambda_2}$ are in A.P., i.e. $\lambda_1,\lambda_3,\lambda_2$ are in H.P. (the PDF has no solution: its solution is a broken image).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use oblique coordinates along $AB$ and $AD$: the line $PR$ has an intercept form, and $Q$ must satisfy it.
solution: With $A$ as origin and axes along $AB,AD$, $P=(\lambda_1,0)$, $R=(0,\lambda_2)$ in the units of the vectors $\vec b,\vec d$.
The line $PR$ (affine coordinates are enough because lines and ratios are preserved) is $\frac{x}{\lambda_1}+\frac{y}{\lambda_2}=1$.

$Q=\frac{\lambda_3}{2}(\vec b+\vec d)$ has coordinates $\left(\frac{\lambda_3}{2},\frac{\lambda_3}{2}\right)$ and lies on the line: $\frac{\lambda_3}{2}\left(\frac1{\lambda_1}+\frac1{\lambda_2}\right)=1$.
So $\frac2{\lambda_3}=\frac1{\lambda_1}+\frac1{\lambda_2}$, which is the H.P. relation.

useful_results: Three points $\alpha\vec b,\ \beta\vec d,\ \gamma(\vec b+\vec d)$ with $\vec b,\vec d$ independent are collinear iff $\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta=\frac1\gamma$ (the intercept relation).

For a line cutting $AB,AD$ and the diagonal $AC$ of a parallelogram at fractions $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu$ of the sides ($AQ=\mu AC$): $\frac1{\lambda_1}+\frac1{\lambda_2}=\frac1\mu$; here $\mu=\frac{\lambda_3}{2}$.
Three points $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ are collinear iff $\vec q=(1-t)\vec p+t\vec r$; compare coefficients of independent vectors.

concepts: Radical centre of three circles
Line through a point meeting a line and parallel to a plane
questions.question: The radical centre of the following set of circles $x^2+y^2-3x-6y+14=0$ ; $x^2+y^2-x-4y+8=0$ , $x^2+y^2+2x-6y+9=0$ is $(\alpha,\beta)$. Find the equations of the straight line passing through the point $(\alpha,\beta,3)$ to intersect the straight line $x+1=2(y-2)=z+4$ and parallel to the plane $x+5y+4z=0$.
questions.key_idea: Radical centre: solve two radical axes; the required line goes through $(1,2,3)$ and a point $Q$ of the given line with $\overrightarrow{PQ}\perp$ normal of the plane.
solution: From (1) and (2): $x=1,\ y=2$, so the radical centre is $(1,2)$, i.e. $(\alpha,\beta)=(1,2)$ and the point is $P(1,2,3)$.
The given line is $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z+4}{2}=\lambda$; a point on it is $Q(2\lambda-1,\ \lambda+2,\ 2\lambda-4)$ (the PDF prints the middle coordinate as $\lambda+1$, a slip).
$\overrightarrow{PQ}=(2\lambda-2,\ \lambda,\ 2\lambda-7)$ must be parallel to the plane $x+5y+4z=0$: $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot(1,5,4)=0$.
$1(2\lambda-2)+5\lambda+4(2\lambda-7)=0\Rightarrow15\lambda-30=0\Rightarrow\lambda=2$.
$Q=(3,4,0)$ and the line $PQ$ is $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-3}{-3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The required line lies in the plane through $P$ and the given line; its direction is perpendicular to that plane's normal and to the normal of the given plane.
solution: The given line passes through $A_0(-1,2,-4)$ with direction $(2,1,2)$; $\overrightarrow{A_0P}=(2,0,7)$.
Normal of the plane through $P$ and the given line: $(2,1,2)\times(2,0,7)=(7,-10,-2)$.
The required line lies in that plane and is parallel to $x+5y+4z=0$, so its direction is $(7,-10,-2)\times(1,5,4)=(-30,-30,45)\parallel(2,2,-3)$.
Hence the line through $(1,2,3)$ is $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac{z-3}{-3}$, the same line.

useful_results: Radical centre of three circles: solve any two of the radical axes $S_i-S_j=0$.
A line through $P$ meeting a given line $L$ lies in the plane through $P$ and $L$: its direction is perpendicular to that plane's normal $(\vec d_L\times\overrightarrow{A_0P})$.
Being parallel to a plane with normal $\vec n$ means direction $\perp\vec n$; the two conditions together give the direction as a cross product of the two normals.

concepts: Angle bisectors and scalar triple product of unit vectors
questions.question: $\hat W$ is a unit vector perpendicular to the plane of two other unit vectors $\hat u$ and $\hat v$. Three unit vectors $\hat x,\hat y$ and $\hat z$ are along the angle bisectors of $\hat u,\hat v$ ; $\hat v,\hat w$ and $\hat w,\hat u$ respectively. If $[\hat x\times\hat y\ \ \hat y\times\hat z\ \ \hat z\times\hat x]=\frac12$ then find the angle between $\hat u$ and $\hat v$.
questions.key_idea: $[\hat x\times\hat y\ \ \hat y\times\hat z\ \ \hat z\times\hat x]=[\hat x\ \hat y\ \hat z]^2$ and $[\hat x\ \hat y\ \hat z]=\sin\frac\alpha2$.
solution: Let the angle between $\hat u$ and $\hat v$ be $\alpha$. $\hat w\perp\hat u,\hat v$ so $\hat w\cdot\hat u=\hat w\cdot\hat v=0$.
$\hat x=\frac{\hat u+\hat v}{2\cos\frac\alpha2}$ (as $|\hat u+\hat v|=2\cos\frac\alpha2$), $\ \hat y=\frac{\hat v+\hat w}{\sqrt2}$, $\ \hat z=\frac{\hat u+\hat w}{\sqrt2}$.
$[\hat x\ \hat y\ \hat z]=\frac{1}{2\cos\frac\alpha2\cdot\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2}[\hat u+\hat v\ \ \hat v+\hat w\ \ \hat u+\hat w]=\frac{1}{4\cos\frac\alpha2}\cdot2[\hat u\ \hat v\ \hat w]$.

$[\hat u\ \hat v\ \hat w]=(\hat u\times\hat v)\cdot\hat w=\sin\alpha$ (as $\hat w\parallel\hat u\times\hat v$, a unit vector), so $[\hat x\ \hat y\ \hat z]=\frac{\sin\alpha}{2\cos\frac\alpha2}=\sin\frac\alpha2$.
$[\hat x\times\hat y\ \ \hat y\times\hat z\ \ \hat z\times\hat x]=[\hat x\ \hat y\ \hat z]^2=\sin^2\frac\alpha2=\frac12$.
$\sin\frac\alpha2=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Rightarrow\frac\alpha2=\frac\pi4\Rightarrow\alpha=\frac\pi2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the Gram determinant of $\hat x,\hat y,\hat z$ (their pairwise dot products are easy), since $[\hat x\ \hat y\ \hat z]^2=\det G$.
solution: With $c=\cos\frac\alpha2$: $\hat x\cdot\hat y=\frac{\hat u\cdot\hat v+\ldots}{\ldots}=\frac{c}{\sqrt2}$, $\ \hat x\cdot\hat z=\frac{c}{\sqrt2}$, $\ \hat y\cdot\hat z=\frac{\hat v\cdot\hat u+1}{2}=c^2$ (using $1+\cos\alpha=2c^2$).
$\det\left(\begin{matrix}1&\frac c{\sqrt2}&\frac c{\sqrt2}\\\frac c{\sqrt2}&1&c^2\\\frac c{\sqrt2}&c^2&1\end{matrix}\right)=(1-c^2)(1+c^2)-c^2(1-c^2)=1-c^2=\sin^2\frac\alpha2$.
So $[\hat x\times\hat y\ \ \hat y\times\hat z\ \ \hat z\times\hat x]=[\hat x\ \hat y\ \hat z]^2=\sin^2\frac\alpha2=\frac12$, giving $\alpha=\frac\pi2$.

useful_results: $[\vec p\times\vec q\ \ \vec q\times\vec r\ \ \vec r\times\vec p]=[\vec p\ \vec q\ \vec r]^2$.
The unit vector along the bisector of unit vectors $\hat u,\hat v$ (angle $\alpha$) is $\frac{\hat u+\hat v}{2\cos\frac\alpha2}$.
For a unit $\hat w$ perpendicular to the plane of $\hat u,\hat v$: $[\hat u\ \hat v\ \hat w]=\pm\sin\alpha$.

concepts: Equilateral triangle in vectors: incentre and perpendicular direction
questions.question: The position vectors of the vertices $A,B$ and $C$ of a triangle are $\hat i+\hat j$, $\hat j+\hat k$ and $\hat i+\hat k$ respectively. Find a unit vector $\vec r$ lying in the plane of $\triangle ABC$ and perpendicular to $IA$, where $I$ is the incentre of the triangle ________.
questions.key_idea: $AB=BC=CA=\sqrt2$, so the triangle is equilateral and $IA\perp BC$: $\vec r\parallel\overrightarrow{BC}$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=-\hat i+\hat k$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=\hat i-\hat j$, $\overrightarrow{CA}=\hat j-\hat k$: $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=|\overrightarrow{BC}|=|\overrightarrow{CA}|=\sqrt2$.
The triangle is equilateral, so the incentre coincides with the circumcentre and $IA$ is perpendicular to $BC$.
A vector in the plane of the triangle and perpendicular to $IA$ is therefore parallel to $BC$: $\vec r=\lambda(\hat i-\hat j)$.
Unit vector: $|\lambda|\sqrt2=1\Rightarrow\lambda=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $\vec r=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\hat i-\hat j)$ (the PDF prints the factor as $\frac12$, which would not be a unit vector).
questions.correction_note: PDF answer and last line give r = +-(1/2)(i - j), which has length 1/sqrt2, not 1. The unit vector parallel to BC = i - j is +-(1/sqrt2)(i - j).

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve with components: $\vec r\perp IA$ and in the plane, using the centroid as $I$.
solution: For an equilateral triangle $I=G=\left(\frac23,\frac23,\frac23\right)$, so $\overrightarrow{IA}=\left(\frac13,\frac13,-\frac23\right)$.
The plane of the triangle is $x+y+z=2$, so a direction in it satisfies $r_1+r_2+r_3=0$.
$\vec r\cdot\overrightarrow{IA}=0$: $r_1+r_2-2r_3=0$. With $r_1+r_2+r_3=0$ this gives $r_3=0$ and $r_1=-r_2$.
Unit vector: $\vec r=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\hat i-\hat j)$.

useful_results: In an equilateral triangle the incentre, centroid, circumcentre and orthocentre coincide, and each median is perpendicular to the opposite side.
A vector lying in a plane with normal $\vec n$ has $\vec r\cdot\vec n=0$ (direction vectors, not position vectors).
A unit vector in direction $\vec v$ is $\frac{\vec v}{|\vec v|}$: check normalisation in the final answer.

concepts: Coplanarity of four points in terms of position vectors
Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
questions.question: Four points with position vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ and $\vec d$ are coplanar such that $(\sin\alpha)\vec a+(2\sin2\beta)\vec b+(3\sin3\gamma)\vec c-\vec d=\vec 0$. Then, the least value of the expression $\sin^2\alpha+\sin^22\beta+\sin^23\gamma$ is $\frac pq$, where $p$ and $q$ are coprime, then find $(p+q)$.
questions.key_idea: Four points with position vectors satisfying a vector relation are coplanar iff the coefficients sum to zero; then Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the sum of squares.
solution: For four coplanar points, $\vec d$ is an affine combination of $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$.
The relation $(\sin\alpha)\vec a+(2\sin2\beta)\vec b+(3\sin3\gamma)\vec c-\vec d=\vec 0$ has coefficients summing to zero: $\sin\alpha+2\sin2\beta+3\sin3\gamma-1=0$.
So $\sin\alpha+2\sin2\beta+3\sin3\gamma=1$.
Cauchy-Schwarz for $(1,2,3)$ and $(\sin\alpha,\sin2\beta,\sin3\gamma)$: $|\sin\alpha+2\sin2\beta+3\sin3\gamma|\le\sqrt{1^2+2^2+3^2}\sqrt{\sin^2\alpha+\sin^22\beta+\sin^23\gamma}$.
$1\le\sqrt{14}\sqrt{\sin^2\alpha+\sin^22\beta+\sin^23\gamma}\Rightarrow\sin^2\alpha+\sin^22\beta+\sin^23\gamma\ge\frac1{14}$.
Equality when $(\sin\alpha,\sin2\beta,\sin3\gamma)=k(1,2,3)$: $k+4k+9k=1$ gives $k=\frac1{14}$, so the values $\frac1{14},\frac2{14},\frac3{14}\in[-1,1]$ are attainable.
The least value is $\frac1{14}$, so $p=1,\ q=14$ and $p+q=15$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Geometric view: minimise the squared distance from the origin to the plane $s_1+2s_2+3s_3=1$.
solution: Let $s_1=\sin\alpha,\ s_2=\sin2\beta,\ s_3=\sin3\gamma$; then $(s_1,s_2,s_3)$ lies on the plane $s_1+2s_2+3s_3=1$.
$s_1^2+s_2^2+s_3^2$ is the squared distance of that point from the origin; its minimum is the squared distance of the plane from the origin: $\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4+9}}\right)^2=\frac{1}{14}$.
The foot of the perpendicular $\frac1{14}(1,2,3)$ has all coordinates in $[-1,1]$, so it is attainable. $p+q=1+14=15$.

useful_results: Four points with position vectors satisfy $\sum k_i\vec p_i=\vec 0$ with $\sum k_i=0$ (not all $k_i=0$) $\iff$ they are coplanar (affine dependence).
Minimum of $\sum s_i^2$ subject to $\sum k_is_i=c$ is $\frac{c^2}{\sum k_i^2}$ (Cauchy-Schwarz), attained at $s_i\propto k_i$.
Check that the minimising values are admissible ($|\sin|\le1$) before accepting the bound.
